$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f.$ Since we're given that $F$ is conservative, we know that such a function exists. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={x}^{2}-y, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & ={y}^{2}-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}-xy.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨0,1⟩, \\ r(2) & =⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡2,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,1)$ and $(3\operatorname{ln}⁡2,4).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(3\operatorname{ln}⁡2,4)-f(0,1) \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}\cdot (3\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{3}+\frac{1}{3}\cdot {4}^{3}-3\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot 4)-(\frac{1}{3}\cdot {0}^{3}+\frac{1}{3}\cdot {1}^{3}-0\cdot 1) \\  & =9{ln}^{3}⁡2+\frac{64}{3}-12\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{1}{3} \\  & =9{ln}^{3}⁡2-12\operatorname{ln}⁡2+21.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186240924 :question/id #uuid "86f7c787-e5df-5794-8bba-c906aa91522f" :question/math-academy-id "q-104739"} {:db/id 17592186240925 :question/id #uuid "7507d02e-e1da-50a2-9a9d-6236d6a7afae" :question/math-academy-id "q-104745" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "16f31b92-c386-50b2-b977-d94225bcfbc5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{\pi }+1" :db/id 17592186238253} {:answer/id #uuid "465fbdf4-7176-5e2a-afb9-7055988a9594" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{{\pi }^{2}-1}" :db/id 17592186238665} {:answer/id #uuid "54e54a33-5402-591a-ac33-570a9653db6c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi {e}^{\pi -1}" :db/id 17592186238789} {:answer/id #uuid "796fc17c-d543-5b01-83ae-f85bfdb65ad5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186239102} {:answer/id #uuid "dfd66caa-a9be-51dd-a8aa-57947da3bed9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\pi }^{2}+1" :db/id 17592186240013}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186238789} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ed60cbe-d21d-5310-989e-903acd1a44f7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240533}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F,$ defined as

$$
F(x,y)=({e}^{y}+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,i+(x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,j.
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the curve $y=x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ].$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

First, we define $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ as follows:

$$
F(x,y)={{({e}^{y}+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{P(x,y)}\,i+{{(x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{Q(x,y)}\,j.
$$

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function $f$ (if it exists) such that $F=∇f.$ Notice that the domain of $F$ is ${R}^{2},$ and

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{y}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ there exists a potential function $f$ such that $F=∇f,$ and we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={e}^{y}+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =x{e}^{y}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Note that we set $C=0$ for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function $f$ that satisfies $∇f=F.$

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. A suitable parametrization of the curve $C$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨t,t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$

The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,1⟩, \\ r(\pi ) & =⟨\pi ,\pi -1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(0,1)$ and $(\pi ,\pi -1).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(\pi ,\pi -1)-f(0,1) \\  & =(\pi \cdot {e}^{\pi -1}+(\pi -1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-(0\cdot {e}^{1}+1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =(\pi {e}^{\pi -1}+0)-0 \\  & =\pi {e}^{\pi -1}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186240926 :question/id #uuid "b5c03f65-0c80-5089-93df-00e7a5829280" :question/math-academy-id "q-104747"} {:db/id 17592186240928 :question/id #uuid $$

"selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240475}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,g(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{2}(t)\}$ equals $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the set $\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{1}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while ${sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =0-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134562 :question/id #uuid "2b04e926-3f28-54fc-a52b-7c1f046fb290" :question/math-academy-id "q-98689"} {:db/id 17592186240950 :question/id #uuid "e18df242-9d5f-58ab-883f-e2f596589751" :question/math-academy-id "q-104871"} {:db/id 17592186240955 :question/id #uuid "e0a44c8c-788c-548d-8b09-deb0ad2858dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-104894"} {:db/id 17592186240978 :question/id #uuid "2794de9d-8dc5-594e-8a2b-e907f92bf64b" :question/math-academy-id "q-105100"} {:db/id 17592186240983 :question/id #uuid "645a82fe-e42f-5dc9-9e79-d8bd0747a894" :question/math-academy-id "q-105136" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09b29cd5-55b5-5722-ba90-23f769345723" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1" :db/id 17592186238150} {:answer/id #uuid "5bc19ba5-b098-5af2-b759-18b7d61fa0df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1" :db/id 17592186238854} {:answer/id #uuid "64e8e822-ab38-5fcf-a7cb-162397992404" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186238937} {:answer/id #uuid "9cd846ec-dcb9-5576-8a82-5cbd0e68c90d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186239418} {:answer/id #uuid "a19047b8-6624-5f0c-b217-a2d6a5d4fcd6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1" :db/id 17592186239462}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186238937} :answer-field/id #uuid "f5a8c5d5-fcb2-5bdd-8555-14fa5c61c1d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240761}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while $\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) & =\frac{-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =\frac{-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}

{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$ 

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={t}^{2},\,g(t)=15t+3

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t)\}$ equals $15t.$" :question/worked-solution "Since the set $\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=15t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{2}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(15t+3)\cdot {t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}15{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{15}{4}{t}^{4}+{t}^{3}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{15}{4}+1)-(\frac{15}{4}-1) \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{f}_{2}(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot {t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{1}{5}{t}^{5}|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}-(-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{2}{(\frac{2}{5})}\cdot {t}^{2}=5{t}^{2}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =15t+5{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}

find the distance between $f(t)=3t$ and $g(t)=-3t+3$ with respect to the inner product." :question/worked-solution "The distance between $f(t)=3t$ and $g(t)=-3t+3$ with respect to the given inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-g(t)‖ \\  & =‖3t-(-3t+3)‖ \\  & =‖6t-3‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨6t-3,6t-3⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$

{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 8 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,B=\{\begin{bmatrix}| \\ {v}_{1} \\ |\end{bmatrix}\,,\begin{bmatrix}| \\ {v}_{2} \\ |\end{bmatrix}\,,\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}\}
$$

Suppose that $V=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}.$ Given that $B$ is an orthogonal basis for $V,$ and that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "We find an orthogonal basis $B$ of $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

**Step 1.** We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2.** We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the usual formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\frac{8}{8}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** We find the vector ${v}_{3}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ using the usual formula:

$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+3y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,y(0)=1
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below to find the solution using Laplace transforms. You may make use of the following results:

$$
L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$

Let $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}.$ Taking the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation and solving for $Y,$ we have

$$
Y(s)={{field-1}}.
$$

The partial fraction decomposition of $Y$ is

$$
Y(s)={{field-2}}.
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={{field-3}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides of the differential equation. Using the linearity property, we have

$$
L\{{y}^{′}\}+3L\{y\}=L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\}+L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\}.
$$

Using the formula for the transform of a derivative $L\{{y}^{′}\}=sY(s)-y(0)$ and the standard trigonometric transforms

$$
L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\}=\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4},\,L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4},
$$

we substitute the known values. Note that $y(0)=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(sY(s)-1)+3Y(s) & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+3)Y(s)-1 & =\frac{s+2}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

We rearrange to solve for $Y(s).$ First, add $1$ to the right-hand side and find a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}(s+3)Y(s) & =1+\frac{s+2}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+4}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{s+2}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+3)Y(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+s+6}{{s}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by $(s+3),$ we obtain

$$
Y(s)=\frac{{s}^{2}+s+6}{(s+3)({s}^{2}+4)}.
$$

Next, we perform a partial fraction decomposition. Since the denominator has a linear factor $(s+3)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+4),$ we write

$$
\frac{{s}^{2}+s+6}{(s+3)({s}^{2}+4)}=\frac{A}{s+3}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
{s}^{2}+s+6=A({s}^{2}+4)+(Bs+C)(s+3)
$$

- Setting $s=-3,$ we have
 

$$
(-3)^{2}+(-3)+6=A((-3)^{2}+4)+0\,⟹\,12=13A\,⟹\,A=\frac{12}{13}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have
  

$$
1=A+B\,⟹\,1=\frac{12}{13}+B\,⟹\,B=\frac{1}{13}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have
 

$$
6=4A+3C\,⟹\,6=4(\frac{12}{13})+3C\,⟹\,C=\frac{10}{13}.
$$

Thus, the decomposition is

$$
Y(s)=\frac{(\frac{12}{13})}{13(s+3)}+\frac{(\frac{1}{13}s+\frac{10}{13})}{{s}^{2}+4}=\frac{12}{13(s+3)}+\frac{s+10}{13({s}^{2}+4)}.
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+3}\} & ={e}^{-3t} \\ {L}^{-1}\{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}\} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ {L}^{-1}\{\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}\} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =\frac{12}{13}{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+3}\}+\frac{1}{13}{L}^{-1}\{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}\}+\frac{5}{13}{L}^{-1}\{\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}\} \\ y(t) & =\frac{12}{13}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{5}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+\frac{1}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186391848 :question/id #uuid "f44dbcab-4002-5eb8-9303-ab06ab01d7f4" :question/math-academy-id "q-343057"} {:db/id 17592186397600 :question/id #uuid "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344564}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ?$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$  

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={({cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={cos}^{4}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{4}{|}_{-\pi /4}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0-(-\frac{\pi }{2})-(-1)) \\  & =\frac{\pi +2}{8}\end{aligned}

\theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{e}^{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(3)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{e}^{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{e}^{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{e}^{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{e}^{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  & =3{\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3{e}^{u}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =3({e}^{3}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =3({e}^{3}-1)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345247 :question/id #uuid "6d3824d0-05f9-53c5-8fe3-dac14910620a" :question/math-academy-id "q-76694"} {:db/id 17592186345250 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =36\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(6)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}36\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 6\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =6{\int }_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}} \\  & =3({(3\sqrt{3})}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =3\cdot 27 \\  & =81\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345254 :question/id #uuid "21e9d3c4-49da-5fcb-92fe-c05185c24062" :question/math-academy-id "q-76767" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "68904330-d856-56ab-ab89-95598aff7f05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2}" :db/id 17592186343132} {:answer/id #uuid "7643286e-f9ff-585d-9aca-43eda7f2b710" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186343260} {:answer/id #uuid "ccc1b583-ed2c-5e36-a6b5-501f45d92300" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi -3}{6}" :db/id 17592186344043} {:answer/id #uuid "eba40804-2b69-5b03-8ebc-fcc8b5946e91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi +1}{2}" :db/id 17592186344303} {:answer/id #uuid "ec2c9374-53c5-5786-8c80-f18bc786264b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi -3}{2}" :db/id 17592186344309}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186344043} :answer-field/id #uuid "e39c6e76-f79f-5404-bd14-1344e4f9c50e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344892}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$ along the polar curve $r=1$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\theta  & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}\theta =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting into the formula for the integration by parts, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3}-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}-0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}+(\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi -3}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362989 :question/id #uuid "05fbe250-8eb4-5b81-83cc-08a815c1aec0" :question/math-academy-id "q-123510"} {:db/id 17592186363534 :question/id #uuid "683e3791-c874-5158-8d10-18c20b047e9d" :question/math-academy-id "q-165417"} {:db/id 17592186364413 :question/id #uuid "13c81ebd-eba4-55aa-a40f-bfa1b49cc9df" :question/math-academy-id "q-76763" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "49adc8e9-1dc5-5cb5-9175-f91e269efe35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "192" :db/id 17592186364415} {:answer/id #uuid "e94aff50-1cf2-58b3-85e2-e76471a133a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "96" :db/id 17592186364416} {:answer/id #uuid "7fdf46cb-8dea-538a-974a-83bf0db567f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "256" :db/id 17592186364417} {:answer/id #uuid "119dacc9-0e3b-5285-87d0-21d3cc26e860" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "512" :db/id 17592186364418} {:answer/id #uuid "bddd3fe2-39af-5dc8-a534-e22068d4a73c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "384" :db/id 17592186364419}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364415} :answer-field/id #uuid "7944764b-8f2e-517b-9311-deccaafc6156" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364414}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}y$ along the polar curve $r=4$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{3}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{3}4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =256{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(4)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}256{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 4\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =1\,024{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1\,024{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =-1\,024{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}/2}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-1\,024\cdot \frac{1}{4}{u}^{4}\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{2}/2} \\  & =-256((\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})^{4}-{1}^{4}) \\  & =-256(-\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =192\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186455435 :question/id #uuid "1b9e5c87-171d-5626-ae59-fa7b69d9a95a" :question/math-academy-id "q-76766"} {:db/id 17592186455484 :question/id #uuid $$
u(t)=\{\begin{aligned}1,\,t\ge 0, \\ 0,\,t<0.\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of $y=u(t)$ is shown below.

![](images/9f/9fb8c20672705e9d68e69d32e7ff3499ec71560e10aa85136b3f3ad75c5fb5ed.png)

Notice that to transform the function $y=u(t)$ to the given function $y=f(t),$ we perform the following transformations:

- First, we reflect $y=u(t)$ in the $y$-axis, which gives $y=u(-t).$

- Next, we shift by two units to the right, giving $y=u(-(t-2))=u(2-t).$

- Finally, we scale by a scale factor of $2$ parallel to the $y$-axis, giving $y=2u(2-t).$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -5 \\ 1 & -6\end{bmatrix}x(t),\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Hint: The matrix has the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4+\text{i}$ with the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$*" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -5 \\ 1 & -6\end{bmatrix}.$ 

We are given the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4+\text{i}$ and the corresponding eigenvector ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

**Note:** The eigenvector corresponding to the second eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}={\overset{―}{\lambda }}_{1}$ is 
${v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}.$ But we do not require this eigenvector for solving our system.

The solution that we obtain for the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4+\text{i}$ and its associated eigenvector is

$$
{x}_{1}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{(-4+\text{i})t}.
$$

We now express this as a real function. Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{(-4+\text{i})t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2+\text{i} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\text{i}{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ {e}^{-4t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\text{i}{e}^{-4t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t}+\text{i}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} \\  & ={\text{w}}_{1}(t)+\text{i}{\text{w}}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${w}_{1}$ and ${w}_{2}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & ={c}_{1}{\text{w}}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{\text{w}}_{2}(t) \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =-\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t}+3\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308582 :question/id #uuid "ee50735a-2690-5859-ba95-03c8e56ae446" :question/math-academy-id "q-334223"} {:db/id 17592186308583 :question/id #uuid :question/problem "Given the orthogonal basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the vector $x$ below, find the value of $15{x}_{1},$ where ${x}_{1}$ is the first component of $[x]_{B}.$

$$
B=\{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\},\,x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${q}_{1},\,{q}_{2}.$ 

Since $B$ is an orthogonal basis, we have that $[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}$, where ${x}_{i}=\frac{x\cdot {q}_{i}}{{q}_{i}\cdot {q}_{i}}.$ Computing ${x}_{1},$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{x\cdot {q}_{1}}{{q}_{1}\cdot {q}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+(-4)\cdot (-3)}{{1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2+12}{1+9} \\  & =\frac{7}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
15{x}_{1}=15\cdot \frac{7}{5}=21.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351220 :question/id #uuid "35f8611c-3990-55b5-9e1a-16081db42aa2" :question/math-academy-id "q-81104" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "029ad763-c8ac-5848-9e51-a53c81228b42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186348476} {:answer/id #uuid "0ec60a61-d3a0-5a3c-9fa3-9f052d615228" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186348574} {:answer/id #uuid "3066946a-f044-5204-ab77-bef3a2693067" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186348877} {:answer/id #uuid "51c171be-4034-5192-89e4-b692911a89f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186349189} {:answer/id #uuid "94ed251c-0d5e-5d2d-94e7-1fb28d07bdcb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186349781}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186348877} :answer-field/id #uuid "cb94e7f6-2fde-5f36-ac5f-9619c1b6e412" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186351061}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given the orthogonal basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the vector $x$ below, find the value of $20{x}_{2},$ where ${x}_{2}$ is the second component of $[x]_{B}.$

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${q}_{1},\,{q}_{2},\,{q}_{3}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =x\cdot {q}_{2} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\sqrt{41} \\ -9 \\ -2\sqrt{41}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{\sqrt{41}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{41}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-15+0-8 \\  & =-23.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
2{x}_{2}=2\cdot (-23)=-46.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186490328 :question/id #uuid "fbba5a71-4786-5f34-9118-2344153343aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-81140" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "35584b0d-5f36-530c-95c4-8d8dec57a042" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3\sqrt{2} \\ -\sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186489635} {:answer/id #uuid "62645a61-af8c-50c1-891a-ec2a1bd6ffa4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} \\ -\sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186489746} {:answer/id #uuid "a7dfba1c-89fc-5799-a7ce-902a9097fb41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186489885} {:answer/id #uuid "b077d275-d97e-5b1d-b7c1-156af5d3749c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-3\sqrt{2} \\ 3\sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186489901} {:answer/id #uuid "cf87e655-37bd-5819-8214-e0383ae42a09" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186489975}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186489635} :answer-field/id #uuid "6f22f005-276f-5d7e-8ec0-5d5973524d87" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186490136}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given the **orthonormal** basis $B=\{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\}$ of ${R}^{2},$ find $[x]_{B}$ if $x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${q}_{1},\,{q}_{2}.$

$$

$$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Solve the inequality $3-2\sqrt{2x+8}>-9.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we isolate the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}3-2\sqrt{2x+8} & >-9 \\ -2\sqrt{2x+8} & >-12 \\ \sqrt{2x+8} & <6\end{aligned}
$$

In this inequality, the square root is being compared to a non-negative number $(6).$ So, we can square both sides of the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\sqrt{2x+8})}^{2} & <{6}^{2} \\ 2x+8 & <36 \\ 2x & <28 \\ x & <14\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the square root. To find the domain of the square root, we recall that the argument of the square root must be greater than or equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+8 & \ge 0 \\ 2x & \ge -8 \\ x & \ge -4\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x<14,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,14).$ But the domain of the square root is $x\ge -4,$ which can be expressed as $[-4,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the square root, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,14)\cap [-4,\infty )=[-4,14)
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [-4,14),$ which can also be written as $-4\le x<14.$"} {:db/id 17592186250336 :question/id #uuid "6c2efa64-c4bf-59c9-a9ea-6f12963b4810" :question/math-academy-id "q-115060"} {:db/id 17592186294866 :question/id #uuid "a5cfa7d0-350c-55fc-a9cc-0e6072e071e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-276744"} {:db/id 17592186294970 :question/id #uuid "f7d6efa8-c53e-51cd-a6ee-3e65231d4543" :question/math-academy-id "q-278280"} {:db/id 17592186294972 :question/id #uuid "bb2e67ae-496a-51b7-b8e8-17bd77bcb9b4" :question/math-academy-id "q-278283"} {:db/id 17592186354591 :question/id #uuid "9fc08219-8cf5-5739-9502-636c289d32a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-87781"} {:db/id 17592186354592 :question/id #uuid "b69bc8b6-ff1c-556f-a4d8-037531c1b6a8" :question/math-academy-id "q-87782"} {:db/id 17592186049055} {:db/id 17592186049595} {:db/id 17592186049674 :topic/difficulty 1.231026047784105 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428816 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. 17592186159566}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A sample ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ of $n$ employees is drawn from a population. The population has employees with two different working hours, $38\,\text{h/week}$ and $40\,\text{h/week},$ distributed in the ratio $3:1.$ Determine the smallest sample size required so that the standard error of the mean is less than  $0.5\,\text{h/week}.$" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the employees in the population have working hours $38\,\text{h/week}$ and $40\,\text{h/week},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $3:1.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $3+1=4$ employees only with the following working hours:

$$
38\,\text{h/week},\,38\,\text{h/week},\,38\,\text{h/week},\,40\,\text{h/week}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{4}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(3\cdot 38+40) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(114+40) \\  & =\frac{154}{4} \\  & =38.5\,\text{h/week},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$

$$

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following conditional probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{{y}^{2}}, & \,0<x<y,\,0<y<1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(\frac{1}{4}<X<\frac{1}{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{5}{8}).$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that 

$$
P(X\in A\,|\,Y=y)={\int }_{A}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x,
$$

where ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ is the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y.$ 

In our case, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\frac{1}{4}<X<\frac{1}{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{5}{8}) & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y=\frac{5}{8})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}\frac{2x}{{(\frac{5}{8})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{64}{25}{\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{64}{25}[{x}^{2}]_{1/4}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{64}{25}(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{64}{25}(\frac{3}{16}) \\  & =\frac{12}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162392 :question/id #uuid "990850d6-75f9-5e72-98e4-4c732056938a" :question/math-academy-id "q-143461" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "76dedc47-c082-5f11-bb91-f5c53a5feef0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186413404} {:answer/id #uuid "b6e703b0-4bd0-5a40-af83-db0c989a5aba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{12}" :db/id 17592186413405} {:answer/id #uuid "db303bfa-69cf-5cf1-86a5-b4a2624334a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186413408} {:answer/id #uuid "efd7c23f-d7a0-5417-baaf-c56cd1849f93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186413410} {:answer/id #uuid "fcf61311-9fef-553a-a566-6bcfee2063e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{8}" :db/id 17592186413411}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186413404} :answer-field/id #uuid "7133b6f3-994d-586b-8bc7-52facdb8edd3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186413413}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following joint probability density function:

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}24xy, & \,0<x<1,0<y<1-x \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Find $P(Y<X\,|\,X=\frac{1}{3}).$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that 

$$
P(Y\in A\,|\,X=x)={\int }_{A}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y,
$$

where ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ is the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x.$ 

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $X,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1-x}24xy\,\text{d}y \\  & =24x{\int }_{0}^{1-x}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =24x{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1-x} \\  & =12x(1-x)^{2}-0 \\  & =12x(x-1)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}12x(x-1)^{2}, & \,0<x<1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)}.
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal density function for $X.$

Now, for $0<x<1,0<y<1-x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{24xy}{12x(x-1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2y}{(x-1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{(x-1)^{2}}, & \,0<x<1,0<y<1-x \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute our probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<X\,|\,X=\frac{1}{3}) & =P(Y<\frac{1}{3}\,|\,X=\frac{1}{3}) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/3}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x=\frac{1}{3})\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/3}\frac{2y}{{(\frac{1}{3}-1)}^{2}}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1/3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1/3} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\frac{1}{18}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186411871 :question/id #uuid "dd343afe-c54e-593d-8dc2-ed57fc5e3a91" :question/math-academy-id "q-143625" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162113 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "184d9e09-3335-5617-8989-e5ab08ca04e7" :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Conditional Probability"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c35ea81-1fba-5743-bc51-d55ebe9293ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{8}" :db/id 17592186411702} {:answer/id #uuid "4668fa6c-efd9-5349-af00-60d3491fb89f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186411715} {:answer/id #uuid "4822c638-df09-5a29-b181-ed51e650cdfc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186411716} {:answer/id #uuid "debe288e-f7cd-5ceb-8f13-e4258cc3d96c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}" :db/id 17592186411803} {:answer/id #uuid "e02c333f-cc9c-5916-848d-431524aca433" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186411804}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "4668fa6c-efd9-5349-af00-60d3491fb89f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186411715} :answer-field/id #uuid "a596b6c7-9c32-5ca9-bbc7-7ea06ecbb649" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186411839}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following conditional probability density function:

$$
P(Y\in A\,|\,X=x)={\int }_{A}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}y,
$$

where ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ is the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y.$ 

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{y}8xy\,\text{d}x \\  & =8y{\int }_{0}^{y}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =8y{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{y} \\  & =4y({y}^{2}-0) \\  & =4{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)={\begin{aligned}4{y}^{3}, & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

Now, for $0\le x\le 1,0\le y\le x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{8xy}{4{y}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2x}{{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)={\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{{y}^{2}}, & \,0\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute our probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\frac{1}{4}<X<\frac{1}{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{2}{3}) & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y=\frac{2}{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}\frac{2x}{{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{4}{\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{4}{[{x}^{2}]}_{1/4}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\frac{3}{16}) \\  & =\frac{27}{64}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186519515 :question/id #uuid "05787bc3-261f-5b82-bb66-810cc0eb28ae" :question/math-academy-id "q-145108"} {:db/id 17592186519563 :question/id #uuid "91a2a3a1-8ae1-5b13-976f-9bc558602e26" :question/math-academy-id "q-143619"} {:db/id 17592186519568 :question/id #uuid "a05be7fd-94f3-5604-ad03-bc6e74737579" :question/math-academy-id "q-143620"} {:db/id 17592186519584 :question/id #uuid "d2c3b01f-8b1d-5c9b-95df-4bf4aec9fac1" :question/math-academy-id "q-143622"} {:db/id 17592186544811 :question/id #uuid "427792fe-a52b-5a35-ba4b-43ed95fe05d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-143573" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a7dd673-0f1c-53a4-bf23-823dac58c3bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{9}" :db/id 17592186544212} {:answer/id #uuid "71a909e6-6f08-5712-bc83-1b6bad8b11a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{18}" :db/id 17592186544339} {:answer/id #uuid "76d4658d-76b6-5b33-aa64-aa0bb388f498" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{24}" :db/id 17592186544351} {:answer/id #uuid "ab42cc66-3ec7-5fba-ba3f-33b3a69e4979" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{18}" :db/id 17592186544454} {:answer/id #uuid "eb3e916a-1d77-5240-920d-86d1b61a5940" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{9}" :db/id 17592186544594}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544351} :answer-field/id #uuid "4824d498-2640-5207-a210-a8d05507618a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544682}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following conditional probability density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2y(2x+3y)}{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{4xy}{5}+\frac{6{y}^{2}}{5})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{2{x}^{2}y}{5}+\frac{6x{y}^{2}}{5}]}_{x=1}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{8y}{5}+\frac{12{y}^{2}}{5}-\frac{2y}{5}-\frac{6{y}^{2}}{5} \\  & =\frac{6{y}^{2}}{5}+\frac{6y}{5} \\  & =\frac{6y(y+1)}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)={\begin{aligned}\frac{6y(y+1)}{5}, & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

Now, for $1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2y(2x+3y)}{5})}{(\frac{6y(y+1)}{5})} \\  & =\frac{2x+3y}{3(y+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8}({y}^{2}+x), & \,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the expression of the conditional probability density function ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ for $0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the formula for the marginal density function for $Y,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3}{8}({y}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{3{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{3x}{8})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3x{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{16}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{6{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{12}{16}-0 \\  & =\frac{3{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}({y}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}({y}^{2}+1), & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

Now, for $1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{8}({y}^{2}+x))}{(\frac{3}{4}({y}^{2}+1))} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}+x}{2({y}^{2}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}+x}{2({y}^{2}+1)}, & \,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544888 :question/id #uuid "e1e5b64b-413b-5b25-a4f6-89eb28f41500" :question/math-academy-id "q-143644" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18eb1c41-b6a4-592b-856a-3cab685afd5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{y-{y}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186544140} {:answer/id #uuid "4d9e076f-f8bc-5761-b656-c6602ea176a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}-y}" :db/id 17592186544254} {:answer/id #uuid "c9c771ea-0ad2-5a82-b2a7-6dd9f49a0d79" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{y}-y}{3}" :db/id 17592186544509} {:answer/id #uuid "ce0a0f68-ff1b-5054-bdc9-b7e07c3e9fbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3(y-{y}^{2})" :db/id 17592186544524} {:answer/id #uuid "fefcf60e-8515-57a8-ab6a-297915943a05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{y}-y" :db/id 17592186544644}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544254} :answer-field/id #uuid "b608e08c-09ce-5c00-b348-3354afe78844" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544738}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following joint probability density function:

Find the expression of the conditional probability density function ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ for $y\le x\le \sqrt{y},\,0<y<1.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the formula for the marginal density function for $Y,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{y}^{\sqrt{y}}6\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot x\,{|}_{y}^{\sqrt{y}} \\  & =6(\sqrt{y}-y).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}6(\sqrt{y}-y), & \,0<y<1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

Now, for $y\le x\le \sqrt{y},\,0<y<1,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{6}{6(\sqrt{y}-y)} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}-y}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}-y}, & \,y\le x\le \sqrt{y},\,0<y<1, \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}

17592186527042}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.6$ | $0$ |

Calculate the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "The covariance of two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint support $S$ is defined as

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}(x-\text{E}[X])(y-\text{E}[Y])f(x,y).
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.6$ | $0$ | $0.6$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.85$ | $0.15$ | $1$ |

We now compute $\text{E}[X]$ and $\text{E}[Y],$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.4+2\cdot 0.6 \\  & =0+1.2 \\  & =1.2 \\ \text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =0\cdot 0.85+1\cdot 0.15 \\  & =0+0.15 \\  & =0.15\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for the covariance, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}(x-\text{E}[X])(y-\text{E}[Y])f(x,y) \\  & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}(x-1.2)(y-0.15)f(x,y) \\  & =(0-1.2)(0-0.15)f(0,0) \\  & +(0-1.2)(1-0.15)f(0,1) \\  & +(2-1.2)(0-0.15)f(2,0) \\  & +(2-1.2)(1-0.15)f(2,1) \\  & =(-1.2)(-0.15)(0.25) \\  & +(-1.2)(0.85)(0.15) \\  & +(0.8)(-0.15)(0.6) \\  & +(0.8)(0.85)(0) \\  & =-0.18.\end{aligned}

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8}(x+{y}^{2}),\, & 0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{5}{4}$ and $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{9}{16},$ calculate the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "The covariance of $X$ and $Y$ can be calculated using the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

To find $\text{E}[XY],$ we use the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}xyf(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}xy\cdot \frac{3}{8}(x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{8}y{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{8}y{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{8}y[\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y+\frac{3}{4}{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{16}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{11}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the covariance formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{11}{16}-(\frac{5}{4})(\frac{9}{16}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{64}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186512880 :question/id #uuid "28314126-6eaa-5326-a420-9e962fb3a315" :question/math-academy-id "q-147950"} {:db/id 17592186512888 :question/id #uuid "57775fd5-4d0c-5406-bb3e-6af6db58e9c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-147945"} {:db/id 17592186512941 :question/id #uuid "cf31f09e-0f29-56f8-9f97-abccd7a0062d" :question/math-academy-id "q-147844"} {:db/id 17592186527202 :question/id #uuid "b5d80cd0-76ca-5260-b15c-cf7c6e9faf1e" :question/math-academy-id "q-146309" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5a8298a5-fac1-5365-b909-1315a53989cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186526687} {:answer/id #uuid "b3de5092-4946-5d3e-b8a7-ad0de03a3d23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}" :db/id 17592186526847} {:answer/id #uuid "b4aaf98a-33ad-537d-a3f0-b7504ddda61e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186526850} {:answer/id #uuid "ec09683f-97e8-5921-86c5-63360bce02d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186526971} {:answer/id #uuid "fc18d19d-57df-5431-9db5-d3ea0a3393eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186527003}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186527003} :answer-field/id #uuid "5e342586-6b50-54ec-9bac-5940a5f9cadc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186527057}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

:answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186412654}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,W=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ above. If the normal equation for the corresponding weighted least-squares problem $W\,A=Wb$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a & 18 \\ 18 & b\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}c \\ 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=\begin{bmatrix}{2}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {1}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 4 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}16 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}24 & 18 \\ 18 & 17\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}18 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=24+17+18=59.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162356 :question/id #uuid "fe1495c6-48c4-58ae-8df8-b0dc82576087" :question/math-academy-id "q-137888" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b7e37e95-9cea-5ab2-a140-cd13a369a582" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "252" :db/id 17592186159339} {:answer/id #uuid "13a4b33f-6cc5-5cf7-ae67-11fc4cec69cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "272" :db/id 17592186159340} {:answer/id #uuid "1a556378-662e-50f4-84e2-69704397f53e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "225" :db/id 17592186159341} {:answer/id #uuid "26188799-c8bd-52c4-8204-93f83b48f701" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "127" :db/id 17592186159342} {:answer/id #uuid "458d0deb-efd4-5187-a31c-bbfaa42d288f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "131" :db/id 17592186159343}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186159343} :answer-field/id #uuid "35881875-1699-51c1-8367-015366562cfb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186159338}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -8 & 16 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -12 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}18 & -36 \\ -36 & 72\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}27 \\ -54\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -36 & 27 \\ -36 & 72 & -54\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}18 & -36 & 27 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{3}{2}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+\frac{b}{c}=2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+\frac{2}{1}=5.

$f(x,y)=2x+y$ on the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $y\ge 0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](images/b5/b5ba69ab02aa13e201b7b9113f6a36e705ad19e6412499504afc4f239459a8f3.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {2}^{2}=2\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,{[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}[2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{8}{3}((2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\cdot \frac{16}{3}=\frac{8}{3\pi }.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281588 :question/id #uuid "636e23a3-a873-5229-81ee-5d1161e02dcd" :question/math-academy-id "q-163070"} {:db/id 17592186281653 :question/id #uuid "9470a948-0cd8-55e7-86d6-65b250b7e800" :question/math-academy-id "q-163260"} {:db/id 17592186281654 :question/id #uuid "9c6dbd46-16b0-53ac-9c25-a6637f9ce3ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-163261"} {:db/id 17592186281662 :question/id #uuid "4da84d34-65b6-5264-9689-a8f568b0485b" :question/math-academy-id "q-163278" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27060319-319a-5c93-87a4-021b464e69b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3\pi }" :db/id 17592186278938} {:answer/id #uuid "96cddbff-aa96-5c15-b451-85bc3b5899ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{3\pi }" :db/id 17592186279926} {:answer/id #uuid "d6297845-0a0a-51e3-9056-3d94de569441" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186280482} {:answer/id #uuid "d932caf8-3377-5328-b82d-2c72ffe1d077" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186280511} {:answer/id #uuid "fb6871d0-cf0d-5786-9a5c-fd24e0463ae0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{5\pi }" :db/id 17592186280794}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280794} :answer-field/id #uuid "d4bf3c23-4651-531a-8ea1-05778a87081e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281209}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "![](images/f8/f84a8fcd4ed668a6b94d5b084ade49dc8fc027feff4baea862e2feaf68221534.png)

Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ on the semicircle shown above." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(-1,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $y=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-2x}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-2x} \\ {y}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}-2x \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-2x \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{4}-{0}^{4})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{4}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{[-\frac{{cos}^{5}⁡\theta }{5}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}({cos}^{5}⁡\pi -{cos}^{5}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}\cdot \frac{4}{5}=\frac{8}{5\pi }.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281663 :question/id #uuid "128ce1a7-9b5d-51fb-9a3d-78ee6a5214c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163279"} {:db/id 17592186374241 :question/id #uuid In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (4-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{[\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2[(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)] \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{4\pi }\cdot 4\pi =1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481407 :question/id #uuid "b0a81f04-6f59-512d-aa20-c54e3b26a51d" :question/math-academy-id "q-163277"} {:db/id 17592186481408 :question/id #uuid
