Let $F(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{0}.$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{[3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{3})]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{3}{2}-3) \\  & =-\frac{3}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186315079 :question/id #uuid "c31042af-d0b1-56e0-8fc6-7b7b6e402e06" :question/math-academy-id "q-341276"} {:db/id 17592186315080 :question/id #uuid "86b3942b-d5fe-58b1-8280-9f2a9124377a" :question/math-academy-id "q-341283" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27402392-ef7b-543e-a95c-51569128931d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{\pi }(\sqrt{2}-2)" :db/id 17592186312273} {:answer/id #uuid "b2388473-f7b4-5371-bdaf-2f5d22ad6092" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4(\sqrt{2}-2)}{\pi}" :db/id 17592186513999}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186513999} :answer-field/id #uuid "f63f2945-3857-5e6d-882c-11e5148b361f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186314680}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=-5x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier cosine series of the **even** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${a}_{n}.$

$\,{a}_{n}=$ {{field-1}}
for $n\ge 1$" :question/worked-solution "For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-5x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{10}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{10}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{10}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{10}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{10}{n\pi }(0+\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{10(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi ))}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{10(1-(-1)^{n})}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167288 :question/id #uuid "a2a82489-ea8c-529e-9b98-bcb721239fc4" :question/math-academy-id "q-340812"} {:db/id 17592186315074 :question/id #uuid $$

$$" :question/worked-solution "For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=3x+1$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(3x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3x+1\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=3 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(3x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{3}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((3\pi +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{3}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0+\frac{3}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{6(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-1)}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{6((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x)∼(1+\frac{3}{2}\pi )+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186315078 :question/id #uuid "9c2ef579-bdc5-59bc-8cd2-73be3fa9875e" :question/math-academy-id "q-341269"} {:db/id 17592186372764 :question/id #uuid 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186164803}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-8\lambda {y}^{′}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and $y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A+B\cdot 0=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}B{e}^{4\lambda }+B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ 2B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{4\lambda }+2B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{4\lambda }(1+2\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require $B\ne 0.$ Thus, since ${e}^{4\lambda }>0,$ we must have

$$
\lambda =-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the corresponding eigenfunction is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =Bx{e}^{4\lambda x} \\  & =Bx{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167269 :question/id #uuid "faaf0705-3b7e-515b-ad1e-e97ff79382c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-338729" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda x}+B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda }+B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ 4A\lambda +B+4B\lambda  & =0 \\ (4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{8\lambda }+2B{e}^{8\lambda }+2(4A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+8B\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(4A\lambda +B+8B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+8A\lambda +2B+16B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+(4+16\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}4\lambda  & 1+4\lambda  \\ 1+8\lambda  & 4(1+4\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\lambda \cdot 4(1+4\lambda )-(1+4\lambda )(1+8\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -(1+8\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -1-8\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )(8\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} {:db/id 17592186314743 :question/id #uuid **Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-16\lambda m+64{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-8\lambda )(m-8\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=8\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{8\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{8\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{8\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{8\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =8A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda x}+B{e}^{8\lambda x}+8B\lambda x{e}^{8\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}8A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (8\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+2(8A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+8B\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(8A\lambda +B+8B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+16A\lambda +2B+16B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+16\lambda )A+(3+16\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(8\lambda )A+B &=0 \\ (1+16\lambda )A+(3+16\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}8\lambda  & 1 \\ 1+16\lambda  & 3+16\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8\lambda (3+16\lambda )-(1)(1+16\lambda ) & =0 \\ 24\lambda +128{\lambda }^{2}-1-16\lambda  & =0 \\ 128{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (16\lambda -1)(8\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{8}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{16}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{8}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{8{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{8{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(8\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+B=0\,⇒\,A=B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=B{e}^{-x}(x+1).
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{16},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{8{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{8{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(8\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+B=0\,⇒\,A=-2B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-2B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-2) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

$$

$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}6A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+2(6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+12A\lambda +2B+12B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+B &=0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}6\lambda  & 1 \\ 1+12\lambda  & 3+12\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\lambda (3+12\lambda )-(1)(1+12\lambda ) & =0 \\ 18\lambda +72{\lambda }^{2}-1-12\lambda  & =0 \\ 72{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda -1)(6\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}

$$

we get

-A+B=0\,⇒\,A=B

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}

$$
(6\lambda )A+B=0

$$

where we have set $C=B.$

:question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-20\lambda {y}^{′}+100{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-20\lambda m+100{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-10\lambda )(m-10\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=10\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{10\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{10\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{10\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{10\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =10A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda x}+B{e}^{10\lambda x}+10B\lambda x{e}^{10\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}10A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda } & =0 \\ 10A\lambda +B+10B\lambda  & =0 \\ (10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{20\lambda }+2B{e}^{20\lambda }+2(10A\lambda {e}^{20\lambda }+B{e}^{20\lambda }+20B\lambda {e}^{20\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(10A\lambda +B+20B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+20A\lambda +2B+40B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+(4+40\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+4(1+10\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+20\lambda )A+4(1+10\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}10\lambda  & 1+10\lambda  \\ 1+20\lambda  & 4(1+10\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}10\lambda \cdot 4(1+10\lambda )-(1+10\lambda )(1+20\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )[40\lambda -(1+20\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )[40\lambda -1-20\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )(20\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{20}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{10}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{10{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{10{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{20},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{10{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{10{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(10\lambda )A+(1+10\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} {:db/id 17592186522787 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-12\lambda {y}^{′}+36{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions.

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda } & =0 \\ 6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda  & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{12\lambda }+2B{e}^{12\lambda }+6(6A\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }+B{e}^{12\lambda }+12B\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+6(6A\lambda +B+12B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+36A\lambda +6B+72B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+8(1+9\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}6\lambda  & 1+6\lambda  \\ 1+36\lambda  & 8+72\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\lambda (8+72\lambda )-(1+6\lambda )(1+36\lambda ) & =0 \\ 48\lambda +432{\lambda }^{2}-(1+42\lambda +216{\lambda }^{2}) & =0 \\ 216{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda +1)(18\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0
$$

we get

$$
-\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{1}{2}B=0
$$

which gives $A=B,$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =B{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0
$$

we get

$$
\frac{1}{3}A+\frac{4}{3}B=0\,⇒\,A=-4B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-4B{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3} \\  & =B{e}^{x/3}(x-4) \\  & =C{e}^{x/3}(x-4)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/3}(x-4).$"} {:db/id 17592186166940 "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+4{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=y(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=y(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ does not correspond to an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+4{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 2\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)=0$ yields

$$
B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\lambda )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
2\lambda =n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167267 :question/id #uuid "733b1be5-001a-56d5-87cc-51209a854a00" :question/math-academy-id "q-338712" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186164792}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+4\lambda y=0,\,y(0)={y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$  {{field-1}}, where $n\in {N}_{0}.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda >0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)={y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not a parameter of the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+4\lambda  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 2\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda })
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
{y}^{′}=2B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
2B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
2\sqrt{\lambda }=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi =\frac{(1+2n)\pi }{2}
$$

for $n\in {N}_{0}.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{(1+2n)^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{16}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186314745 :question/id #uuid "1cf1150e-7ecc-59c2-a214-35eca3b99cbc" :question/math-academy-id "q-338915" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter corresponding to the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+25\lambda  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 5\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda })
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
{y}^{′}=-5A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda })+5B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-5A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+5B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields

$$
-5A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi \sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
5\pi \sqrt{\lambda }=n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{{n}^{2}}{25}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365869 :question/id #uuid "f6852602-1069-51f1-8d48-415f065da706" :question/math-academy-id "q-338912"} {:db/id 17592186391695 :question/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+49{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(2)=0,\,0\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter corresponding to the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+49{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 7\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\lambda x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}=-7A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(7\lambda x)+7B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(7\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-7A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+7B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
-7A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(14\lambda )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
14\lambda =n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{14}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050221 :topic/difficulty 0.5216133198934195 :topic/id #uuid "3748163a-70f7-518f-9382-77b8230a6624" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186166899 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfy the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ satisfy the inhomogeneous system
${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)+f(t).$
Which of the following is **always** a solution of the same inhomogeneous system?

I. $2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$

II. ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)$

III. $3\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${x}_{h}(t)$ satisfies a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution to an inhomogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ then ${x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$ is also a solution to the same inhomogeneous system.

Additonally, the *linearity principle* for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if ${x}_{1}(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t),…,{x}_{k}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ then any linear combination 

$$
{c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)+⋯+{c}_{k}{x}_{k}(t)
$$

with ${c}_{1},{c}_{2},…,{c}_{k}\in R$ is also a solution of the same homogeneous system. 

With that in mind, let's examine the given expression.

- Option I is a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Indeed, notice that the linear combination 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)=2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)
$$

is a solution to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ according to the linearity principle. Thus, 

$$
{{2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{h}(t)}+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

is a solution to our inhomogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t).$

- Option II might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because it lacks the particular solution term ${x}_{p}(t).$

- Option III might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that $3\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier $3$ next to the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186304815 :question/id #uuid "d7119481-1ac5-5669-b8e8-7afd953dbdf9" :question/math-academy-id "q-330309"} {:db/id 17592186379411 :question/id #uuid "ec98e74e-e68c-5045-a599-d3ec1260eaf6" :question/math-academy-id "q-330299"} {:db/id 17592186379418 :question/id #uuid "028e3468-5c29-5e67-a28b-97b2d534ac0d" :question/math-academy-id "q-330306"} {:db/id 17592186049852} {:db/id 17592186048395 :topic/difficulty 0.5681913796417801 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428988 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?" :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186305099 :question/id #uuid "f20c0d44-466d-592f-adfd-5535d1164b77" :question/math-academy-id "q-332705"} {:db/id 17592186305100 :question/id #uuid "1e70744b-cd4d-5289-8a1e-db4fcf31bc45" :question/math-academy-id "q-332707"} {:db/id 17592186305101 :question/id #uuid "cd958f9f-ce7e-5925-b2cc-b90dad87e64d" :question/math-academy-id "q-332710" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24c87346-c0ee-53c3-94ac-95b49a1375c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-4y(t)\end{aligned}\right." :db/id 17592186302693} {:answer/id #uuid "8c1993f9-8087-5c6b-a1ad-dedd2a035b5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=4y(t)\end{aligned}\right." :db/id 17592186303328} {:answer/id #uuid "c5e742a2-b236-57f3-8979-a3b9a473fc05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=4y(t)\end{aligned}\right." :db/id 17592186303672} {:answer/id #uuid "d10f1558-a4b7-543d-abeb-1abd68004cee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-4y(t)\end{aligned}\right." :db/id 17592186303745} {:answer/id #uuid "ff1b612c-1d62-5b79-aa3b-7cf7a714c584" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-5y(t)\end{aligned}\right." :db/id 17592186304063}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186303672} :answer-field/id #uuid "fe78fafd-1fb0-5c2f-9ba1-e3c0b222dbf4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186304760}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/83/83a565accc834d7c16091de22eb43ba80c0ce9c4290f567d1e0ccc009beca565.png)

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-4t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/a2/a2196ea04e12f3c706300e0c9d15806606e408f5e582d3e4f2b9c62f0efc343f.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-2t})^{′}}=\frac{-4{c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}}{-2{c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/a2/a2c81ff3c50013c149dc6a5db67bbe11cccdbbef22ce2c0712101f4a358bcb8c.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{2t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{2t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{t})^{′}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}}{{c}_{1}{e}^{t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to \pm \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

"$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-4y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Select the correct options below regarding the given decoupled system of linear differential equations.

$\,$
The $x$-axis is a {{field-1}} line.

$\,$
The $y$-axis is a {{field-2}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a saddle point}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

17592186527029}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "The displacement $r,$ in meters, of a particle $P$ of mass $3\,\text{kg}$ is given by

$$
r=⟨{t}^{3},\,{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}⟩,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force acting on the particle when $t=4\,\text{s}.$ Round your final answer to the nearest Newton." :question/worked-solution "Newton’s second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we first differentiate $r$ to get the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}-{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},\,4{t}^{3}-2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate the velocity vector to get the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{3}-2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨6t,\,12{t}^{2}-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =3\cdot ⟨6t,\,12{t}^{2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨18t,\,36{t}^{2}-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=4\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(4) & =⟨18(4),\,36({4}^{2})-6⟩ \\  & =⟨72,\,570⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of $F(4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|F(4)| & =\sqrt{(72)^{2}+{(570)}^{2}} \\  & ≈575\,\text{N}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
f(\theta ,ϕ)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\text{_____},\,5\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $f(\theta ,ϕ)$ above parametrizes the ellipsoid defined in Cartesian coordinates as $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+4{y}^{2}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{25}=1.$ What is the second component of $f?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the following substitution:

$$
x=2X,\,y=\frac{1}{2}Y,\,z=5Z
$$

Substituting the above into the Cartesian equation of our ellipsoid, we get

$$
{X}^{2}+{Y}^{2}+{Z}^{2}=1,
$$

which is the equation of a sphere of radius $1$ centered at the origin in $(X,Y,Z)$ coordinates.
In spherical polar coordinates, this sphere has the equation $\rho =1.$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical polar coordinates of a point, then its $(X,Y,Z)$ coordinates can be found using the following formulas:

$$
X=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,Y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,Z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ.
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨2X,\frac{1}{2}Y,5Z⟩ \\  & =⟨2\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\frac{1}{2}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,5\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩ \\  & =⟨2\cdot 1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,5\cdot 1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,5\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ and $ϕ\in [-\pi ,\pi ].$

Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$"} {:db/id 17592186241113 :question/id #uuid "246d3e23-2beb-5fb6-85c7-306f6b17e271" 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "![](images/de/dea7eed9213ddf1bb3293950e2490b120a061e9add1172d3b850ccbc58f90454.png)

Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(y+x)\,i+x\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4$ traversed from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y+x)\,i+x\,j \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2(-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,dt \\  & =[\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =[-1+0]-[1-0] \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345268 :question/id #uuid "1c70d6fc-ab49-5aab-b1d0-4a65a7ea2b5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-77032"} {:db/id 17592186345269 :question/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/de/de3e018fa1382ee2250d1b2e256e3b47cafef346852007f0e6afb84342d7cb04.png)

Consider the vector field $F=3x\,i-2y\,j$ and a rectangle $C$ with base $4$ and height $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/09/0950c559d5d6df93cf40afd8fdbd07f090f864fa462083bfd496246e7f2bded9.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(3x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =3{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-3,3].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =3{\int }_{-3}^{3}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{-3}^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =6\cdot 6 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=36.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(3x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+3j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-2{\int }_{-2}^{2}3\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =(-6)\cdot 4 \\  & =-24.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=-24.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 36+2\cdot (-24)=24.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186420916 :question/id #uuid "ab737fa4-bfd8-53e2-9695-4ad4cbdcb6c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-226136"} {:db/id 17592186421470 :question/id #uuid "f9f7d0a1-c461-5247-ab30-95b875686e93" :question/math-academy-id "q-226134"} {:db/id 17592186050793} {:db/id 17592186049462 :topic/difficulty 0.686470580486518 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186429230 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Any $6\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
- **II.** The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}$ has one negative singular value.
- **III.** Any $4\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $6\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $4\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186493969 :question/id #uuid "dfba6eb1-d0b6-5cbc-ac16-d682a2e1cc93" :question/math-academy-id "q-95286" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08b31b5f-4d45-56bb-9d27-10f181056843" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186493405} {:answer/id #uuid "1f5ebfbd-349c-5710-ab1d-bffdb6d4d025" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186493445} {:answer/id #uuid "21c0505d-1159-59fb-ba8b-2bd5ac4199de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186493447} {:answer/id #uuid "94c66a12-70a7-529f-ba21-ac7f034b13c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186493623} {:answer/id #uuid "e4ada2c6-ebf0-5d58-9a21-8f0d7d2bddb7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186493752}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493447} :answer-field/id #uuid "6457d0d0-1968-5324-849a-7bcaae3a3d7b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493831}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}2-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 8-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ 16-2\lambda -8\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -10) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =10,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{10} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186184877 :question/id #uuid "e9152817-159b-5a54-868d-fe52d19640cc" :question/math-academy-id "q-94981" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a7d4ed93-75bb-5db0-9900-2362979d6c53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4,\,3,\,0" :db/id 17592186404734} {:answer/id #uuid "aac056f1-2c7a-51fc-b3b8-c7516856527b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3,\,2,\,0" :db/id 17592186404735} {:answer/id #uuid "2ef4562a-20e9-5af5-80a4-ced17b367b83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2,\,2,\,0" :db/id 17592186404736} {:answer/id #uuid "fd4157e7-a2cf-562a-af6a-fea80f5a7f86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16,\,9,\,0" :db/id 17592186404737} {:answer/id #uuid "95d80c78-37a1-5b82-8b12-a47780191024" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9,\,4,\,0" :db/id 17592186404738}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186404735} :answer-field/id #uuid "ce3dc232-fc1d-50e4-99b4-15ed1b8fa187" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186404733}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}10 & -6 \\ -6 & 10\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}10-\lambda  & -6 \\ -6 & 10-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )(10-\lambda )-36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +100-36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-20\lambda +64 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda -16) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =16,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta }.$ 

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta .$ 

Using the fact that $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
x=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ,\,y=1.
$$

Then, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }=0.
$$

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(0)}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544858 :question/id #uuid "9dac1de0-3399-5e2c-82ff-248d3a51fed2" :question/math-academy-id "q-133230"} {:db/id 17592186188282 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=2]$ given that the conditional probability mass function ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)$ is shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{X|2}=2.2.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=2] & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)]-{\mu }_{X|2}^{2} \\  & =[(1)^{2}\cdot 0.3+(2)^{2}\cdot 0.45+(4)^{2}\cdot 0.25]-(2.2)^{2} \\  & =0.3+1.8+4-4.84 \\  & =1.26.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186188328 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188035 :question/id #uuid "49a039ae-dbe1-5faa-a9a7-014bd9549c03" :question/math-academy-id "e-10306"} :knowledge-point/id Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=2]$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{X|2}=8.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y,$ corresponding to the column totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=5$ | $\frac{2}{9}$ | $\frac{2}{9}$ |
| $X=10$ | $\frac{2}{9}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $\frac{4}{9}$ | $\frac{5}{9}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y:$

| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=5$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{2}{5}$ |
| $X=10$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{5}$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=2] & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)]-{\mu }_{X|2}^{2} \\  & =[{5}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{5}+{10}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{5}]-{8}^{2} \\  & =10+60-64 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186511491 :question/id #uuid "4b9363aa-00d2-51a2-9bff-045f9cb8f2d6" :question/math-academy-id "q-146278" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "66d1570e-0fc2-5b26-944e-0848dd40f138" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186510998} {:answer/id #uuid "7e4bbbd8-2767-5014-b1ea-d2f03b69e408" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186511040} {:answer/id #uuid "82fe3a83-b24a-5a3c-bffb-cf8e5344fd6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186511051} {:answer/id #uuid "9f3745f3-2e12-5887-955e-9fd687c8f6c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186511116} {:answer/id #uuid "b3aef80f-ba63-5a2a-892f-31618b540913" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186511153}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186511153} :answer-field/id #uuid "798593a5-cfe0-5f7d-84fa-43e7795c761a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186511372}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | $Y=8$ |

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |

| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ |

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=0]$ given that $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{Y|0}=1.$" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ let's first find the marginal distribution for $X,$ corresponding to the row totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x$ is

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding row total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x:$

| ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $1$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=0] & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)]-{\mu }_{Y|0}^{2} \\  & =[{0}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}+{1}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}+{2}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}]-{(1)}^{2} \\  & =0+\frac{1}{2}+1-1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186188687 :question/id #uuid "e6e8480d-863e-574b-98a7-52fe067fa786" :question/math-academy-id "q-146230" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f4abe7f7-40a7-5fee-8c26-2ce6a49da4ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{25}" :db/id 17592186186403} {:answer/id #uuid "02c37c21-5706-5110-839d-3b7f23f1c8c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}" :db/id 17592186186404} {:answer/id #uuid "28522e3b-eba5-534c-bcd9-5ef42a50ee9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186186405} {:answer/id #uuid "42159274-25fc-5902-8f54-b1273ec708fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{25}" :db/id 17592186186406} {:answer/id #uuid "56837666-e2e8-5a77-9c5c-5bd3b0c1b2ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186186407}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186186403} :answer-field/id #uuid "8b741eef-9c5a-588c-9901-de8a736211a9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186186402}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "![](images/9a/9a66f9263c9009f634668e826f0a84320103589b9c270360d7b2465c71e74592.png)

Evaluate the triple integral 
${∭}_{R}2xz\,dV$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the top one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*" :question/worked-solution "![](images/49/49a3333a52a6b7d7451095dbc46ab1009df491c92726436929a6f93cff38db60.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type I region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le 3-2x\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/df/dfa0a80bc323401f050d1302dc42c92558d8b566d9b0f985e955d34eb5cc15bd.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 3-2x\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2xz\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3-2x}2xz\,dz\,dy\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ and $y$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3-2x}2xz\,dz\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{3-2x}2xz\,dz]dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}[x{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=3-2x}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}x(3-2x)^{2}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3})\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3})\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2}(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3})\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3}){[y]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(18x-24{x}^{2}+8{x}^{3})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(18x-24{x}^{2}+8{x}^{3})\,dx & ={[9{x}^{2}-8{x}^{3}+2{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =[9-8+2] \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050165} {:db/id 17592186050524} {:db/id 17592186049016 :topic/id #uuid "d40c7f73-0923-5b33-8a87-c53afe20cdeb" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186198371 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Change the order of integration in the integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.
$$

so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $x,$ and then $z.$" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le x\le \operatorname{tan}⁡y\}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type II region, we first sketch the projection onto the $yz$-plane, given by

$$
E=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{4}\}.
$$

as shown below.

![](images/e3/e32a019900b77c0bb84b4599b8899e3d0d32ae07d9674da126db34394b97ea24.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $0\le x\le \operatorname{tan}⁡y.$

![](images/af/af629672ff2fd31eeae585ad4941fb8682941444cd34383392fb0a6bec24396e.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](images/04/04dc917237ab002263e35fb4a84c264fef240fefaa456c5249d6e24d0c8ebe28.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
x=\operatorname{tan}⁡y\,⟹\,y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x.
$$

- The right boundary of the region is

$$
y=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/b2/b2a6fc02441bb6013b6f54d49ceefafc1468b291ae4149847290135bbf2d2e56.png)

We now consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xz$-plane with the top curve given by 

$$
x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=1.
$$

![](images/b9/b942dbfba8276421620df6258c9951c2b91a5d2dea18c84260c90b6cbe6f760b.png)

Hence, we have that

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{4}\}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $x,$ then $z,$ we obtain

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\operatorname{arctan}⁡x}^{\pi /4}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281479 :question/id #uuid "4f5b1d02-5004-52a1-b833-f3c606e282e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-162482"} {:db/id 17592186281482 :question/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-2.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}-(-2)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198562 :question/id #uuid "48e09a9b-efe0-5a6d-96f4-c82dbcd33806" :question/math-academy-id "q-138095" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198442 :knowledge-point/id #uuid Recall that:

$$

$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get

$25{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=100.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ -8 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=5$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{5},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ -8 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -16 \\ -40 & -20\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}20 & -80 \\ -80 & -100\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}20-\lambda  & -80 \\ -80 & -100-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (20-\lambda )(-100-\lambda )-6\,400 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+80\lambda -8\,400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -60)(\lambda +140) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =60,\,-140\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-140.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186284641 :question/id #uuid "80991c77-0c00-52ac-bae2-41a3b83ff730" :question/math-academy-id "q-170515" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "01f3ea30-3f9d-5508-ab40-ee2dba4f0888" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "70" :db/id 17592186281708} {:answer/id #uuid "2a5452df-294d-5701-b4af-bbf16d6e0530" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "50" :db/id 17592186282056} {:answer/id #uuid "4e6d984c-3905-5e24-bf07-c5dd11a46a31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "100" :db/id 17592186282364} {:answer/id #uuid "bb2908d2-0e8d-5999-a64a-a03cd4b68ae9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "90" :db/id 17592186283306} {:answer/id #uuid "c1eb5798-946a-56c8-9937-6c6a91e2207e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "80" :db/id 17592186283374}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186283306} :answer-field/id #uuid "e3ab9ad5-298c-5e24-9d44-dc14f057d818" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284336}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-18{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+81{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:
