$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =\begin{bmatrix}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{bmatrix}+72\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186389643 :question/id #uuid "546ae5ae-d06c-5386-b960-6a8c9d016f97" :question/math-academy-id "q-170514" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e97a677c-7cd3-5ab4-a853-3e58af95ef68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389645} {:answer/id #uuid "d626e8f2-6f92-5b4c-b77d-4433976b4f8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389646} {:answer/id #uuid "388c0d7a-2358-5cd2-b7be-8784a5eb4f83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389647} {:answer/id #uuid "5bee8a5d-5168-5c30-886c-aa5b72b8ba65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389648} {:answer/id #uuid "34eaf1be-fb4e-53d6-9abd-f05704e7c071" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389649}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389648} :answer-field/id #uuid "807b9eea-f22c-56a9-981a-517ef2430f4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389644}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-30{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-50{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+25{x}_{2}^{2}=100,$ is $-250.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$

$$

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

$$

:answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186460695}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
{u}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$
- **II.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthogonal
- **III.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}=18-18=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})$ is not a unit vector since

$$
‖Q({u}_{1})‖=‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{{9}^{2}+{6}^{2}}\ne 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} {:db/id 17592186198750 :question/id #uuid "e6d806a7-8383-51f7-a460-be3b003d424b" :question/math-academy-id "q-177315"} {:db/id 17592186284748 :question/id #uuid "1e67e934-1049-5a47-aaca-94c1d2a3bfc1" :question/math-academy-id "q-177118" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5a4ade3a-303a-5eec-9df3-e43d050e7127" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465651} {:answer/id #uuid "bfb5336b-989f-5a31-b653-6429b31a077f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465652}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465651} :answer-field/id #uuid "50d64a07-1676-5fda-bef0-6a4849be81d2" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466669} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6722f30e-e2af-5a70-879f-cfff27425f84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465653} {:answer/id #uuid "dc3d0a9a-fffb-56ce-a7bd-59c663e5f87e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465654}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465653} :answer-field/id #uuid "c9cb2af9-89d8-5f3d-8d83-90156885a877" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466670} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9ff5d22d-d9d1-5f3d-acef-b6be4a77c7ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465655} {:answer/id #uuid "bb044ed9-c0d7-5063-b76d-362678932554" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465656}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465655} :answer-field/id #uuid "3cba7c41-2ad1-5047-8e7d-0cc187a92400" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466671}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

- **III.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}=-\frac{12}{25}+\frac{12}{25}=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, both $Q({u}_{1})$ and $Q({u}_{2})$ are unit vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q({u}_{1})‖ & =‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{4}{5})^{2}+(\frac{3}{5})^{2}}=1 \\ ‖Q({u}_{2})‖ & =‖{u}_{2}‖=\sqrt{(-\frac{3}{5})^{2}+(\frac{4}{5})^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following are orthogonal sets?
- **U.** $U={Q(\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$
- **W.** $W={Q(\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix})}$
- **V.** $V={Q(\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}),Q(\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix})}$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

Let's denote the elements of $U,W,$ and $V$ respectively as 

$\,$ ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})},\,$ ${Q({w}_{1}),Q({w}_{2})},\,$ and $\,{Q({v}_{1}),Q({v}_{2}),Q({v}_{3})}.$ 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- $Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2})=0,\,Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0,\,Q({v}_{2})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2}) & ={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}=18-18=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthogonal.

- For the set $W,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2}) & ={w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=1-1=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthogonal.

- For the Set $V,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2}) & ={v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=2+12-5=9\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$U$ and $W$ only"."} {:db/id 17592186411865 :question/id #uuid "8d807e12-6960-57f6-b74d-aa3fe66f0f76" :question/math-academy-id "q-178271" :knowledge-point/_questions 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

- **II.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthogonal
- **III.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=12-12=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})$ is not a unit vector since

$$
‖Q({u}_{1})‖=‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-6)^{2}}\ne 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} {:db/id 17592186446168 :question/id #uuid "ac6fbe63-89e3-55f0-b383-00653c46559a" :question/math-academy-id "q-178025" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "85bffa49-25ed-5277-8eb0-2bf0d83a3acf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186446158} {:answer/id #uuid "acfdb839-bbb9-5d75-a684-8e0ba2f1180c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "None of the statements are true." :db/id 17592186446161} {:answer/id #uuid "e4112fbf-91d8-5bb1-acad-1777ebe798bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186446162} {:answer/id #uuid "eb713c79-d5f4-5d03-8da7-db12deacf3d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186446164} {:answer/id #uuid "f04b535e-e446-5693-b598-2a2ae8017998" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186446165}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186446162} :answer-field/id #uuid "5243b6a3-407c-5377-9662-ad587ee4e1e3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186446167}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
{u}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$

II. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthogonal

III. $\{Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})\}$ is orthonormal" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{5}=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, both $Q({u}_{1})$ and $Q({u}_{2})$ are unit vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q({u}_{1})‖ & =‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}+(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}}=1 \\ ‖Q({u}_{2})‖ & =‖{u}_{2}‖=\sqrt{(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}+(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}})^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} {:db/id 17592186485518 :question/id #uuid "3a3b6415-46fa-5ac6-8f1e-cce0985c5f71" :question/math-academy-id "q-40515"} {:db/id 17592186485595 :question/id #uuid "fd59782d-c853-5fe4-812d-f8b2814488a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-140567"} {:db/id 17592186525984 :question/id #uuid "01fe6b4b-89e7-5f7d-85f4-05ba3856f335" :question/math-academy-id "q-178268" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d3fe7ca-ea29-5f3f-8066-d8716cb13a68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "None of the statements are true." :db/id 17592186525269} {:answer/id #uuid "32717fe3-a7f3-56f5-9f8f-5f4636b81c3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186525330} {:answer/id #uuid "4d91a2bf-fdbf-56b8-8e4e-20e5996d747e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186525401} {:answer/id #uuid "80bb61ff-4612-53a2-9ac0-e8606aaa9455" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186525527} {:answer/id #uuid "9ef395c5-e379-5f31-abfb-14bad75b8656" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186525611}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186525269} :answer-field/id #uuid "7be66281-82ba-5671-8686-d76669d37ebe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186525907}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

"selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186356969}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+L\{2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t{e}^{2t}\} & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$"} {:db/id 17592186304984 :question/id #uuid "8e2260d5-2c33-5f8d-aede-72fd6d295719" :question/math-academy-id "q-332133"} {:db/id 17592186304995 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{2{e}^{-3t}+7{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\  & =L\{2{e}^{-3t}\}+L\{7{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\  & =2L\{{e}^{-3t}\}+7L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} & =\frac{2}{(s-5)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =2L\{{e}^{-3t}\}+7L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{5t}\} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{s+3}+7\cdot \frac{2}{(s-5)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{s+3}+\frac{14}{(s-5)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{2t}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$

$$

$$

$$

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=x+y,\,y(0)=0
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with two steps to approximate $y(1)$ and $y(2),$ rounded to two decimal places.

$$
y(1)≈{{field-1}},\,y(2)≈{{field-2}}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

First, note that we are given $y(0)$ and asked to find $y(2).$ The distance from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is $2,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{2-0}{2}=1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((x+y)+({x}_{\text{new}}+{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+y)+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+y)+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y)+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve for the general formula for ${y}_{\text{new}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to calculate our approximations of $y(1)$ and $y(2).$

**Step 1**.

From the initial conditions, we have

$$
x=0,\,y=0.
$$

Therefore, the new $x$ value is 

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+1=1.
$$

Hence, the new $y$ value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y \\  & =0+1+3\cdot 0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**.

From the previous step, we have

$$
x=1,\,y=1.
$$

Therefore, the new $x$ value is 

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

Hence, the new $y$ value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y \\  & =1+2+3\cdot 1 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
y(1)≈1.00,\,y(2)≈6.00.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186314870 :question/id #uuid "1460acee-63ea-51f1-b97f-adf5a4da0829" :question/math-academy-id "q-339859"} {:db/id 17592186314871 :question/id #uuid :db/id 17592186307849}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\pm 3\text{i}.$*

| ${e}^{At}=\frac{1}{3}\,\,$ |  | $3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ | $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3\text{i}t) & ={e}^{3\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot 3\text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+3{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5{\alpha }_{1}t & =-5\cdot \frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308658 :question/id #uuid "b1c86e08-63ee-5a97-b95f-27068e31ae61" :question/math-academy-id "q-334635"} {:db/id 17592186308659 :question/id #uuid "0448b3a1-752c-5dfe-8b80-002c75e77e8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-334636"} {:db/id 17592186308660 :question/id #uuid "94b786d3-6c88-5e7c-b171-415f525959f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-334637"} {:db/id 17592186370129 :question/id #uuid "eace89bb-5f6d-586f-b6ba-d2d1f4b38da0" :question/math-academy-id "q-334633"} {:db/id 17592186532679 :question/id #uuid "900adaef-859d-5d14-9981-202d2269e069" :question/math-academy-id "q-334626" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9a8db4e8-f732-5d22-9704-09e0ccf298b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\cos(3t)+\sin(3t)" :db/id 17592186532285}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186532285} :answer-field/id #uuid "3247c73e-d754-5617-80f3-a0beacefea90" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186532515} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f84eb7c6-9806-5d01-aade-ce5ce09883c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sin(3t)" :db/id 17592186532472}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186532472} :answer-field/id #uuid "4788b925-6ee1-5536-8ffa-a6478b71d51d" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186532525}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}].$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$

$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((2+3\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(2+3\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(2+3\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\ (2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+3{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5\cdot \frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t+{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3\cdot \frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t \\  & =-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

17592186045485} :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $3,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $3t$ | $1-3t$ |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(3t) &={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
3t{e}^{3t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}(1-3t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =6{e}^{3t}t+{e}^{3t}(1-3t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(1+3t), \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3{e}^{3t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1+3t & -3t \\ 3t & 1-3t\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308671 :question/id #uuid "3361c13c-b482-5551-8d22-7ff3a0ff8596" :question/math-academy-id "q-334732"} {:db/id 17592186308672 :question/id #uuid "4bf1a0f0-bb87-5dac-ad3b-1ce93c87e2a8" :question/math-academy-id "q-334733" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "52b1d7ae-e4dd-5799-9115-e6e7b1fd12ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12t" :db/id 17592186305951}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305951} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dde19ef-9af0-5255-a3d4-655b000140c4" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307818} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0fc7ea02-06bd-5e6c-aed2-4751d80186b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+6t" :db/id 17592186305289}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305289} :answer-field/id #uuid "893c4189-3f31-573e-94ae-26b874312a53" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307952}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}8 & -3 \\ 12 & -4\end{bmatrix}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -3 \\ 12 & -4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 12{\alpha }_{1}t & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t) &={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t) &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =8{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1+6t) \\ 12{\alpha }_{1}t & =12{e}^{2t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}1+6t & -3t \\ 12t & 1-6t\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308673 :question/id #uuid "05e36fef-5d87-510d-a2e4-12cce4dfd1e8" :question/math-academy-id "q-334734"} {:db/id 17592186308674 :question/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &={x}^{2}(t)+2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-3x(t)+{y}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$

| ${u}^{′}=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+2y \\ -3x+{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2y)=2 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3x+{y}^{2})=-3,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3x+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x & 2 \\ -3 & 2y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2(0) & 2 \\ -3 & 2(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186368152 :question/id #uuid "a7c1fead-d116-5ff5-8a51-16479e32a1be" :question/math-academy-id "q-335143"} {:db/id 17592186368175 :question/id #uuid "396d0927-5f69-505a-80d1-a119800f214e" :question/math-academy-id "q-336900" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ed2047a8-8982-5263-b25f-46e01db0123d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186368177}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186368177} :answer-field/id #uuid "0a3a8240-1762-543d-99d2-3372e89367f7" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186368176} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a2da43c9-f82c-5c88-b1e6-691df9d8c9c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186368179}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186368179} :answer-field/id #uuid "2d3bca15-6c24-52f3-baa6-76c81a9a965b" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186368178} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "57371dc2-00f9-5847-bcf0-bf21a9eee108" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186368181}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186368181} :answer-field/id #uuid "dd8f71a2-83e7-5924-ab0b-12a5484830f6" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186368180} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7e2d6566-7c2c-5700-9daf-b1f1f46b1e04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186368183}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186368183} :answer-field/id #uuid "3396f4c5-a888-5322-87d4-018f368e9efa" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186368182}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[2,\text{ }1]^{T}?$

|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+2y-6 \\ x-3y+{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2y-6)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2y-6)=2 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-3y+{y}^{2})=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-3y+{y}^{2})=-3+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x & 2 \\ 1 & 2y-3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2(2) & 2 \\ 1 & 2(1)-3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y-1\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186368184 :question/id #uuid "764d1d84-2f88-5b8f-983f-958d465089bf" :question/math-academy-id "q-336904"} {:db/id 17592186444533 :question/id #uuid $$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}4x+{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-5y\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+{y}^{2})=4,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-5y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-5y)=-5\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2y \\ 2x & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & -5\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186221419 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221183 :question/id #uuid "fd2d2d61-53a6-51c1-811c-41393270ddba" :question/math-academy-id "e-21676"} :knowledge-point/id {{field-1}}{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=\begin{bmatrix}xy+y \\ -2x-y\end{bmatrix}.$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+y)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+y)=x+1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2x-y)=-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2x-y)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}y & x+1 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}-\lambda  & 1 \\ -2 & -1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-1-\lambda )-(-2)(1) & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +1)+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\text{i}.$

Finally, since we have two complex eigenvalues with negative real parts, our equilibrium is an $\text{asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$"} {:db/id 17592186444535 :question/id #uuid $$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}xy-{y}^{2}-1 \\ -{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+5\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-{y}^{2}-1)=y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-{y}^{2}-1)=x-2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+5)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+5)=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}y & x-2y \\ -2x & -2y\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}(1) & 2-2(1) \\ -2(2) & -2(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ -4 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(-2-\lambda ) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-2,1.$

Finally, since we have two real eigenvalues with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$"} {:db/id 17592186050600} {:db/id 17592186048912 :topic/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=2x-2y-3,\,y(0)=1
$$

To approximate the solution, one step of the Runge-Kutta method has already been computed, resulting in the following estimate:

$$
y(1)≈0
$$

Use the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method with one step to approximate $y(2).$

*Hint: The corrector equation of the two-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is defined as*

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx
$$

*where ${y}_{p}$ denotes the predictor at the current step, and ${y}_{-1}^{′}$ is the estimated slope at the previous point.*" :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (ABM $2$-step) Method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the current point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{-1}^{′}=f({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point (${x}_{-1},{y}_{-1}),$ and

- ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the estimated slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

Before we start, let's add the initial condition data and Runge-Kutta step data to a table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Now, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=2,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=2-1=1.
$$

First, we compute the values of ${y}^{′}$ at each point according to the given rule:

- The slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})=(0,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{-1}^{′} & =2{x}_{-1}-2{y}_{-1}-3 \\  & =2\cdot 0-2\cdot 1-3 \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

- The slope at the current point $(x,y)=(1,0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x-2y-3 \\  & =2\cdot 1-2\cdot 0-3 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ |  |  |  |  |

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot (-1)-(-5))\cdot 1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ |  |  |  |

So, the coordinates of the predicted new point are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=0+1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ |  |  |

Hence, the slope at this predicted point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =2{x}_{\text{new}}-2{y}_{p}-3 \\  & =2\cdot 2-2\cdot 1-3 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot (-1)+8\cdot (-1)-(-5))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot (-8) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=2.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =0+(-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈-\frac{2}{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186308490 :question/id #uuid "e92e1b49-1def-5e1c-b19c-ef83416fc895" :question/math-academy-id "q-333686"} {:db/id 17592186308491 17592186307684}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A numerical method is used to approximate the solution to an initial value problem.

- With step size $Δx=0.08,$ the observed local truncation error is $τ(0.08)=0.13.$

- With step size $Δx=0.02,$ the observed local truncation error is $τ(0.02)=0.002.$

Estimate the order of the numerical method." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.08$ to $0.02.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.08}{0.02}=4.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={4}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.13$ to $0.002.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.13}{0.002}=65.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{p+1} & ≈65 \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{4}⁡(65) \\ p+1 & ≈3.011… \\ p & ≈2.011….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is $2.$"} {:db/id 17592186221987 :question/id #uuid "36473f35-3093-5439-832b-c821da150814" :question/math-academy-id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "The local truncation error (LTE) of a numerical method with step size $Δx$ is

$$
τ(Δx)=4(Δx)^{3}-(Δx)^{4}.
$$

Complete the following sentences.$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.3,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.1,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Decreasing from $Δx=0.3$ to $Δx=0.1,$ the LTE is reduced by a factor of $≈$
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ According to this data, the order of the method is approximately
{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.3,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.3) & =4(0.3)^{3}-(0.3)^{4} \\  & =4\cdot 0.027-0.008\,1 \\  & =0.108-0.008\,1 \\  & =0.099\,9 \\  & ≈0.100.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.1,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.1) & =4(0.1)^{3}-(0.1)^{4} \\  & =4\cdot 0.001-0.000\,1 \\  & =0.004-0.000\,1 \\  & =0.003\,9 \\  & ≈0.004.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.3$ to $0.1.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.3}{0.1}=3.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={3}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.099\,9$ to $0.003\,9.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.099\,9}{0.003\,9}=25.615\,38…≈25.615.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{p+1} & ≈25.615\,38… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(25.615\,38…) \\ p+1 & ≈2.952… \\ p & ≈1.952….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$2.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:

$$
τ(Δx)=4(Δx)^{3}-(Δx)^{4}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{3})=O\,((Δx)^{2+1}),\,Δx\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $2.$"} {:db/id 17592186396412 :question/id #uuid "191ac454-645f-542b-be97-450b5f3d1a65" :question/math-academy-id "q-334710"} {:db/id 17592186396437 :question/id $$

- For the LTE expression $τ(Δx)=(Δx)^{4}-2(Δx)^{5},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $(Δx)^{4}=(Δx)^{3+1}.$ So, statement III corresponds to an order $3$ method.

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A numerical method for approximating a solution to an initial value problem is known to be order $3.$  Suppose that using step size $Δx=0.2$ produces a global truncation error (GTE) of $e(0.2)≈0.064.$  If we instead use a step size $Δx=0.1,$ what GTE should we expect?

$e(0.1)≈$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.2$ to $0.1.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.2}{0.1}=2.
$$

Now, since the numerical method is of order $3,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of

$$
{k}^{3}={2}^{3}=8.
$$

Therefore, using a step size of $Δx=0.1,$ the expected GTE is

$$
e(0.1)≈\frac{0.064}{8}=0.008.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308686 :question/id #uuid "5e9fb99c-0502-586a-b64c-76d5a0146e7d" :question/math-academy-id "q-334781"} {:db/id 17592186308687 :question/id #uuid "d047c5c7-9757-5ee5-9e01-a79118905089" :question/math-academy-id "q-334796" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d077e1b-69a5-5689-b7f2-27863f84eb6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.01" :db/id 17592186305418}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305418} :answer-field/id #uuid "c9664d18-5c13-5c23-a303-4d40a0de2cc7" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186308149}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A numerical method for approximating a solution to an initial value problem is known to be order $2.$  Suppose that using step size $Δx=0.15$ produces a global truncation error (GTE) of $e(0.15)≈0.0225.$  If we instead use a step size $Δx=0.10,$ what GTE should we expect?

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-y=0,\,y(1)=-1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2
$$

Use Euler's Method with two steps to approximate $y(2)$ and ${y}^{′}(2).$

$$
y(2)≈{{field-1}},\,{y}^{′}(2)≈{{field-2}}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′} &=f(x,y,z)\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-y & =0 \\ {x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =y-4{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{y-4{y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=2.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} &=z,\, && y(1)=-1, \\ {z}^{′} &=\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}},\, && z(1)=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z={y}^{′}$ at $x=1$ and asked to find their values at $x=2.$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=2$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=-1$ and $z(1)=2.$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ |  |  | $2$ |  |  |

**Step 1**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the first row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=2 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{-1-4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}}=-9 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=2\cdot \frac{1}{2}=1 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=-9\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{9}{2} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=-1+1=0 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=2-\frac{9}{2}=-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-9$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $0$ |  |  | $-\frac{5}{2}$ |  |  |

**Step 2**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the second row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=-\frac{5}{2} \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{0-4(-\frac{5}{2})}{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}}=\frac{10}{(\frac{9}{4})}=\frac{40}{9} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{5}{4} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{40}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{20}{9} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0-\frac{5}{4}=-\frac{5}{4} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{20}{9}=-\frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-9$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $0$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $-\frac{5}{4}$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{40}{9}$ | $\frac{20}{9}$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{5}{4}$ |  |  | $-\frac{5}{18}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(2)≈-\frac{5}{4}$
and
${y}^{′}(2)=z(2)≈-\frac{5}{18}.$"} {:db/id 17592186308538 :question/id #uuid "fb1abd48-adcc-5047-a986-a35aa0061fc5" :question/math-academy-id "q-333997"} {:db/id 17592186308540 :question/id #uuid following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=3x-{y}^{2},\,y(0)=1
$$

Use the implicit Euler method with one step and Newton's method to approximate $y(0.4).$ Round your answer to two decimal places.

$y(0.4)≈$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}),
$$

the implicit Euler method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=0.4,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=0.4-0=0.4.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the implicit Euler method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(3({x}_{\text{new}})-({y}_{\text{new}})^{2})\cdot 0.4 \\  & =1.2({x}_{\text{new}})-0.4({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy$ and move all terms to the left-hand side and define the resulting expression as $g({y}_{\text{new}}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+1.2({x}_{\text{new}})-0.4({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
0.4({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-1.2({x}_{\text{new}})=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=0.4$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.4({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-1.2({x}_{\text{new}}).
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is ${x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+0.4=0.4.$ Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.4({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1-1.2(0.4) \\  & =0.4({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1.48.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method. 

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=0.8({y}_{\text{new}})+1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.4(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}+({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-1.48}{0.8(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})+1}
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(0)=1,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & =1.044444 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈1.044014 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈1.044014\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(0.4)≈1.04,$ rounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186308430 :question/id #uuid "faf897e3-cf50-5b4e-b765-c864f4378034" :question/math-academy-id "q-333286"} {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if

$$
{y}^{″}+9y=5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot (t-3)^{2}\,,\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,
$$

where ${u}_{3}(t)=u(t-3)$ is the unit step function." :question/worked-solution "First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{″}+9y\} & =L\{5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot (t-3)^{2}\} \\ L\{{y}^{″}\}+9L\{y\} & =L\{5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot (t-3)^{2}\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{″}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of the second derivative and the initial conditions $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
L\{{y}^{″}\}={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
5{u}_{3}(t)\cdot (t-3)^{2}
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=3$ and $f(t)=5(t-3)^{2}.$

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\}={e}^{-as}\cdot L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

  

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{5u(t-3)\cdot (t-3)^{2}\} & ={e}^{-3s}\cdot L\{5((t+3)-3)^{2}\} \\  & ={e}^{-3s}\cdot L\{5{t}^{2}\} \\  & ={e}^{-3s}\cdot 5\cdot \frac{2!}{{s}^{2+1}} \\  & =\frac{10{e}^{-3s}}{{s}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{″}\}+9L\{y\} & =L\{5{u}_{3}(t)(t-3)^{2}\} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s)+9Y(s) & =\frac{10{e}^{-3s}}{{s}^{3}} \\ ({s}^{2}+9)Y(s) & =\frac{10{e}^{-3s}}{{s}^{3}} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{10{e}^{-3s}}{{s}^{3}({s}^{2}+9)}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186377466 :question/id #uuid "98a09fe6-32c9-5c80-965f-f0e147575e4d" :question/math-academy-id "q-345251"} {:db/id 17592186377473 :question/id #uuid "5c8533a8-1f90-5b54-be02-41e34f166ed3" :question/math-academy-id "q-345255" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "070cb125-df6a-5a6e-a3c1-eebd12e71978" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y(s)=\frac{18{e}^{-s}}{({s}^{2}+9)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186377475} {:answer/id #uuid "f4013812-37ba-5064-ab55-54d4b4b78e12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y(s)=\frac{18{e}^{-2s}}{({s}^{2}+9)({s}^{2}+4s+13)}" :db/id 17592186377476} {:answer/id #uuid "b3afdc87-a5c1-502d-b40f-2421236c8cf8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y(s)=\frac{18{e}^{-s}}{({s}^{2}+9)({s}^{2}+4s+13)}" :db/id 17592186377477} {:answer/id #uuid "436278c2-b580-52a1-8e49-b07bf5e41e0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y(s)=\frac{18{e}^{-s}}{{s}^{2}+4s+13}" :db/id 17592186377478} {:answer/id #uuid "665b8f05-7e39-58e8-bd72-72806cf6ff9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y(s)=\frac{9{e}^{-s}}{({s}^{2}+9)({s}^{2}+4s+13)}" :db/id 17592186377479}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186377477} :answer-field/id #uuid "443034ac-6f38-5490-9b31-4ff0cd1c4442" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186377474}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if

$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{′}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of the first derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=0$:

$$
L\{{y}^{′}\}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{″}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of the second derivative and the initial conditions $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0$:

$$
L\{{y}^{″}\}={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)
$$

For the right-hand side, we use the second shifting theorem:

$$
L\{u(t-a)f(t-a)\}={e}^{-as}F(s)
$$

Here, $a=1$ and $f(t-1)=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-1))$, so $f(t)=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$ The transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
F(s)=L\{6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\}=6\cdot \frac{3}{{s}^{2}+{3}^{2}}=\frac{18}{{s}^{2}+9}.
$$

Applying the shift, we get

$$
L\{6{u}_{1}(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-1))\}={e}^{-s}\cdot \frac{18}{{s}^{2}+9}=\frac{18{e}^{-s}}{{s}^{2}+9}.
$$

Substituting these into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)+4sY(s)+13Y(s) & =\frac{18{e}^{-s}}{{s}^{2}+9} \\ ({s}^{2}+4s+13)Y(s) & =\frac{18{e}^{-s}}{{s}^{2}+9} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{18{e}^{-s}}{({s}^{2}+9)({s}^{2}+4s+13)}\end{aligned}

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the solution $y(t)$ given that the Laplace transform of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}(t)+3{y}^{′}(t)+2y(t)={u}_{2}(t),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,
$$

is given by

$$
{s}^{2}Y(s)+3sY(s)+2Y(s)=\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}.
$$

The solution is $y(t)=u(t-2)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}-{e}^{-(t-2)}\,+\,$
{{field-1}}
$).$" :question/worked-solution "Using the transformed equation, we solve for $Y(s)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)+3sY(s)+2Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s} \\ ({s}^{2}+3s+2)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s} \\ (s+1)(s+2)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s} \\ Y(s) & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot \frac{1}{s(s+1)(s+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the inverse transform, we first use partial fraction decomposition on the algebraic part:

$$
\frac{1}{s(s+1)(s+2)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{s+1}+\frac{C}{s+2}
$$

Solving for the constants, we find $A=\frac{1}{2}$, $B=-1$, and $C=\frac{1}{2}$, giving:

$$
\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+3s+2)}=\frac{1}{2s}-\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{1}{2(s+2)}
$$

Now, we apply the inverse Laplace transform. Let 

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{2s}-\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{1}{2(s+2)},
$$

then, we have 

$$
f(t)=\frac{1}{2}-{e}^{-t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2t}.
$$

According to the second shifting theorem, 

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}={u}_{a}(t)f(t-a).
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-2s}F(s)\} \\ y(t) & ={u}_{2}(t)\,f(t-2) \\ y(t) & =u(t-2)(\frac{1}{2}-{e}^{-(t-2)}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2(t-2)}).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186377480 :question/id #uuid "3731bc55-d35c-5b26-9516-425a707e0d99" :question/math-academy-id "q-345263" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c35b6c1e-f747-5862-8863-fe053c5aa6c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\operatorname{cos}(t-1)" :db/id 17592186377482} {:answer/id #uuid "143176f2-5f66-5c47-bc95-252c5655a68f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\cos(t-1)" :db/id 17592186517527}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186517527} :answer-field/id #uuid "2c74efd7-0f5a-5f39-afee-3b02924def1a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186377481}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find the solution $y(t)$ given that the Laplace transform of the initial value problem

$$

is given by

$$
{s}^{2}Y(s)+6sY(s)+5Y(s)=\frac{20{e}^{-4s}}{s}.

$$

To find the inverse transform, we first use partial fraction decomposition on the algebraic part:

$$
\frac{20}{s(s+1)(s+5)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{s+1}+\frac{C}{s+5}
$$

Solving for the constants, we find $A=4,$ $B=-5,$ and $C=1,$ giving:

$$
\frac{20}{s(s+1)(s+5)}=\frac{4}{s}-\frac{5}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s+5}
$$

Now, we apply the inverse Laplace transform. Let 

$$
F(s)=\frac{4}{s}-\frac{5}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s+5},
$$

then, we have

$$
f(t)=4-5{e}^{-t}+{e}^{-5t}.
$$

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}={u}_{a}(t)f(t-a).
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-4s}F(s)\} \\ y(t) & ={u}_{4}(t)\,f(t-4) \\ y(t) & =u(t-4)\cdot (4-5{e}^{-(t-4)}+{e}^{-5(t-4)}).\end{aligned}

calculus states that

$$
\int_a^b f'(x)\,\textrm d x = f(b) - f(a).
$$

A similar result, known as **the fundamental theorem for line integrals,** exists for line integrals of conservative vector fields. This theorem can be stated as follows:

*Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ Then,*

$$
\int_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

 

We'll discuss how this theorem is proved in simple cases at the end of the lesson. :step/content {:db/id 17592186135127 :tutorial/content "Let's apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals to evaluate

$$
\int_C \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},
$$

where $f(x,y) = x^2y^3$ and $C$ is the path along the curve $y=x^2$ for $x \in [0,2].$ 

First, we must parameterize the curve $C.$ A suitable parametrization is 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t, \: t^2\right\rangle, \qquad t \in [0,2].
$$

The position vectors of the endpoints of $C$ are given by

$$
\mathbf{r}(0)	= \left\langle 0, 0\right\rangle, \qquad
\mathbf{r}(2)	= \left\langle 2, 4\right\rangle.
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the path's endpoints defined by $C$ are $(0,0)$ and $(2,4).$

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(r(2))-f(r(0)) \\  & =f(2,4)-f(0,0) \\  & ={2}^{2}\cdot {4}^{3}-{0}^{2}\cdot {0}^{3} \\  & =4\cdot 64 \\  & =256.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice how much faster it is to evaluate a line integral when we can use the fundamental theorem." :tutorial/id #uuid "8ce39e74-c98d-54af-8d93-20f6b5bca39a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5829 :tutorial/title "A Concrete Example"} :step/id #uuid "15f14408-48b8-5f0f-8c55-d5009dc56e57" :step/math-academy-id 35721 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134824}} {:db/id 17592186134861 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135128 :tutorial/content "Here, we prove the fundamental theorem of line integrals in the two-dimensional case. The three-dimensional case is similar.

Let $C$ be a smooth curve $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and suppose that $f(x,y)$ is a differentiable function of two variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ We wish to show that

$$
\int_C \nabla f \cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

Using our usual formula for calculating line integrals, we can write the left-hand side as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}∇f\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the chain rule, the integrand above is simply the derivative of $f(\mathbf r(t))$ with respect to $t.$ Thus, we can write this integral as

$$
\int_a^b \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d t}(f(\mathbf r(t)))\,\textrm d t.
$$

Finally, by the fundamental theorem of calculus, this is equal to 

$$
f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

This concludes the proof in the case where $C$ is smooth. It's easy to show that the theorem also holds for piecewise smooth curves." :tutorial/id #uuid "0ef0926c-7a69-5fc8-91f0-7f40e3be9be9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5830 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Fundamental Theorem for Smooth Curves"} :step/id #uuid "48691aa9-a37a-52cd-a44c-e9ef2b10ea85" :step/math-academy-id 35722}] :activity/title "The Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186133996} {:db/id 17592186134760 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135084 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $f(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b].$ The fundamental theorem of calculus states that

$$
\int_a^b f'(x)\,\textrm d x = f(b) - f(a).
$$

A similar result, known as **the fundamental theorem for line integrals,** exists for line integrals of conservative vector fields. This theorem can be stated as follows:

*Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $\nabla f$ is continuous on $C.$ Then,*

$$
\int_{C} \nabla f \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf r = f(\mathbf r(b)) - f(\mathbf r(a)).
$$

 

We'll discuss how this theorem is proved in simple cases at the end of the lesson. But for now, let's take a look at a concrete example of how to apply this theorem." :tutorial/id #uuid "0c3e4762-a85a-5881-81ad-857e0bec5a48" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4306 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e063a5e6-8819-5814-8c62-dae890a57d71" :step/math-academy-id 26178 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134860}} {:db/id 17592186135084 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $f(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b].$ The fundamental theorem of calculus states that

Given that $C$ is the path along the curve $y={x}^{3}+1$ for $x\in [1,2],$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

We start by parametrizing the curve $C.$ A suitable parametrization is

$$
r(t)=⟨t,{t}^{3}+1⟩,\,t\in [1,2].
$$

Then, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨1,2⟩, \\ r(2) & =⟨2,9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by $C$ are $(1,2)$ and $(2,9).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$

$$

Then, the position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ r(\pi ) & =⟨\pi ,2\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
