Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/a2/a2c81ff3c50013c149dc6a5db67bbe11cccdbbef22ce2c0712101f4a358bcb8c.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{2t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{2t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{t})^{′}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}{e}^{2t}}{{c}_{1}{e}^{t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to \pm \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?" :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$

$$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-3t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-2t})^{′}}=\frac{-3{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}}{-2{c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}}=\frac{3{c}_{2}}{2{c}_{1}}{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?" :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ae3c91ec-0646-58d2-a00b-c0e68120022f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186525123}} {:db/id 17592186525104 :step/content {:db/id 17592186391169 :question/answer-fields \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-5y(t)\end{aligned}\right.

Select the correct options below regarding the given decoupled system of linear differential equations.$\,$
The $x$-axis is a {{field-1}} line.

$\,$
The $y$-axis is a {{field-2}} line.

The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-4t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis and also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a stable node (sink)}.$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/b1/b1efa82f75d22a304e29adc5a791086bb9d9bf43b2f5c97ba8563f43fd13cc4a.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-3t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-2t})^{′}}=\frac{-3{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}}{-2{c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}}=\frac{3{c}_{2}}{2{c}_{1}}{e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-4t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

$$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

lie on the $y$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{6t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/24/2473117cdca4318187b94374820c0a12576e998e7f631a6e7bf51e56c985be43.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{4t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{6t})^{′}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}}{6{c}_{1}{e}^{6t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=1$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$

The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ with the eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a saddle point}.$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{6t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{6t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/24/2473117cdca4318187b94374820c0a12576e998e7f631a6e7bf51e56c985be43.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{6t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{4t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{6t})^{′}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}}{6{c}_{1}{e}^{6t}}=\frac{2{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r .
$$

This integral represents the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle from an initial point $A$ to a terminal point $B$ along the curve.

If the curve can be parameterized by the function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ then we can calculate the line integral using the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r= \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,\textrm dt
$$

Often, the trickiest part is finding a parameterization for $C.$ In this lesson, we'll consider several different cases" :tutorial/id #uuid "ec010a30-571c-5ad5-b30a-c18ffdd997e1" "81974eea-7a73-591a-8f79-590de81df808" :step/math-academy-id 45752 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199396}} {:db/id 17592186199393 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199515 :tutorial/content "If $A$ is the matrix corresponding to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ then:  

- The maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}$ of $A,$ and the maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}$ of $A,$ and the minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{min}}.$

We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-10\: \! x_1x_2+x_2^2
$$

 

when $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1$ is $6.$ Let's use this to find a unit vector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}$ where this maximum value is attained. 

So first, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/a6/a6165f41eb43e8f6e8fd4399f1c428f73481de9d4b5ec41293f3ec0e4f062fc6.svg)

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=6{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 \\ -5 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/30/30699c4f0abcb099a6f7a76cbd76674757c3f7de313e034d0870d1fce27fdd8c.svg) 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 

![](images/ef/ef14ea5facf5010b99721cf915f44162dfa52e089508fb78c2d02d9aad66f1a4.svg)  

Let's check that this is indeed the vector we were looking for: 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{\text{max}}) & ={(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}-10(\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}})(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})+{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{10}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =6\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c50ae6a7-1f29-5274-bd82-d2d8acfef6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7954 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "08dd4ae6-a6ab-54da-a4ca-840835781b76" :step/math-academy-id :step/next {:db/id 17592186199404}} {:db/id 17592186199396 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_1x_2+x_2^2,
$$

 over the ellipse $4x_1^2+x_2^2=4$ equals $5.$ How can we find a vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which this maximum is attained?

We can find this vector by applying a suitable change of variable. This change of variable should transform our problem into one where we need to maximize a related quadratic form $Q'$ on the unit circle. Let's see how this is done.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](images/7b/7b1fd813963e16887c57d6c10be1bfe288e3209fd3a02ca6e6236b7261feb7b1.svg)

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
{x_1^2}+ \dfrac{x_2^2}{2^2}=1
$$

which  represents an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the $x_2$-axis). 

If we introduce new variables

$$
y_1={x_1}, \qquad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{2},
$$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

![](images/80/80f8e821a60b63dde0f314460adfd31faca5d82315243fb2a3ebdec75bc61538.svg) 

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}=Q'(\mathbf{y}).
$$

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in the new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, the goal is to maximize $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ which we do using our usual methods.  

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $5,$ we have

$$
\max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\max} = 5.
$$

Next, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{max}}=5{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-5I)\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/4b/4b51afece6e21c2fe073a5346557f42f9f03ae3400407d18ed6af3af8f32e310.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get 

![](images/ce/ce571338fc1d83f0b0892a356bca56073c096a1f5191a21a4baef56b6d5a399f.svg) 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$

![](images/80/80f8e821a60b63dde0f314460adfd31faca5d82315243fb2a3ebdec75bc61538.svg)

$$

$$

*The maximum value of a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x},$ when $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$* 

$$
\max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}
$$

*The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}}.$*

**Note:** We'll show only the first part (about the maximum value) since a similar argument can be used to prove the second part (about the minimum value).

Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ symmetric matrix corresponding to a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)\mathbin.$ As a result, there must be an *orthonormal* matrix $P$ such that 

- $D=P^{-1}AP=P^TAP,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

- The diagonal entries of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,$ where $\lambda_{\textrm{max}} = \lambda_1.$

- The columns $\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_n$ of $P$ form an orthonormal set of unit eigenvectors of $A.$ So, $\mathbf{u}_{\textrm{max}} = \mathbf{u}_1.$

Take $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y.$ Since, $P$ is orthonormal, we have

$$
\|\mathbf x\| = \|P \mathbf y \| = \|\mathbf y\|
$$

and

$$
Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T\!A\mathbf x = (P\mathbf y)^T\!A(P\mathbf y) = \mathbf{y}^T (P^T\!AP) \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y}
$$

for all $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

- $\|\mathbf x\| =1 \Longleftrightarrow \|\mathbf y\| =1$ for all $\mathbf y$ such that $\mathbf x=P\mathbf y$

- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\mathbf y)= \mathbf y^T D\mathbf y$ coincide: 

$$
\{\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x: \: \: \|\mathbf x\|=1\}= \{\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y: \: \: \|\mathbf y\|=1\}  \subset \mathbb R
$$

Now, for any unit vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{′}(y) \\  & ={\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & \le {\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\  & ={\lambda }_{\text{max}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that  that 

$$
M = \max \{ Q(\mathbf{x}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{x} \| = 1 \} = \max \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \:  \| \mathbf{y} \| = 1 \} \le \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.
$$

 

On the other hand, if we take ![](images/53/53a051ea36059c9222e717c65adc6531bc313c9807d44a39b262433acfdcbc5c.svg) then $Q(P\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\mathbf{e}_1) = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$

Finally, since $\mathbf{u}_1 = P\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that 
$Q(\mathbf u_1) =  \mathbf e_1^T D \mathbf e_1 = \lambda_{\textrm{max}}.$ 
Therefore, the maximum value is attained at $\mathbf u_{\textrm{max}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "364005f5-f0fc-5d17-9d6b-288d52abe715" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8176 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Main quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}

The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}-4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0d7e6a3a-4e90-51f7-9e6d-1f36e15dea08" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410203}} {:db/id 17592186410200 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410197 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410169} {:answer/id #uuid "3bb153c6-9455-5e09-b9d4-e4c936682c6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410172} {:answer/id #uuid "566bcdea-96b1-557a-bdcd-81a53378a8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410173} {:answer/id #uuid "a93b100e-c392-5adc-a3ed-bee963bcaac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410185} {:answer/id #uuid "b119d151-632a-5e08-8a6e-94f8c7ba763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410186}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410169} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5b0d1a4-b3d8-5bd2-80e4-83dea5aa94c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dea55e7b-1cc0-500b-8640-ae39dddce75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170560" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:db/id 17592186410201 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27fa6c83-fea5-559c-b3af-e6a7e1618346" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "80ab5b9e-fd44-5cd4-b555-7638c14ed974" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410200}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id $$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

"First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =\begin{bmatrix}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{bmatrix}-25\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

"q-170525" :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)=-3{x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+12{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 16 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 16 \\ 16 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-12-\lambda  & 16 \\ 16 & 12-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-12-\lambda )(12-\lambda )-256 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -20)(\lambda +20) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =20,\,-20\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-250.

$$

$$

"Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 0 & -12 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -12 & 0 & 14\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 0 & -12 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -12 & 0 & 14\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 0 & -12 \\ 0 & -19 & 0 \\ -12 & 0 & -6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-20I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d3d621c0-f7fd-55c5-881a-bf98c73f81f7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422489}} {:db/id 17592186422489 :step/content {:db/id 17592186389643 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e97a677c-7cd3-5ab4-a853-3e58af95ef68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389645} {:answer/id #uuid "d626e8f2-6f92-5b4c-b77d-4433976b4f8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389646} {:answer/id #uuid "388c0d7a-2358-5cd2-b7be-8784a5eb4f83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389647} {:answer/id #uuid "5bee8a5d-5168-5c30-886c-aa5b72b8ba65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389648} {:answer/id #uuid "34eaf1be-fb4e-53d6-9abd-f05704e7c071" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186389649}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389648} :answer-field/id #uuid "807b9eea-f22c-56a9-981a-517ef2430f4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389644}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "546ae5ae-d06c-5386-b960-6a8c9d016f97" :question/math-academy-id "q-170514" :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-30{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-50{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+25{x}_{2}^{2}=100,$ is $-250.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have

$$
min\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{min}=-250.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-250:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =\begin{bmatrix}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{bmatrix}+250\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8691c397-86b9-56c4-bc27-77cec1d7f354" :step/next {:db/id 17592186422486}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e97a677c-7cd3-5ab4-a853-3e58af95ef68" :answer/type {:db/id $$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-9{x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-10.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-10:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-10)I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}+10\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}11 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-10)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "92250051-c04a-54d1-8629-4491dfcb275a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442117}} {:db/id 17592186442117 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1579c753-1597-556d-8bd8-51a8deed3084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410166} {:answer/id #uuid "1c96736a-b709-578c-8d05-cc73305aecdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410168} {:answer/id #uuid "31146e93-a5b1-5fe1-90a1-7f9c284f1056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410171} {:answer/id #uuid "5dd5c912-e67d-530f-a2c1-baaeaac814c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410177} {:answer/id #uuid "a21806c6-2164-532f-ac84-142d42881117" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186410184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410168} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dc24884-5d5e-5b11-b5e7-3763c0022ada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410191}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3f433543-b9f1-5f20-b0ed-749a73af3fa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170506" :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{bmatrix}-20\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5f8ca3b8-f2b1-5dda-8678-447d69f170dd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442119}} {:db/id 17592186442119 :step/content {:db/id 17592186378969 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fea291ee-6497-5ad3-94fc-370909961651" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378971} {:answer/id #uuid "d36d82c5-f411-510f-b777-9fca82b43277" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378972} {:answer/id #uuid "34611fcc-fc75-5837-8815-4b563c9bc527" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378973} {:answer/id #uuid "a08c13c3-88ad-550d-9cc8-cabd76a06564" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378974} {:answer/id #uuid "a6d304bd-fbab-5bd6-8c82-afcb34c6646e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378975}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378971} :answer-field/id #uuid "59fbad7d-97f9-581f-9baa-b0e8b8e58fe8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378970}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "6d3c8fe2-1d6d-57e9-bf5c-5e70cb30abf3" :question/math-academy-id "q-170561" :question/problem "The minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}-4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "203e3740-ec3e-5f05-bb23-784b804df740" :step/next {:db/id 17592186502182}} {:db/id 17592186502174 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284645 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "58e43fd8-bedb-54d5-9723-4873762018ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186282444} {:answer/id #uuid "6080b967-b1e5-508e-9eb9-b06f08ffc56b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186282507} {:answer/id #uuid "b44dda1b-d74d-5302-ac25-2322f81791f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186283250} {:answer/id #uuid "f9c243a3-3d78-5363-a946-67271923a982" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186283874} {:answer/id #uuid "fdac630b-fc7e-5910-8320-fe5c826d997e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "17" :db/id 17592186283913}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186282444} :answer-field/id #uuid "b28de760-832c-5bd3-997a-40bc410c2fcb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284244}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "315ff370-acb2-54c0-a94c-7932c53e50d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170525" :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)=-3{x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+12{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 8 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 16 \\ 8 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-12 & 16 \\ 16 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}-12-\lambda  & 16 \\ 16 & 12-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (-12-\lambda )(12-\lambda )-256 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-400 & =0 \\ (\lambda -20)(\lambda +20) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =20,\,-20\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2d9889da-3200-5318-891b-ae6984507147" :step/next {:db/id 17592186502189}} {:db/id 17592186502182 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284641 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "01f3ea30-3f9d-5508-ab40-ee2dba4f0888" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "70" :db/id 17592186281708} {:answer/id #uuid "2a5452df-294d-5701-b4af-bbf16d6e0530" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "50" :db/id 17592186282056} {:answer/id #uuid "4e6d984c-3905-5e24-bf07-c5dd11a46a31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "100" :db/id 17592186282364} {:answer/id #uuid "bb2908d2-0e8d-5999-a64a-a03cd4b68ae9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "90" :db/id 17592186283306} {:answer/id #uuid "c1eb5798-946a-56c8-9937-6c6a91e2207e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "80" :db/id 17592186283374}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186283306} :answer-field/id #uuid "e3ab9ad5-298c-5e24-9d44-dc14f057d818" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284336}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "80991c77-0c00-52ac-bae2-41a3b83ff730" :question/math-academy-id "q-170515" :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-18{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+81{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$

$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -6 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -18 \\ -6 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}18 & -18 \\ -18 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

:question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $0.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The  maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{bmatrix}-0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$  

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a61dcaf7-f154-5c88-a2cc-4dd236b50f6e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186519632}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d9e2ab8-f0d5-5abe-b74e-db6a46609bb7" :answer/type {:db/id "08180a9a-2473-5b5c-bf97-d2ef2156c578" :step/math-academy-id 43194 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199310}} {:db/id 17592186199307 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199474 :tutorial/content "Consider the following repeated integral:

$$
\displaystyle
\int_0^1 \int_0^{1-x} \int_0^{1-x-y} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x
$$

For this repeated integral, the integration domain is the type I region

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 1-x, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1-x-y \right\}
$$

as shown below.

![](images/56/56ef205e4a92cf96d2ddb81635b5776ededf880d4507e68db1d66ae045533705.png)

Suppose we wish to change the order of integration so that we integrate first with respect to $y,$ then over a region $D$ in the $xz$-plane. In other words, we wish to express our repeated integral in the form

$$
\int_0^1 \int_0^{1-x} \int_0^{1-x-y} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x
=
\iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{u_1(x,z)}^{u_2(x,z)} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}A.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x$ to $\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}A,$ we write $R$ as a type III region. 

To visualize $R$ as a type III region, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](images/3c/3c444ce37b1799e950b52789d7837b699938bec602e274fed7c91640a31812a2.png)

The arrow enters the region through the back boundary and leaves through the front boundary:

- The front boundary of the region is

$$
z = 1-x-y,
$$

and writing this in the form $y = u_2(x,z),$ we have

$$
y = 1-x-z.
$$

- The back boundary of the region is $y = 0.$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is 

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (x,z) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 1-x-z \right\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/31/31c74e0c21a02898e584d141e942037cedf392680b9bc3bd84ae8831fb55224c.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $y$ and then over $D,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}{\int }_{0}^{1-x-y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{1-x-z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b266db14-83cd-503a-9a9a-0a046db8b914" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7667 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4ef19e30-5711-5c99-9378-bdff12e2c640" :step/math-academy-id 44543 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199271}} {:db/id 17592186199310 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198396 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198038 :question/id #uuid "15684778-4ac6-5741-b17b-4ba9f8a193e4" :question/math-academy-id "e-12405"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c1eaf02c-e29b-58dd-aa24-8b0bb70183a0" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198969} {:db/id 17592186198970} {:db/id 17592186281480} {:db/id 17592186281481} {:db/id 17592186326734} {:db/id 17592186365185} {:db/id 17592186365206} {:db/id 17592186366104}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Triple Integral by Swapping the Order of Integration"} :step/id #uuid "bdf0c9c2-cbc5-5ca4-8248-c9b49ffdbda4" :step/math-academy-id 44564}] :activity/title "Changing the Order of Integration in Triple Integrals: Changing Region" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198491} {:db/id 17592186199307 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199474 :tutorial/content "Consider the following repeated integral:

Suppose we wish to change the order of integration so that we integrate first with respect to $y,$ then over a region $D$ in the $xz$-plane. In other words, we wish to express our repeated integral in the form

$$
\int_0^1 \int_0^{1-x} \int_0^{1-x-y} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x
=
\iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{u_1(x,z)}^{u_2(x,z)} f(x,y,z) \:\textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}A.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\textrm{d}z\:\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}x$ to $\textrm{d}y\:\textrm{d}A,$ we write $R$ as a type III region. 

To visualize $R$ as a type III region, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](images/3c/3c444ce37b1799e950b52789d7837b699938bec602e274fed7c91640a31812a2.png)

The arrow enters the region through the back boundary and leaves through the front boundary:

- The front boundary of the region is

$$
z = 1-x-y,
$$

and writing this in the form $y = u_2(x,z),$ we have

$$
y = 1-x-z.
$$

- The back boundary of the region is $y = 0.$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is 

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (x,z) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 1-x-z \right\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/31/31c74e0c21a02898e584d141e942037cedf392680b9bc3bd84ae8831fb55224c.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $y$ and then over $D,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}{\int }_{0}^{1-x-y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{1-x-z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.\end{aligned}

"Recall that if the solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $A\mathbf x=\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ lies in $\textrm{Col}(A).$ Furthermore, $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the vector in $\textrm{Col}(A)$ that's closest to $\mathbf b.$ 

In terms of vector spaces, the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$ Therefore, the error vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A).$

![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png)

A similar property holds for weighted least-squares solutions:

*If the solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the least-squares problem $W\!A\mathbf x=W\mathbf{b}$ is unique, then
$A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i,
$$

 
where the $w_i$'s are the weights from the main diagonal of the weight matrix $W.$* 

We previously considered the weighted least-squares problem $W\!Ax=W\mathbf{b},$ where

![](images/d4/d44c48deb0864fb8fd6aa92ce8af408b600de8abf2039a3f3cd7397fabc7d9fe.svg)

It's easy to show (using the usual techniques) that the unique weighted least-squares solution is given by 

![](images/db/db8f62fcb085d8c1fcfc22bb53cb8f22bd9a65b211e5fd5d4017e30bf9bdb4c7.svg)

Computing our error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}ε & =A\hat{x}-b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}10 \\ 4 \\ 14\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 0 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $\mathbf a_1$ and $\mathbf a_2$ denote the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$ 
![](images/3f/3fbafcf3f9d80d2d54089647b2f0239662dcbe56c9ba68539e2303ce752d28ee.svg)

Notice that the error vector $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ is *not* orthogonal to the columns of $A\mathbin{:}$

- Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{1} & =⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}⟩ \\  & =(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\  & =-3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Computing $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf a_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}ε\cdot {a}_{2} & =⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}⟩ \\  & =(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\  & =3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

However, if we check the orthogonality with respect to the *weighted* dot product 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2 x_i y_i = 4x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 + x_3y_3,
\quad
$$

 

we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{⟨ε,{a}_{1}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}⟩}_{W} \\  & =4(1)(1)+(4)(1)+(-4)(2) \\  & =0\,✓ \\ {⟨ε,{a}_{2}⟩}_{W} & ={⟨\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}⟩}_{W} \\  & =4(1)(-1)+(4)(0)+(-4)(-1) \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b}$ is orthogonal to $\textrm{Col}(A)$ with respect to the weighted dot product. We can write this as

$$
A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \perp_W \textrm{Col}(A).
$$

In terms of vector spaces, the vector $A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ is the orthogonal projection with respect to $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_W$ of the vector $\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$ 

Furthermore, the weighted least-squares problem with weight matrix $W$ is equivalent to finding a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\Vert  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \Vert_W
$$

is as small as possible." :tutorial/id #uuid "91e0f414-7785-5748-bba9-04278c6519ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6084 :tutorial/title "A Geometric Interpretation of the Weighted Least-Squares Solution"} :step/id #uuid "373b333f-64bb-5518-823a-a53a7c7b2614" :step/math-academy-id 37006}] :activity/title "Weighted Least-Squares" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162229} {:db/id 17592186163036 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163308 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the least-squares problem $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where

$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$

$$
