$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix},
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -16 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -10\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & ={\begin{bmatrix}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9\cdot 8-(-2)\cdot (-2)}\begin{bmatrix}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{68}\begin{bmatrix}68 \\ -68\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d99942ec-6a5c-5573-82e8-6cbe4cc7bec4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186483475}} {:db/id 17592186483470 :step/content {:db/id 17592186278195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1837262d-ff49-5dc0-83dc-18a2a52a47d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186275702} {:answer/id #uuid "83ad3cee-ea0e-56c1-b1e1-0033f7ef2b3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-17" :db/id 17592186276660} {:answer/id #uuid "a6db5086-e388-525f-b82e-43ab2607f8e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186276982} {:answer/id #uuid "da92de70-9727-5c4f-a7b9-538c8d5065dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186277394} {:answer/id #uuid "ddd8000e-3029-5f03-9736-b53484ed1a2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{17}" :db/id 17592186277423}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186277394} :answer-field/id #uuid "ebadb5d8-fe72-566c-b39f-5c8e9dc439a5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186278139}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "36a6e17d-f83c-53ad-b495-79ac2ba0a0eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-158458" :question/problem "$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {1}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix},
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 1 \\ -6 & -4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 1 \\ -6 & -4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 1 \\ -6 & -4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 4 & -8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 1 \\ -6 & -4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}17 & -34 \\ -34 & 68\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}17 & -34 & 3 \\ -34 & 68 & -6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}17 & -34 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{3}{17}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{17}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{17} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
17a+\frac{b}{c}=17(\frac{3}{17})+\frac{2}{1}=5.

$$

$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}45 & 30 & 60 \\ 30 & 20 & 40\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}45 & 30 & 60 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{4}{3}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$

inequality, we can cube both sides of the inequality.

For example, to solve the inequality

$$
\sqrt[3]{x-2} \leq 4,
$$

we can cube both sides and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\sqrt[3]{x-2})}^{3} & \le {4}^{3} \\ x-2 & \le 64 \\ x & \le 66.\end{aligned}
$$

The reason why we're allowed to cube both sides of an inequality is that cubing preserves the order of numbers. That is to say, if $a < b,$ then $a^3 < b^3.$

To see this concretely, consider the following order of numbers:

$$
-2 < -1 < 0 < 0.5 < 1 < 2 < 3
$$

If we take the cubes of all the numbers above, they stay in the same order:

$$
\underbrace{-8}_{ (-2)^3 } < \underbrace{-1}_{ (-1)^3 } < \underbrace{0}_{ 0^3 } < \underbrace{0.125}_{ (0.5)^3 } < \underbrace{1}_{ 1^3 } < \underbrace{8}_{ 2^3 } < \underbrace{27}_{ 3^3 }
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "372baf4e-1214-5c31-9cee-48762b863105" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4653 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d46966b9-f04d-56e3-9df8-7ed2c4d8af6b" :step/math-academy-id 468025 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158386}} {:db/id 17592186158386 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157442 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157132 :question/id #uuid "813b7b5f-0da8-5a92-b4ff-f7208c5f059f" :question/math-academy-id "e-7654"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "bf6a3dbb-52b3-5384-b640-0fbf29a6cc98" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048784} {:db/id 17592186049986}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157891} {:db/id 17592186157894} {:db/id 17592186250333} {:db/id 17592186294915} {:db/id 17592186294921} {:db/id 17592186294922} {:db/id 17592186354585}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving an Inequality Involving a Cube Root"} :step/id #uuid "fd5a0c08-cb93-5a8d-9608-af5e2a089f47" :step/math-academy-id 468026 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158387}} {:db/id 17592186158387 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158504 :tutorial/content "When we have a square root in an inequality, we *can't* always square both sides. $$
\begin{aligned}(-4)^{2} & ≮{3}^{2} \\ 16 & ≮9\end{aligned}
$$

However, if we're comparing a square root to a negative number, there's no need to take the square root. The key is to remember that the square root of a number is always positive.

- If a square root is less than (or equal to) a negative number, then there is no solution.

For example, if

$$
\sqrt{x+1} < -3,
$$

then there is no solution because the square root $\sqrt{x+1}$ can never be negative.

- If a square root is greater than (or equal to) a negative number, then any number we can substitute into the square root will satisfy the inequality. So, the solution is the domain of the square root.

For example, if

$$
\sqrt{x+1} > -3,
$$

then the solution consists of all $x$ in the domain of $\sqrt{x+1}$ because $\sqrt{x+1}$ is zero or positive for all $x$ in its domain. To find the domain, we recall that the inside of the square root must be greater than or equal to $0{:}$

$$

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "21c64dd2-31f7-5c73-a9b1-a82a67d65615" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4651 :tutorial/title "Comparing a Square Root to a Negative Number"} :step/id #uuid "a7b132c4-8966-5562-a68f-5bcc071c84e8" :step/math-academy-id 468029 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158388}} {:db/id 17592186158388 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157443 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186157133 :question/id #uuid "bc44bc68-a615-5f25-b686-8a775fcac64c" :question/math-academy-id "e-7655"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "24f2c5a5-dc56-5f78-8138-8f7b3a6280e2" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186157890} {:db/id 17592186157892} {:db/id 17592186250334} {:db/id 17592186250335} {:db/id 17592186294865} {:db/id 17592186294923} {:db/id 17592186294924} {:db/id 17592186294959} {:db/id 17592186354587} {:db/id 17592186354588} {:db/id 17592186354589}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving an Inequality Involving a Square Root Compared to a Negative Number"} :step/id #uuid "1c597805-9cb4-559b-bb63-8db421b0801d" :step/math-academy-id 468030 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158389}} {:db/id 17592186158389 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158505 :tutorial/content "If we have an inequality that compares a square root to a non-negative number, we can square both sides of the equation.

For example, consider the following inequality:

$$
\sqrt{x+1} < 3
$$

In this inequality, the square root is being compared to a non-negative number $(3).$ So, we can square both sides of the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\sqrt{x+1})}^{2} & <{3}^{2} \\ x+1 & <9 \\ x & <8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the square root. To find the domain of the square root, we recall that the argument of the square root must be greater than or equal to zero:

$$
x+1 \geq 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x \geq -1
$$

Our solution is $x < 8,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty, 8).$ But the domain of the square root is $x \geq -1,$ which can be expressed as $[-1, \infty).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the square root, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty, 8) \cap [-1, \infty) = [-1, 8)
$$

A.$

Also, since $A^T \! A$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A$ must be always non-negative real numbers.

Let's compute the singular values of the matrix $A,$ given by 

![](images/a9/a9edbe1fee59758c9557d95ea8f62468f9f3cb98449c437a274bdbf5c30f7dc6.svg)

Now, since

- $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix, and

- $A^T$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix,

then $A^T \! A$  must be a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times {\large 3}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A} = 
\underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 2}}{A^T \! A}
$$

Let's now compute our singular values. First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\,0 & \,2 \\ \,\,-2 & \,0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the eigenvalues of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -9)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- When listing the singular values of a matrix, we usually write them in descending order.

- If $A$ is a $m\times n$ matrix, then $A^T A$ is a $n\times n$ positive semi-definite matrix. This means that $A$ has *at most* $n$ distinct singular values." :tutorial/id #uuid "6230f35e-b526-5e84-be30-86c8cdcbd301" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4891 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid $$

$$

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-1) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

Select all that apply.

- **I.** Any $6\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
- **II.** The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}$ has one negative singular value.
- **III.** Any $4\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $6\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a11d8c53-0d85-5382-8004-1a8f6e94884d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186508139}} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046644} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186509031} :activity/id #uuid "25c36865-a3f4-539d-ab87-b42995a49a22" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049462 :topic/id #uuid "f7488799-2322-5ff9-8065-6852954f5eb5" :topic/math-academy-id 3819} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186509001 :step/content {:db/id 17592186493969 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08b31b5f-4d45-56bb-9d27-10f181056843" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186493405} {:answer/id #uuid "1f5ebfbd-349c-5710-ab1d-bffdb6d4d025" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186493445} {:answer/id #uuid "21c0505d-1159-59fb-ba8b-2bd5ac4199de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186493447} {:answer/id #uuid "94c66a12-70a7-529f-ba21-ac7f034b13c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186493623} {:answer/id #uuid "e4ada2c6-ebf0-5d58-9a21-8f0d7d2bddb7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186493752}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493447} :answer-field/id #uuid "6457d0d0-1968-5324-849a-7bcaae3a3d7b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493831}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "dfba6eb1-d0b6-5cbc-ac16-d682a2e1cc93" :question/math-academy-id "q-95286" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $6\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $6$ distinct singular values.

II. Any $8\times 9$ matrix $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

III. The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ has at most two non-negative distinct singular values." :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $6\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $8\times 9$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $9\times 8$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $9\times 9$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{9\times 8}\times {A}_{8\times 9}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{9\times 9}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed, all singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "08b16f9c-1a48-5e48-899f-7bdd30c63128" :step/next {:db/id 17592186509043}} {:db/id 17592186509031 :step/content {:db/id 17592186184876 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15ac2533-62db-535c-8dc9-3e42649cc9f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$10$ and $2$" :db/id 17592186368873} {:answer/id #uuid "40993328-f48a-5d16-8477-6064543ac098" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$3$ and $0$" :db/id 17592186368874} {:answer/id #uuid "02e843f4-0fc7-5f0b-a07b-3fa3bfc2abd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\sqrt{10}$ and $0$" :db/id 17592186368875} {:answer/id #uuid "98d65d3b-180c-559c-9c5f-db57ec8866a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$3$ and $2$" :db/id 17592186368876} {:answer/id #uuid "f0117d76-d5c6-543b-9609-b905ac185a64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$10$ and $0$" :db/id 17592186368877}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186368875} :answer-field/id #uuid "9f0db150-06f0-53a7-8afc-b9734abea2f1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186368872}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5015d1af-a116-557e-a448-94566c652f07" :question/math-academy-id "q-94773" :question/problem "What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & 0 & -12 \\ 0 & 16-\lambda  & 0 \\ -12 & 0 & 16-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (16-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & -12 \\ -12 & 16-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (16-\lambda )((9-\lambda )(16-\lambda )-144) & =0 \\ (16-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda -16\lambda +144-144) & =0 \\ (16-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-25\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -16)(\lambda -25) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =25,\,16,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{9\times 8}\times {A}_{8\times 9}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{9\times 9}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed, all singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

drawn from a population with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2,$ then the sample mean, denoted $\overline{X},$ is given by

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
$$

The sample mean is a random variable whose probability distribution (also called the **sampling distribution**) has an expected value of $\mu\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu
$$

 

In other words, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean $\mu.$

Let's now find the variance of the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}.$ Using the properties of variance for sums of independent random variables, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}] & =\text{Var}[\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}] \\  & ={(\frac{1}{n})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{X}_{i}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \text{Var}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}] \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot (\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+⋯+\text{Var}[{X}_{n}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot ({\sigma }^{2}+{\sigma }^{2}+⋯+{\sigma }^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\cdot n{\sigma }^{2} \\  & =\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize, we have the following important result:

$$
\textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}
$$

It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}.$ What we *do* know is that whatever the sampling distribution of $\overline{X}$ is, it has mean $\mu$ and variance and the standard error is given by

$$

We're told that the nails in the population have lengths $5\,\text{cm}$ and $\text{10}\,\text{cm},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $4:1.$ Therefore, to compute the population mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $4+1=5$ nails only with the following lengths:

$$
5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm}\,10\,\text{cm}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot 5+10) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(20+10) \\  & =\frac{30}{5} \\  & =6\,\text{cm},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot {5}^{2}+{10}^{2})-{6}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(200)-36 \\  & =40-36 \\  & =4\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sample size $n=3,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}=\frac{4}{3}\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}≈1.15\,\text{cm}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1+4\cdot 0.5) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1+2) \\  & =\frac{3}{5} \\  & =$0.6,\end{aligned}

$$

:topic/math-academy-id 3211} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167900 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168037 :tutorial/content "In a homogeneous boundary value problem (BVP) that depends on a parameter $\lambda$, most values of $\lambda$ lead only to the trivial solution $y\equiv 0$.  

The special values of $\lambda$ that produce *nontrivial* solutions are called **eigenvalues**, and the corresponding nontrivial solutions are called **eigenfunctions**.

For example, consider the boundary value problem

$$
y'' - 18\lambda y' + 81\lambda^2y  = 0, \quad y(0) = 0, \quad 4y(3) + 5y'(3) = 0, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 3, \quad \lambda \in\mathbb R.
$$

Let's find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. 

The method for solving the differential equation depends on whether $\lambda = 0$ or $\lambda \neq 0.$ To find the eigenvalues, we must therefore investigate these two possibilities as separate cases.

On the next slide, we will analyze the case where $\lambda = 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1378993d-8bac-50d2-b1ea-4f7c3a1f5ec2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14646 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id {:db/id 17592186391720} {:db/id 17592186397263} {:db/id 17592186413439} {:db/id 17592186522793} {:db/id 17592186543510}] :knowledge-point/title "Trigonometric Eigenfunctions"} :step/id #uuid "dc1ec685-f38d-51a2-9240-4f3a1f1346e1" :step/math-academy-id 592748} {:db/id 17592186167903 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168038 :tutorial/content "When the auxiliary equation has purely imaginary roots, the solutions are trigonometric, and the boundary conditions usually force $\lambda$ to take on a discrete set of values.
So, we again look for values of $\lambda$ that allow a nontrivial solution.

We will now find the **eigenvalues** and **eigenfunctions** for the boundary value problem:

$$
y'' + 9\lambda^2 y = 0, \qquad y'(0) = 0, \quad y(4) = 0, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 4, \quad \lambda \geq 0.
$$

We consider two cases based on the value of $\lambda,$ since they correspond to different forms of the general solution.

**Case 1: $\lambda = 0$**

Setting $\lambda = 0$ gives the equation $y'' = 0.$
Integrating this equation twice gives the general solution:

$$
y = Ax + B.
$$

To apply the boundary conditions, we first find the derivative, $y' = A.$

- Applying $y'(0) = 0$ gives $A = 0.$ The solution becomes $y = B.$

- Applying $y(4) = 0$ then gives $B = 0.$

This yields the trivial solution $y \equiv 0.$ Since an eigenfunction must be nontrivial, $\lambda = 0$ is *not* an eigenvalue.

**Case 2: $\lambda > 0$**

The auxiliary equation is $m^2 + 9\lambda^2 = 0,$ which has roots $m = \pm 3i\lambda.$
The general solution is therefore

$$
y = A\cos (3\lambda x) + B\sin (3\lambda x).
$$

Now we apply the boundary conditions. First, we find the derivative:

$$
y' = -3A\lambda\sin(3\lambda x) + 3B\lambda\cos(3\lambda x).
$$

- Applying the condition $y'(0) = 0$ yields:

$$
-3A\lambda\sin(0) + 3B\lambda\cos(0) = 0 \quad\implies\quad 3B\lambda = 0.
$$

Since we are in the case where $\lambda > 0,$ this requires $B = 0.$ The solution simplifies to:

$$
y = A\cos (3\lambda x).
$$

- Next, applying the condition $y(4) = 0$ yields:
 

$$
A\cos (12\lambda) = 0.
$$

 For a nontrivial solution, we must have $A \neq 0,$ which means we require
 

$$
\cos (12\lambda) = 0.
$$

 This condition is met when $12\lambda$ is an odd multiple of $\pi/2:$

$$
12\lambda = \dfrac{(2n+1)\pi}{2}, \quad \text{for } n = 0, 1, 2, \dots
$$

Solving for $\lambda$ gives the set of **eigenvalues**:

$$
\lambda_n = \dfrac{(2n+1)\pi}{24}.
$$

The corresponding **eigenfunctions** are 

$$
y_n(x) = A_n \cos(3\lambda_n x) , \quad A_n \in \mathbb{R}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2e52b01a-4f53-5d27-9984-dd731308d87d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14650 :tutorial/title "Trigonometric Eigenfunctions"} :step/id #uuid "3e7ba88a-596c-53db-b70b-6b89ee975318" :step/math-academy-id 592751 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167902}} {:db/id 17592186167958 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168055 :tutorial/content "Next, we consider the case $\lambda \neq 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions of 

$$
y'' - 18\lambda y' + 81\lambda^2y  = 0,
$$

for $\lambda \neq 0,$ we set $y = e^{m x}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-18\lambda m+81{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-9\lambda )(m-9\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives a repeated root $m = 9\lambda.$ The general solution is

$$
y = Ae^{9\lambda x} + Bxe^{9\lambda x}.
$$

Now we apply the boundary conditions.

- Applying the first boundary condition, $y(0) = 0,$ yields

$$
y(0) = Ae^{0} + B(0)e^{0} = 0 \quad \implies \quad A = 0.
$$

So, the solution simplifies to $y = Bxe^{9\lambda x}.$ Its derivative is

$$
y' = Be^{9\lambda x} + 9B\lambda xe^{9\lambda x}.
$$

- Applying the second boundary condition, $4y(3) + 5y'(3) = 0,$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}4(3B{e}^{27\lambda })+5(B{e}^{27\lambda }+27B\lambda {e}^{27\lambda }) & =0 \\ 12B{e}^{27\lambda }+5B{e}^{27\lambda }+135B\lambda {e}^{27\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{27\lambda }(17+135\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For a nontrivial solution (an eigenfunction), we require $B\neq 0.$ Since $e^{27\lambda}$ is never zero, we must have

$$
17+135\lambda = 0 \quad \implies \quad \lambda = -\dfrac{17}{135}.
$$

This is our **eigenvalue**. The corresponding **eigenfunction** is

$$
y(x) = Bxe^{9(-17/135) x} = Bxe^{-17x/15}.
$$

Note that any nonzero constant multiple of this function is also an eigenfunction." :tutorial/id #uuid "f4d9fb35-7991-5b49-bfd6-c82ad2ef1c69" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14892 :tutorial/title "Non-Trivial Solution of the Eigenvalue Problem"} :step/id #uuid "81f0071e-ac02-5b8f-ba91-88209136e903" :step/math-academy-id 608067 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167901}} {:db/id 17592186167959 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168056 :tutorial/content "We begin by considering  the case $\lambda = 0.$

Setting $\lambda = 0$ in the original equation, $y'' - 18\lambda y' + 81\lambda^2y  = 0,$ gives a much simpler equation:

$$
y'' = 0.
$$

Integrating this equation twice with respect to $x$ gives the general solution

$$
y = Ax + B.
$$

Now we apply the boundary conditions. 

- The first condition, $y(0) = 0,$ implies:

$$
y(0) = A(0) + B = 0 \quad \implies \quad B=0.
$$

So the solution must be of the form $y = Ax.$

- For the second condition, we first find the derivative, $y' = A.$ Applying the condition $4y(3) + 5y'(3) = 0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}4(A\cdot 3)+5(A) & =0 \\ 12A+5A & =0 \\ 17A & =0\,\,⟹\,\,A=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since both $A=0$ and $B=0,$ we are left with the trivial solution $y \equiv 0.$ By definition, an eigenfunction must be a *nontrivial* solution.

Therefore, $\lambda = 0$ is *not* an eigenvalue. 

Next, we will check the case where $\lambda \neq 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b3458843-3f77-548b-b991-69c3d163d75d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14893 :tutorial/title "Trivial Solution of the Eigenvalue Problem"} :step/id #uuid "d95ffe14-fb14-518a-ac26-6970a9d57acf" :step/math-academy-id 608068 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167958}}] :activity/title "Eigenvalues and Eigenfunctions of Homogeneous BVPs" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166995} {:db/id 17592186167900 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168037 :tutorial/content "In a homogeneous boundary value problem (BVP) that depends on a parameter $\lambda$, most values of $\lambda$ lead only to the trivial solution $y\equiv 0$.  

The special values of $\lambda$ that produce *nontrivial* solutions are called **eigenvalues**, and the corresponding nontrivial solutions are called **eigenfunctions**.

For example, consider the boundary value problem

$$
y'' - 18\lambda y' + 81\lambda^2y  = 0, \quad y(0) = 0, \quad 4y(3) + 5y'(3) = 0, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 3, \quad \lambda \in\mathbb R.
$$

Let's find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. 

The method for solving the differential equation depends on whether $\lambda = 0$ or $\lambda \neq 0.$ To find the eigenvalues, we must therefore investigate these two possibilities as separate cases.

On the next slide, we will analyze the case where $\lambda = 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1378993d-8bac-50d2-b1ea-4f7c3a1f5ec2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14646 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "887046eb-da38-509e-bc00-d45adf4aa497" :step/math-academy-id 592744 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167959}} {:db/id 17592186168037 :tutorial/content "In a homogeneous boundary value problem (BVP) that depends on a parameter $\lambda$, most values of $\lambda$ lead only to the trivial solution $y\equiv 0$.

For example, consider the boundary value problem

$$
y'' - 18\lambda y' + 81\lambda^2y  = 0, \quad y(0) = 0, \quad 4y(3) + 5y'(3) = 0, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 3, \quad \lambda \in\mathbb R.
$$

Let's find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. 

The method for solving the differential equation depends on whether $\lambda = 0$ or $\lambda \neq 0.$ To find the eigenvalues, we must therefore investigate these two possibilities as separate cases.

On the next slide, we will analyze the case where $\lambda = 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1378993d-8bac-50d2-b1ea-4f7c3a1f5ec2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14646 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186167959 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168056 :tutorial/content "We begin by considering  the case $\lambda = 0.$

Setting $\lambda = 0$ in the original equation, $y'' - 18\lambda y' + 81\lambda^2y  = 0,$ gives a much simpler equation:

$$
y'' = 0.
$$

Integrating this equation twice with respect to $x$ gives the general solution

$$
y = Ax + B.
$$

Now we apply the boundary conditions. 

- The first condition, $y(0) = 0,$ implies:

$$
y(0) = A(0) + B = 0 \quad \implies \quad B=0.
$$

So the solution must be of the form $y = Ax.$

- For the second condition, we first find the derivative, $y' = A.$ Applying the condition $4y(3) + 5y'(3) = 0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}4(A\cdot 3)+5(A) & =0 \\ 12A+5A & =0 \\ 17A & =0\,\,⟹\,\,A=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since both $A=0$ and $B=0,$ we are left with the trivial solution $y \equiv 0.$ By definition, an eigenfunction must be a *nontrivial* solution.

Therefore, $\lambda = 0$ is *not* an eigenvalue. 

Next, we will check the case where $\lambda \neq 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b3458843-3f77-548b-b991-69c3d163d75d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14893 :tutorial/title "Trivial Solution of the Eigenvalue Problem"} :step/id #uuid "d95ffe14-fb14-518a-ac26-6970a9d57acf" :step/math-academy-id 608068 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167958}} {:db/id 17592186167901 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166939 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166566 :question/id #uuid "877e1518-96ed-5b31-9e05-22990ce1cb72" :question/math-academy-id "e-21808"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ba4d320f-517e-5dc6-9c6d-02d1c2488472" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049937} {:db/id 17592186050433} {:db/id 17592186050906}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167268} {:db/id 17592186167269} {:db/id 17592186314743} {:db/id 17592186314744} {:db/id 17592186365845} {:db/id 17592186365858} {:db/id 17592186397210} {:db/id 17592186397223} {:db/id 17592186397252} {:db/id 17592186522787}] :knowledge-point/title "Exponential Eigenfunctions"} :step/id #uuid "4251a9bf-5cd3-5cfc-ae56-c1aa466b5998" :step/math-academy-id 592745 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167903}} {:db/id 17592186167903 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168038 :tutorial/content "When the auxiliary equation has purely imaginary roots, the solutions are trigonometric, and the boundary conditions usually force $\lambda$ to take on a discrete set of values.
So, we again look for values of $\lambda$ that allow a nontrivial solution.

We will now find the **eigenvalues** and **eigenfunctions** for the boundary value problem:

$$
y'' + 9\lambda^2 y = 0, \qquad y'(0) = 0, \quad y(4) = 0, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 4, \quad \lambda \geq 0.
$$

We consider two cases based on the value of $\lambda,$ since they correspond to different forms of the general solution.

**Case 1: $\lambda = 0$**

Setting $\lambda = 0$ gives the equation $y'' = 0.$
Integrating this equation twice gives the general solution:

$$
y = Ax + B.
$$

To apply the boundary conditions, we first find the derivative, $y' = A.$

- Applying $y'(0) = 0$ gives $A = 0.$ The solution becomes $y = B.$

- Applying $y(4) = 0$ then gives $B = 0.$

This yields the trivial solution $y \equiv 0.$ Since an eigenfunction must be nontrivial, $\lambda = 0$ is *not* an eigenvalue.

**Case 2: $\lambda > 0$**

The auxiliary equation is $m^2 + 9\lambda^2 = 0,$ which has roots $m = \pm 3i\lambda.$
The general solution is therefore

$$
y = A\cos (3\lambda x) + B\sin (3\lambda x).
$$

Now we apply the boundary conditions. First, we find the derivative:

$$
y' = -3A\lambda\sin(3\lambda x) + 3B\lambda\cos(3\lambda x).
$$

- Applying the condition $y'(0) = 0$ yields:

$$
-3A\lambda\sin(0) + 3B\lambda\cos(0) = 0 \quad\implies\quad 3B\lambda = 0.
$$

Since we are in the case where $\lambda > 0,$ this requires $B = 0.$ The solution simplifies to:

$$
y = A\cos (3\lambda x).
$$

- Next, applying the condition $y(4) = 0$ yields:
 

$$
A\cos (12\lambda) = 0.
$$

 For a nontrivial solution, we must have $A \neq 0,$ which means we require
 

$$
\cos (12\lambda) = 0.
$$

 This condition is met when $12\lambda$ is an odd multiple of $\pi/2:$

$$
12\lambda = \dfrac{(2n+1)\pi}{2}, \quad \text{for } n = 0, 1, 2, \dots
$$

Solving for $\lambda$ gives the set of **eigenvalues**:

$$
\lambda_n = \dfrac{(2n+1)\pi}{24}.
$$

The corresponding **eigenfunctions** are 

$$
y_n(x) = A_n \cos(3\lambda_n x) , \quad A_n \in \mathbb{R}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2e52b01a-4f53-5d27-9984-dd731308d87d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14650 :tutorial/title "Trigonometric Eigenfunctions"} :step/id #uuid "3e7ba88a-596c-53db-b70b-6b89ee975318" :step/math-academy-id 592751 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167902}} {:db/id 17592186167902 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166940 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166565 :question/id #uuid "738bd502-dec6-589b-b198-5040fe7e3906" :question/math-academy-id "e-21806"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "472cbb79-e22b-50d2-a997-93130ff66c22" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048289} {:db/id 17592186049936} {:db/id 17592186049937}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167266} {:db/id 17592186167267} {:db/id 17592186314745} {:db/id 17592186314746} {:db/id 17592186365869} {:db/id 17592186391695} {:db/id 17592186391709} {:db/id 17592186391720} {:db/id 17592186397263} {:db/id 17592186413439} {:db/id 17592186522793} {:db/id 17592186543510}] :knowledge-point/title "Trigonometric Eigenfunctions"} :step/id #uuid "dc1ec685-f38d-51a2-9240-4f3a1f1346e1" :step/math-academy-id 592748} {:db/id 17592186168038 :tutorial/content "When the auxiliary equation has purely imaginary roots, the solutions are trigonometric, and the boundary conditions usually force $\lambda$ to take on a discrete set of values.

To find the fundamental solutions of 

$$
y'' - 18\lambda y' + 81\lambda^2y  = 0,
$$

for $\lambda \neq 0,$ we set $y = e^{m x}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-18\lambda m+81{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-9\lambda )(m-9\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives a repeated root $m = 9\lambda.$ The general solution is

$$
y = Ae^{9\lambda x} + Bxe^{9\lambda x}.
$$

Now we apply the boundary conditions.

- Applying the first boundary condition, $y(0) = 0,$ yields

$$
y(0) = Ae^{0} + B(0)e^{0} = 0 \quad \implies \quad A = 0.
$$

So, the solution simplifies to $y = Bxe^{9\lambda x}.$ Its derivative is

$$
y' = Be^{9\lambda x} + 9B\lambda xe^{9\lambda x}.
$$

- Applying the second boundary condition, $4y(3) + 5y'(3) = 0,$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}4(3B{e}^{27\lambda })+5(B{e}^{27\lambda }+27B\lambda {e}^{27\lambda }) & =0 \\ 12B{e}^{27\lambda }+5B{e}^{27\lambda }+135B\lambda {e}^{27\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{27\lambda }(17+135\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For a nontrivial solution (an eigenfunction), we require $B\neq 0.$ Since $e^{27\lambda}$ is never zero, we must have

$$
17+135\lambda = 0 \quad \implies \quad \lambda = -\dfrac{17}{135}.
$$

This is our **eigenvalue**. The corresponding **eigenfunction** is

$$
y(x) = Bxe^{9(-17/135) x} = Bxe^{-17x/15}.
$$

Note that any nonzero constant multiple of this function is also an eigenfunction." :tutorial/id #uuid "f4d9fb35-7991-5b49-bfd6-c82ad2ef1c69" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14892 :tutorial/title "Non-Trivial Solution of the Eigenvalue Problem"} :step/id #uuid "81f0071e-ac02-5b8f-ba91-88209136e903" :step/math-academy-id 608067 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167901}} {:db/id 17592186168055 :tutorial/content "Next, we consider the case $\lambda \neq 0.$

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c6e87982-ab6f-5e96-94e7-996ae7f3b605" :question/math-academy-id "q-338845" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-10\lambda {y}^{′}+25{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-10\lambda m+25{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-5\lambda )(m-5\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=5\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{5\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{5\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{5\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{5\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda x}+B{e}^{5\lambda x}+5B\lambda x{e}^{5\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda }+B{e}^{5\lambda }+5B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ 5A\lambda +B+5B\lambda  & =0 \\ (5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{10\lambda }+2B{e}^{10\lambda }+2(5A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(5A\lambda +B+10B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+10A\lambda +2B+20B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+(4+20\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}5\lambda  & 1+5\lambda  \\ 1+10\lambda  & 4(1+5\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\lambda \cdot 4(1+5\lambda )-(1+5\lambda )(1+10\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -(1+10\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -1-10\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )(10\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

:question/math-academy-id "q-338917" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+9\lambda y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(3)=0,\,0\le x\le 3,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda >0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(3)=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter corresponding to eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+9\lambda  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 3\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda })
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
{y}^{′}=-3A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda })+3B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-3A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+3B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(3)=0$ yields

$$
-3A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(9\sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
9\sqrt{\lambda }=n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{81}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "35485800-4576-505b-b01c-a3a46dd2634c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186418252}} {:db/id 17592186418252 :step/content {:db/id 17592186391720 :question/answer-fields boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-12\lambda {y}^{′}+36{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}6A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+2(6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+12A\lambda +2B+12B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+B &=0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}6\lambda  & 1 \\ 1+12\lambda  & 3+12\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\lambda (3+12\lambda )-(1)(1+12\lambda ) & =0 \\ 18\lambda +72{\lambda }^{2}-1-12\lambda  & =0 \\ 72{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda -1)(6\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+B=0\,⇒\,A=B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=B{e}^{-x}(x+1).
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+B=0\,⇒\,A=-2B
$$

$$
{y}^{″}-10\lambda {y}^{′}+25{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-10\lambda m+25{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-5\lambda )(m-5\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=5\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{5\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{5\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{5\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{5\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda x}+B{e}^{5\lambda x}+5B\lambda x{e}^{5\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda }+B{e}^{5\lambda }+5B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ 5A\lambda +B+5B\lambda  & =0 \\ (5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{10\lambda }+2B{e}^{10\lambda }+2(5A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(5A\lambda +B+10B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+10A\lambda +2B+20B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+(4+20\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}5\lambda  & 1+5\lambda  \\ 1+10\lambda  & 4(1+5\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\lambda \cdot 4(1+5\lambda )-(1+5\lambda )(1+10\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -(1+10\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -1-10\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )(10\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} :step/id #uuid "10ec5288-96c7-54f4-a406-4dc3fa372454" and the general solution is

$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\lambda (3+12\lambda )-(1)(1+12\lambda ) & =0 \\ 18\lambda +72{\lambda }^{2}-1-12\lambda  & =0 \\ 72{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda -1)(6\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}

:question/math-academy-id "q-338915" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+9\lambda y=0,\,y(0)={y}^{′}(2)=0,\,0\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in {N}_{0}.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda >0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)={y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ does not correspond to an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+9\lambda  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 3\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda })
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
{y}^{′}=3B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
3B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
6\sqrt{\lambda }=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi =\frac{(1+2n)\pi }{2}
$$

for $n\in {N}_{0}.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{(1+2n)^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{144}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1cab76e5-6c1e-514f-a717-d9c42a4499b0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186441530}} {:db/id 17592186441530 :step/content {:db/id 17592186391709 :question/answer-fields :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "868ac7c6-b3e9-504e-8014-26f63ba38d5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-338722" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-8\lambda {y}^{′}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and $y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A+B\cdot 0=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$

"q-338729" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-8\lambda {y}^{′}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda x}+B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda }+B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ 4A\lambda +B+4B\lambda  & =0 \\ (4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{8\lambda }+2B{e}^{8\lambda }+2(4A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+8B\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(4A\lambda +B+8B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+8A\lambda +2B+16B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+(4+16\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}4\lambda  & 1+4\lambda  \\ 1+8\lambda  & 4(1+4\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\lambda \cdot 4(1+4\lambda )-(1+4\lambda )(1+8\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -(1+8\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -1-8\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )(8\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} :step/id #uuid "f8b73451-fda1-5086-8156-fc15d81c7a88" $$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda >0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=y(5)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ does not correspond to an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16\lambda  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 4\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x\sqrt{\lambda })
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(5)=0$ yields

$$
B\operatorname{sin}⁡(20\sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
20\sqrt{\lambda }=n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{400}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8a1cfa99-80c5-51a8-869c-32eec8bcaf70"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "66f6bef1-778e-54ac-8bca-389bd469b61a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value $$
{y}^{″}-8\lambda {y}^{′}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and $y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A+B\cdot 0=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}B{e}^{4\lambda }+B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ 2B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{4\lambda }+2B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{4\lambda }(1+2\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require $B\ne 0.$ Thus, since ${e}^{4\lambda }>0,$ we must have

$$
\lambda =-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the corresponding eigenfunction is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =Bx{e}^{4\lambda x} \\  & =Bx{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f1e042a8-1faa-5865-8d30-e1ea1fe82b24" :step/next {:db/id 17592186441532}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7708b0c3-fc6f-5c9e-b153-91f22444d86e" :answer/type {:db/id "q-338729" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-8\lambda {y}^{′}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda x}+B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}4A\lambda {e}^{4\lambda }+B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ 4A\lambda +B+4B\lambda  & =0 \\ (4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{8\lambda }+2B{e}^{8\lambda }+2(4A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+8B\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(4A\lambda +B+8B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+8A\lambda +2B+16B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+(4+16\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+8\lambda )A+4(1+4\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}4\lambda  & 1+4\lambda  \\ 1+8\lambda  & 4(1+4\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\lambda \cdot 4(1+4\lambda )-(1+4\lambda )(1+8\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -(1+8\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )[16\lambda -1-8\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+4\lambda )(8\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{8},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{4{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(4\lambda )A+(1+4\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} :step/id #uuid "f8b73451-fda1-5086-8156-fc15d81c7a88" {y}^{″}+25{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,0\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ does not correspond to an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+25{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 5\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\lambda x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}=5B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(5\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
5B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(10\lambda )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
10\lambda =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi =\frac{(2n+1)\pi }{2}
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{(2n+1)\pi }{20}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2a58e732-9b94-5f3d-88a9-7a4d9823485f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186522856}} {:db/id 17592186522842 :step/content {:db/id 17592186522787 :question/answer-fields 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d3e4d429-39a4-5565-a491-a0dbab9cb6bc" :question/math-academy-id "q-338898" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-12\lambda {y}^{′}+36{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions.

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda } & =0 \\ 6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda  & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{12\lambda }+2B{e}^{12\lambda }+6(6A\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }+B{e}^{12\lambda }+12B\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+6(6A\lambda +B+12B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+36A\lambda +6B+72B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+8(1+9\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B &=0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}6\lambda  & 1+6\lambda  \\ 1+36\lambda  & 8+72\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\lambda (8+72\lambda )-(1+6\lambda )(1+36\lambda ) & =0 \\ 48\lambda +432{\lambda }^{2}-(1+42\lambda +216{\lambda }^{2}) & =0 \\ 216{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda +1)(18\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0
$$

we get

$$
-\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{1}{2}B=0
$$

which gives $A=B,$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =B{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0
$$

we get

$$
\frac{1}{3}A+\frac{4}{3}B=0\,⇒\,A=-4B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-4B{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3} \\  & =B{e}^{x/3}(x-4) \\  & =C{e}^{x/3}(x-4)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/3}(x-4).$"} :step/id #uuid "4affdd5b-9eb0-5e02-a8fc-15da98d24def" $$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda >0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)={y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not a parameter of the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+4\lambda  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 2\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda })
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
{y}^{′}=2B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
2B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
2\sqrt{\lambda }=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi =\frac{(1+2n)\pi }{2}
$$

for $n\in {N}_{0}.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{(1+2n)^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{16}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
