the Solution to an Initial Value Problem Using The ABM 2-Step Method"} :step/id #uuid "40865e2e-2c40-5544-acb9-196c8c726a9f" :step/math-academy-id 611751 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222414}} {:db/id 17592186222414 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222485 :tutorial/content "Where do the predictor and corrector equations of the two-step Adams–Bashforth–Moulton method come from?

The method consists of two parts: the **Adams-Bashforth** (**AB2**) **predictor**, and **Adams-Moulton** (**AM2**) **corrector**.
We'll begin by deriving the AB2 predictor.

Consider an initial value problem:

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a)=c
$$

Writing the differential equation in integral form, we have

$$
y_\text{new} = y + \int_{x}^{x_\text{new}} f(t, y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Delta y = \int_{x}^{x_\text{new}} f(t, y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Let $\Delta x = x_\text{new} - x$ be the step size, and define the change of variables

$$
\theta = \dfrac{t - x}{\Delta x}.
$$

Then, $t = x + \theta\cdot\Delta x$ and $\mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,$ so the integral becomes

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 f(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x, y(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x))\,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x.
$$

Now, define a new function $g$ of $\theta$ as the integrand:

$$
g(\theta) = f(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x, y(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x))
$$

The Adams formulas result from approximating $g(\theta)$ by a simple function that agrees with its known values, and then integrating that approximation from $0$ to $1.$ We now determine some known values.

- Evaluating $g$ at $\theta = 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}g(0) & =f(x+0\cdot Δx,y(x+0\cdot Δx)) \\  & =f(x,y) \\  & ={y}^{'}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, evaluating $g$ at $\theta=-1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-1) & =f(x+(-1)\cdot Δx,y(x+(-1)\cdot Δx)) \\  & =f(x-Δx,y(x-Δx)) \\  & =f({x}_{-1},y({x}_{-1})) \\  & ={y}_{-1}^{'},\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_{-1}$ is the previous $x$-value and $y'_{-1}$ is the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})).$

Since we have two known values, the simplest reasonable approximation to $g(\theta)$ is a *straight line* passing through these two points: $(0,y')$ and $(-1,y'_{-1}).$
This straight line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\theta ) & ={y}^{'}+\frac{{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}}{0-(-1)}(\theta -0) \\  & ={y}^{'}+({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by integrating this approximation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}p(\theta )\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{'}+({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\theta )\,d\theta  \\  & ={({y}^{'}\theta +\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}){\theta }^{2})|}_{\theta \,=\,0}^{\theta \,=\,1} \\  & ={y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the approximation of the increment in $y$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy={\int }_{0}^{1}g(\theta )\,d\theta \cdot Δx\approx {\int }_{0}^{1}p(\theta )\,d\theta \cdot Δx=\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

It is this approximation that we define as the AB2 predictor:

$$
\Delta y_p = \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
$$

The Adams formulae result from approximating [math]g(\theta)[/math] by a polynomial interpolant constructed from known function values and integrating that polynomial from [math]0[/math] to [math]1.[/math]

Notice that evaluating [math]g[/math] at [math]\theta = 0,[/math] we have
\begin{align*}
g(0) &= f(x + 0\cdot\Delta x, y(x + 0\cdot\Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x, y) \\[5pt]
&= y'.
\end{align*}

Similarly, evaluating [math]g[/math] at [math]\theta=-1[/math], we get
\begin{align*}
g(-1)
&= f(x + (-1)\cdot\Delta x, y(x + (-1)\cdot\Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x - \Delta x, y(x - \Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})) \\[5pt]
&= y'_{-1},
\end{align*}

where [math]y'_{-1}[/math] is the slope at the previous point [math](x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})).[/math]
So, to derive the AB2 predictor, we can approximate [math]g(\theta)[/math] by a *linear* interpolant using its values at [math]\theta=0[/math] and [math]\theta=-1.[/math]

The Lagrange basis polynomials are
\[
\ell_0(\theta) = \theta + 1,\qquad
\ell_{-1}(\theta) = -\theta,
\]

so the interpolant is
\begin{align*}
p(\theta) &= g(0)\ell_0(\theta) - g(-1)\ell_{-1}(\theta) \\[5pt]
&= y'\cdot(\theta + 1) - y'_{-1}\cdot\theta.
\end{align*}

Finally, by integrating the interpolant, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta
&= \int_0^1 \big(y'\cdot(\theta + 1) - y'_{-1}\cdot\theta\big) \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= y'\int_0^1 (\theta + 1) \,\mathrm{d}\theta - y'_{-1} \int_0^1 \theta \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= y'\left[\dfrac12\theta^2 + \theta\right]_0^1 - y'_{-1}\left[\dfrac12\theta^2\right]_0^1 \\[5pt]
&= y'\left(\dfrac12 + 1 - 0\right) - y'_{-1}\left(\dfrac12 - 0\right) \\[5pt]
&= \dfrac32y' - \dfrac12y'_{-1}.
\end{align*}

Therefore, the AB2 predictor is
\begin{align*}
\Delta y \approx \Delta y_p &= \int_0^1 p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta \cdot \Delta x \\[5pt]
&= \left(\dfrac32y' - \dfrac12y'_{-1}\right)\cdot\Delta x \\[5pt]
&= \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "dee56e00-8f80-598d-a5ea-b99a6322bddd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14478 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the AB2 Predictor"} :step/id #uuid "d6baca6f-a078-54e6-b8c4-a3e52eb82476" :step/math-academy-id 611754 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222415}} {:db/id 17592186222415 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222486 :tutorial/content "So far, we have derived the AB2 predictor. We are left to derive the AM2 corrector.

Recall that we wrote the differential equation in integral form as

$$
y_\text{new} = y + \int_x^{x_\text{new}} f(t,y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Delta y = \int_x^{x_\text{new}} f(t,y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

With the change of variables

$$
\theta = \dfrac{t-x}{\Delta x},
$$

we had $t = x + \theta\cdot\Delta x$ and $\mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,$ so

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 f(x+\theta\Delta x,y(x+\theta\Delta x))\,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,
$$

and we defined

$$
g(\theta) = f(x+\theta\Delta x,y(x+\theta\Delta x)).
$$

For the predictor, we considered two known values of $g(\theta){:}$ 

- For $\theta = 0,$ we have $g(0) = y'.$

- For $\theta = -1,$ we have $g(-1) = y'_{-1}.$

Then, we approximated $g$ with a linear function passing through these two points.

Now, for the corrector, we use *three* known values, and approximate $g(\theta)$ by a *quadratic* passing through these three points.

To obtain a third value, we also want the slope at the *new* $x$-value $x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x.$ But, the true value $y_\text{new}$ is not yet known.

Instead, we evaluate the slope at the new point estimated by the AB2 predictor! This corresponds to $\theta = 1{:}$

$$
g(1) = f(x + \Delta x, y(x + \Delta x)) \approx f(x_\text{new}, y_p) = y'_p,
$$

where $y_p$ is the new $y$-value predicted by AB2, and $y'_p$ is the slope evaluated at $(x_\text{new}, y_p).$
So, our three points are

$$
(-1,y'_{-1}), \quad (0,y'), \quad (1,y'_p).
$$

Let $q(\theta)$ be the quadratic that passes through these three points. After simplifying, this quadratic can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}q(\theta ) & =\frac{1}{2}\theta (\theta +1){y}_{p}^{'}-(\theta -1)(\theta +1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}\theta (\theta -1){y}_{-1}^{'} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}+\theta ){y}_{p}^{'}-({\theta }^{2}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}-\theta ){y}_{-1}^{'}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate this approximation from $0$ to $1{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}q(\theta )\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}+\theta ){y}_{p}^{'}-({\theta }^{2}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}-\theta ){y}_{-1}^{'})\,d\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2}){y}_{p}^{'}-(\frac{1}{3}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}){y}_{-1}^{'}-0 \\  & =\frac{5}{12}{y}_{p}^{'}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{'}-\frac{1}{12}{y}_{-1}^{'} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{'}+8{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the approximation of the increment in $y$ is

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 g(\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x
\approx \int_0^1 q(\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x
= \dfrac1{12}(5y'_p + 8y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
$$

It is this approximation that we use as the AM2 corrector. Putting it together, the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{'}+8{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5aa97723-f737-5f47-be29-c04919e09c0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14479 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the AM2 Corrector"} :step/id #uuid "5990a7fa-57e1-5d5e-9ae3-587f865f923b" :step/math-academy-id 611755}] :activity/title "The ABM2 Method" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221477} {:db/id 17592186222406 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222483 :tutorial/content "For a first-order initial value problem, we have already seen ways to approximate the increment in $y$ over a step, including:

- the modified Euler method, which predicts using Euler's method and then corrects that prediction, and

- the RK4 method, which combines several slope evaluations within a single step.

Another group of methods, called the **Adams-Bashforth-Moulton methods**, takes a different approach. Rather than computing multiple slopes at new points, these methods reuse slopes from previous steps in a predictor-corrector framework, giving high accuracy with relatively little additional work.

In this lesson, we'll focus on one of the simplest: the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method. For an initial value problem

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a) = c,
$$

the predictor equation of the **$2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method** (**ABM $2$-step**) with step size $\Delta x$ is

$$
\Delta y_p = \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1}) \cdot \Delta x,
$$

where

- $y' = f(x,y)$ is the slope at the current point $(x,y),$ and

- $y'_{-1} = f(x_{-1}, y_{-1})$ is the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}),$ where $x_{-1} = x-\Delta x.$

The initially predicted new $y$-value is then given by $y_p = y + \Delta y_p.$

Since ABM $2$-step uses the slope from the previous step, it cannot be started from a single initial condition alone. 
Instead, we initialize the method by computing the first step with a one-step method, typically the RK4 method.

Once the prediction $y_p$ is computed, we apply a corrector equation to refine our approximation. We'll return to this step shortly.
Before that, let's see an example of how to apply the predictor equation." :tutorial/id #uuid "50a2f37b-38d8-5a6f-bc13-9086af674ed7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14412 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5af445aa-9ec9-5489-9176-c4332bff0a03" :step/math-academy-id 611738 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222407}} {:db/id 17592186222483 :tutorial/content "For a first-order initial value problem, we have already seen ways to approximate the increment in $y$ over a step, including:

- the modified Euler method, which predicts using Euler's method and then corrects that prediction, and

- the RK4 method, which combines several slope evaluations within a single step.

Another group of methods, called the **Adams-Bashforth-Moulton methods**, takes a different approach. Rather than computing multiple slopes at new points, these methods reuse slopes from previous steps in a predictor-corrector framework, giving high accuracy with relatively little additional work.

In this lesson, we'll focus on one of the simplest: the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method. For an initial value problem

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a) = c,
$$

the predictor equation of the **$2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method** (**ABM $2$-step**) with step size $\Delta x$ is

$$
\Delta y_p = \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1}) \cdot \Delta x,
$$

where

- $y' = f(x,y)$ is the slope at the current point $(x,y),$ and

- $y'_{-1} = f(x_{-1}, y_{-1})$ is the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}),$ where $x_{-1} = x-\Delta x.$

The initially predicted new $y$-value is then given by $y_p = y + \Delta y_p.$

Since ABM $2$-step uses the slope from the previous step, it cannot be started from a single initial condition alone. 
Instead, we initialize the method by computing the first step with a one-step method, typically the RK4 method.

Once the prediction $y_p$ is computed, we apply a corrector equation to refine our approximation. We'll return to this step shortly.
Before that, let's see an example of how to apply the predictor equation." :tutorial/id #uuid "50a2f37b-38d8-5a6f-bc13-9086af674ed7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14412 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186222407 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222510 :tutorial/content "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
y' = 4x - 2y, \qquad y(0) = 1
$$

Let's begin the process of applying the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method to approximate the value of $y(1).$

We know $y(0)$ and wish to estimate $y(1).$ Since the method takes $2$ steps (one to initialize, one to approximate), we will use a step size of

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{1-0}2 = \dfrac12.
$$

We will use a table to keep track of known values. First, we add the initial condition data:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  |  |  |

Next, we initialize the ABM $2$-step method by making a preliminary step with a one-step method.

Applying the RK4 method with step size $\Delta x = \dfrac12,$ we obtain the slope $y'=-2,$ increment $\Delta y = -\dfrac14,$ and approximation

$$
y\left(\dfrac12\right)\approx 1 + \left(-\dfrac14\right) = \dfrac34.
$$

We add the slope to the table, and the approximation in a new row.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ |  |  |  |

Note that, since RK4 is not a predictor-corrector method, there is no increment $\Delta y_p$ or predictor $y_p$ for this step. So, we leave these entries in the first row blank.

Now, we continue from this point, using the ABM $2$-step method.
First, we compute the value of $y'$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =4x-2y \\  & =4\cdot (\frac{1}{2})-2\cdot (\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ |  |  |

From the table, we see that the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}) = \left(0, 1\right)$ is $y'_{-1} = -2.$

Next, we compute $\Delta y_p$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot (\frac{1}{2})-(-2))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{7}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this value to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ |  |

Hence, according to the predictor equation, the initially predicted new $y$-value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{7}{8} \\  & =\frac{13}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the completed table is as given below.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ |

Therefore, our initial prediction for $y(1)$ is $y_p = \dfrac{13}8.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3c403981-071d-5b27-8ff8-99c1ea98715b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14615 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "fb2bf195-d713-5c11-b38c-0b93be4ea2b8" :step/math-academy-id 611739 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222408}} {:db/id 17592186222510 :tutorial/content "Consider the following initial value problem:

Next, we initialize the ABM $2$-step method by making a preliminary step with a one-step method.

Applying the RK4 method with step size $\Delta x = \dfrac12,$ we obtain the slope $y'=-2,$ increment $\Delta y = -\dfrac14,$ and approximation

y\left(\dfrac12\right)\approx 1 + \left(-\dfrac14\right) = \dfrac34.
$$

We add the slope to the table, and the approximation in a new row.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ |  |  |  |

Note that, since RK4 is not a predictor-corrector method, there is no increment $\Delta y_p$ or predictor $y_p$ for this step. So, we leave these entries in the first row blank.

Now, we continue from this point, using the ABM $2$-step method.
First, we compute the value of $y'$ according to the given rule:

\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =4x-2y \\  & =4\cdot (\frac{1}{2})-2\cdot (\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ |  |  |

From the table, we see that the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}) = \left(0, 1\right)$ is $y'_{-1} = -2.$

Next, we compute $\Delta y_p$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot (\frac{1}{2})-(-2))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{7}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this value to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ |  |

Hence, according to the predictor equation, the initially predicted new $y$-value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{7}{8} \\  & =\frac{13}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the completed table is as given below.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ |

Therefore, our initial prediction for $y(1)$ is $y_p = \dfrac{13}8.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3c403981-071d-5b27-8ff8-99c1ea98715b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14615 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:db/id 17592186222408 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221458 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221161 :question/id #uuid "c736760f-414e-5ab2-adfa-c09acce10d5e" :question/math-academy-id "e-21539"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "874de02f-c5be-54ed-8d66-a3b1f1f23c9a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049048} {:db/id 17592186050891}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221937} {:db/id 17592186221958} {:db/id 17592186308367} {:db/id 17592186308372} {:db/id 17592186308373}] :knowledge-point/title "Completing a Table Using the Predictor Equation of the ABM 2-Step Method"} :step/id #uuid "183435e5-3131-5485-8b09-dfbc5b6bc6b9" :step/math-academy-id 611740 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222409}} {:db/id 17592186222409 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222479 :tutorial/content "For an initial value problem

$$
y' = 4x-2y, \qquad y(0) = 1
$$

We will now complete our approximation of the value of $y(1)$ using the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method.

First, recall that we previously initialized with the RK4 method and completed the predictor step of the ABM $2$-step method, resulting in the following values:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ |  |  |

Now, the slope at the point $(x_\text{new},y_p) = \left(\dfrac12+\dfrac12, \dfrac{13}8\right) = \left(1, \dfrac{13}8\right)$ estimated by the predictor is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{'} & =4{x}_{\text{new}}-2{y}_{p} \\  & =4\cdot 1-2\cdot \frac{13}{8} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ | $\dfrac34$ |  |

Looking at the partially filled table, we note the following:

- From the second row, the slope at the current point $(x, y) = \left(\dfrac12, \dfrac34\right)$ is $y' = \dfrac12.$

- From the first row, the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}) = \left(0, 1\right)$ is $y'_{-1} = -2.$

Finally, we compute $\Delta y$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{'}+8{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot \frac{3}{4}+8\cdot \frac{1}{2}-(-2))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}\cdot \frac{39}{4} \\  & =\frac{13}{32}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the completed row is as given below.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac{13}{32}$ |

We know the value of $x$ in the next row is $x_\text{new}=1.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $\Delta y$ to $y{:}$

$$
y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y = \dfrac34 + \dfrac{13}{32} = \dfrac{37}{32}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac{13}{32}$ |
| $1$ | $\dfrac{37}{32}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(1) \approx \dfrac{37}{32}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "098a5bb7-0ece-59ec-8400-a8e3efe1b00a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14385 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "702af9a1-f869-585a-9d62-8b4e15161407" :step/math-academy-id 611744 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222411}} {:db/id 17592186222480 :tutorial/content "Let's return to the following initial value problem:

"40865e2e-2c40-5544-acb9-196c8c726a9f" :step/math-academy-id 611751 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222414}} {:db/id 17592186222414 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222485 :tutorial/content "Where do the predictor and corrector equations of the two-step Adams–Bashforth–Moulton method come from?

The method consists of two parts: the **Adams-Bashforth** (**AB2**) **predictor**, and **Adams-Moulton** (**AM2**) **corrector**.
We'll begin by deriving the AB2 predictor.

Consider an initial value problem:

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a)=c
$$

Writing the differential equation in integral form, we have

$$
y_\text{new} = y + \int_{x}^{x_\text{new}} f(t, y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Delta y = \int_{x}^{x_\text{new}} f(t, y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Let $\Delta x = x_\text{new} - x$ be the step size, and define the change of variables

$$
\theta = \dfrac{t - x}{\Delta x}.
$$

Then, $t = x + \theta\cdot\Delta x$ and $\mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,$ so the integral becomes

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 f(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x, y(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x))\,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x.
$$

Now, define a new function $g$ of $\theta$ as the integrand:

$$
g(\theta) = f(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x, y(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x))
$$

The Adams formulas result from approximating $g(\theta)$ by a simple function that agrees with its known values, and then integrating that approximation from $0$ to $1.$ We now determine some known values.

- Evaluating $g$ at $\theta = 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}g(0) & =f(x+0\cdot Δx,y(x+0\cdot Δx)) \\  & =f(x,y) \\  & ={y}^{'}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, evaluating $g$ at $\theta=-1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-1) & =f(x+(-1)\cdot Δx,y(x+(-1)\cdot Δx)) \\  & =f(x-Δx,y(x-Δx)) \\  & =f({x}_{-1},y({x}_{-1})) \\  & ={y}_{-1}^{'},\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_{-1}$ is the previous $x$-value and $y'_{-1}$ is the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})).$

Since we have two known values, the simplest reasonable approximation to $g(\theta)$ is a *straight line* passing through these two points: $(0,y')$ and $(-1,y'_{-1}).$
This straight line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\theta ) & ={y}^{'}+\frac{{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}}{0-(-1)}(\theta -0) \\  & ={y}^{'}+({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by integrating this approximation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}p(\theta )\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{'}+({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\theta )\,d\theta  \\  & ={({y}^{'}\theta +\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}){\theta }^{2})|}_{\theta \,=\,0}^{\theta \,=\,1} \\  & ={y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the approximation of the increment in $y$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy={\int }_{0}^{1}g(\theta )\,d\theta \cdot Δx\approx {\int }_{0}^{1}p(\theta )\,d\theta \cdot Δx=\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

It is this approximation that we define as the AB2 predictor:

$$
\Delta y_p = \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
$$

The Adams formulae result from approximating [math]g(\theta)[/math] by a polynomial interpolant constructed from known function values and integrating that polynomial from [math]0[/math] to [math]1.[/math]

Notice that evaluating [math]g[/math] at [math]\theta = 0,[/math] we have
\begin{align*}
g(0) &= f(x + 0\cdot\Delta x, y(x + 0\cdot\Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x, y) \\[5pt]
&= y'.
\end{align*}

Similarly, evaluating [math]g[/math] at [math]\theta=-1[/math], we get
\begin{align*}
g(-1)
&= f(x + (-1)\cdot\Delta x, y(x + (-1)\cdot\Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x - \Delta x, y(x - \Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})) \\[5pt]
&= y'_{-1},
\end{align*}

where [math]y'_{-1}[/math] is the slope at the previous point [math](x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})).[/math]
So, to derive the AB2 predictor, we can approximate [math]g(\theta)[/math] by a *linear* interpolant using its values at [math]\theta=0[/math] and [math]\theta=-1.[/math]

The Lagrange basis polynomials are
\[
\ell_0(\theta) = \theta + 1,\qquad
\ell_{-1}(\theta) = -\theta,
\]

so the interpolant is
\begin{align*}
p(\theta) &= g(0)\ell_0(\theta) - g(-1)\ell_{-1}(\theta) \\[5pt]
&= y'\cdot(\theta + 1) - y'_{-1}\cdot\theta.
\end{align*}

Finally, by integrating the interpolant, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta
&= \int_0^1 \big(y'\cdot(\theta + 1) - y'_{-1}\cdot\theta\big) \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= y'\int_0^1 (\theta + 1) \,\mathrm{d}\theta - y'_{-1} \int_0^1 \theta \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= y'\left[\dfrac12\theta^2 + \theta\right]_0^1 - y'_{-1}\left[\dfrac12\theta^2\right]_0^1 \\[5pt]
&= y'\left(\dfrac12 + 1 - 0\right) - y'_{-1}\left(\dfrac12 - 0\right) \\[5pt]
&= \dfrac32y' - \dfrac12y'_{-1}.
\end{align*}

Therefore, the AB2 predictor is
\begin{align*}
\Delta y \approx \Delta y_p &= \int_0^1 p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta \cdot \Delta x \\[5pt]
&= \left(\dfrac32y' - \dfrac12y'_{-1}\right)\cdot\Delta x \\[5pt]
&= \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "dee56e00-8f80-598d-a5ea-b99a6322bddd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14478 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the AB2 Predictor"} :step/id #uuid "d6baca6f-a078-54e6-b8c4-a3e52eb82476" :step/math-academy-id 611754 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222415}} {:db/id 17592186222485 :tutorial/content "Where do the predictor and corrector equations of the two-step Adams–Bashforth–Moulton method come from?

\begin{aligned}g(-1) & =f(x+(-1)\cdot Δx,y(x+(-1)\cdot Δx)) \\  & =f(x-Δx,y(x-Δx)) \\  & =f({x}_{-1},y({x}_{-1})) \\  & ={y}_{-1}^{'},\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_{-1}$ is the previous $x$-value and $y'_{-1}$ is the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})).$

Since we have two known values, the simplest reasonable approximation to $g(\theta)$ is a *straight line* passing through these two points: $(0,y')$ and $(-1,y'_{-1}).$
This straight line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\theta ) & ={y}^{'}+\frac{{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}}{0-(-1)}(\theta -0) \\  & ={y}^{'}+({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by integrating this approximation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}p(\theta )\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{'}+({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\theta )\,d\theta  \\  & ={({y}^{'}\theta +\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}){\theta }^{2})|}_{\theta \,=\,0}^{\theta \,=\,1} \\  & ={y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the approximation of the increment in $y$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy={\int }_{0}^{1}g(\theta )\,d\theta \cdot Δx\approx {\int }_{0}^{1}p(\theta )\,d\theta \cdot Δx=\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

It is this approximation that we define as the AB2 predictor:

$$
\Delta y_p = \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
$$

The Adams formulae result from approximating [math]g(\theta)[/math] by a polynomial interpolant constructed from known function values and integrating that polynomial from [math]0[/math] to [math]1.[/math]

Notice that evaluating [math]g[/math] at [math]\theta = 0,[/math] we have
\begin{align*}
g(0) &= f(x + 0\cdot\Delta x, y(x + 0\cdot\Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x, y) \\[5pt]
&= y'.
\end{align*}

Similarly, evaluating [math]g[/math] at [math]\theta=-1[/math], we get
\begin{align*}
g(-1)
&= f(x + (-1)\cdot\Delta x, y(x + (-1)\cdot\Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x - \Delta x, y(x - \Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})) \\[5pt]
&= y'_{-1},
\end{align*}

where [math]y'_{-1}[/math] is the slope at the previous point [math](x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})).[/math]
So, to derive the AB2 predictor, we can approximate [math]g(\theta)[/math] by a *linear* interpolant using its values at [math]\theta=0[/math] and [math]\theta=-1.[/math]

The Lagrange basis polynomials are
\[
\ell_0(\theta) = \theta + 1,\qquad
\ell_{-1}(\theta) = -\theta,
\]

so the interpolant is
\begin{align*}
p(\theta) &= g(0)\ell_0(\theta) - g(-1)\ell_{-1}(\theta) \\[5pt]
&= y'\cdot(\theta + 1) - y'_{-1}\cdot\theta.
\end{align*}

Finally, by integrating the interpolant, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta
&= \int_0^1 \big(y'\cdot(\theta + 1) - y'_{-1}\cdot\theta\big) \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= y'\int_0^1 (\theta + 1) \,\mathrm{d}\theta - y'_{-1} \int_0^1 \theta \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= y'\left[\dfrac12\theta^2 + \theta\right]_0^1 - y'_{-1}\left[\dfrac12\theta^2\right]_0^1 \\[5pt]
&= y'\left(\dfrac12 + 1 - 0\right) - y'_{-1}\left(\dfrac12 - 0\right) \\[5pt]
&= \dfrac32y' - \dfrac12y'_{-1}.
\end{align*}

Therefore, the AB2 predictor is
\begin{align*}
\Delta y \approx \Delta y_p &= \int_0^1 p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta \cdot \Delta x \\[5pt]
&= \left(\dfrac32y' - \dfrac12y'_{-1}\right)\cdot\Delta x \\[5pt]
&= \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "dee56e00-8f80-598d-a5ea-b99a6322bddd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14478 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the AB2 Predictor"} {:db/id 17592186222415 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222486 :tutorial/content "So far, we have derived the AB2 predictor. We are left to derive the AM2 corrector.

Recall that we wrote the differential equation in integral form as

$$
y_\text{new} = y + \int_x^{x_\text{new}} f(t,y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Delta y = \int_x^{x_\text{new}} f(t,y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

With the change of variables

$$
\theta = \dfrac{t-x}{\Delta x},
$$

we had $t = x + \theta\cdot\Delta x$ and $\mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,$ so

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 f(x+\theta\Delta x,y(x+\theta\Delta x))\,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,
$$

and we defined

$$
g(\theta) = f(x+\theta\Delta x,y(x+\theta\Delta x)).
$$

For the predictor, we considered two known values of $g(\theta){:}$ 

- For $\theta = 0,$ we have $g(0) = y'.$

- For $\theta = -1,$ we have $g(-1) = y'_{-1}.$

Then, we approximated $g$ with a linear function passing through these two points.

Now, for the corrector, we use *three* known values, and approximate $g(\theta)$ by a *quadratic* passing through these three points.

To obtain a third value, we also want the slope at the *new* $x$-value $x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x.$ But, the true value $y_\text{new}$ is not yet known.

Instead, we evaluate the slope at the new point estimated by the AB2 predictor! This corresponds to $\theta = 1{:}$

$$
g(1) = f(x + \Delta x, y(x + \Delta x)) \approx f(x_\text{new}, y_p) = y'_p,
$$

where $y_p$ is the new $y$-value predicted by AB2, and $y'_p$ is the slope evaluated at $(x_\text{new}, y_p).$
So, our three points are

$$
(-1,y'_{-1}), \quad (0,y'), \quad (1,y'_p).
$$

Let $q(\theta)$ be the quadratic that passes through these three points. After simplifying, this quadratic can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}q(\theta ) & =\frac{1}{2}\theta (\theta +1){y}_{p}^{'}-(\theta -1)(\theta +1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}\theta (\theta -1){y}_{-1}^{'} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}+\theta ){y}_{p}^{'}-({\theta }^{2}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}-\theta ){y}_{-1}^{'}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate this approximation from $0$ to $1{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}q(\theta )\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}+\theta ){y}_{p}^{'}-({\theta }^{2}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}-\theta ){y}_{-1}^{'})\,d\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2}){y}_{p}^{'}-(\frac{1}{3}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}){y}_{-1}^{'}-0 \\  & =\frac{5}{12}{y}_{p}^{'}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{'}-\frac{1}{12}{y}_{-1}^{'} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{'}+8{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the approximation of the increment in $y$ is

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 g(\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x
\approx \int_0^1 q(\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x
= \dfrac1{12}(5y'_p + 8y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
$$

It is this approximation that we use as the AM2 corrector. Putting it together, the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{'}+8{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5aa97723-f737-5f47-be29-c04919e09c0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14479 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the AM2 Corrector"} :step/id #uuid "5990a7fa-57e1-5d5e-9ae3-587f865f923b" :step/math-academy-id 611755} {:db/id 17592186222486 :tutorial/content "So far, we have derived the AB2 predictor. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5aa97723-f737-5f47-be29-c04919e09c0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14479 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the AM2 Corrector"} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186231839} :activity/id #uuid "b8c77116-13b1-5351-9553-d047fa93cd04" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049590 :topic/id #uuid "02cc8363-d667-570b-9679-eb87a01109a9" :topic/math-academy-id 6728} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186231839 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231995 :tutorial/content "In previous lessons, we solved second-order initial value problems using Laplace transforms when the forcing term was an ordinary function of $t.$

In this lesson, we extend the same method to **time-delayed forcing**, where the right-hand side turns on at a specific time. This type of forcing is modeled using the **unit step function**.

For a fixed constant $a>0,$ we write $$u_a(t) = u(t-a),$$ which represents a signal that is zero for $t< a$ and turns on at $t = a.$ For example, $u(t-3)$ remains zero until $t=3,$ at which point it jumps to $1.$

When a second-order differential equation includes a term involving $u_a(t),$ we still begin by taking the Laplace transform of both sides and solving for $Y(s)=\mathcal L\{y(t)\}$ (for $s>0$). The left-hand side is handled exactly as before, using the Laplace transforms of derivatives and the given initial conditions.

The main new idea is how the unit step function affects the transform of the forcing term. We will see how to account for this delay and how it changes the algebraic equation for $Y(s).$ To do this, we first need to determine the transform of the step function itself. Let's find some Laplace transforms." :tutorial/id #uuid "932cf723-31f5-5d76-95e4-d384feb59c11" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14810 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c3d26acf-ed42-5d5f-9088-64b3a8a9e309" :step/math-academy-id 612666 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231840}} {:db/id 17592186231840 :step/content {:db/id 17592186232000 :tutorial/content "Consider a second-order initial value problem with step function forcing, such as $$y'' + y = u_2(t), \qquad y(0)=0,\qquad y'(0)=0,$$ where $u_2(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.

**Step 1: Transform the left-hand side.**

We begin by taking the Laplace transform of both sides. Let $Y(s)=\mathcal L\{y(t)\}.$ Using the formula for the second derivative and the initial conditions, we have $$\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y(s)-sy(0)-y'(0) = s^2Y(s).$$

**Step 2: Transform the right-hand side.**

From the table of Laplace transforms, the unit step function satisfies $$\mathcal L\{u_2(t)\}=\frac{e^{-2s}}{s},$$ which is valid for $s>0.$

**Step 3: Solve for $Y(s).$**

Substituting these results into the transformed equation gives $$s^2Y(s)+Y(s)=\frac{e^{-2s}}{s}.$$ We now collect terms and solve algebraically for $Y(s){:}$ $$\begin{aligned}({s}^{2}+1)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s({s}^{2}+1)}\end{aligned}$$

Aside from the exponential factor $e^{-2s},$ the steps are exactly the same as in problems without time delay." :tutorial/id #uuid "f7be86fb-5367-564f-906a-5ce064205685" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14834 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "f07d73a0-6354-56ab-81e4-4b5131af3c8c" :step/math-academy-id 612667 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231841}} {:db/id 17592186231841 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231432 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231403 :question/id #uuid "7ff7cc10-3649-5ffe-9a8a-6aedd7954ea5" :question/math-academy-id "e-6664"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0baa73e5-19ee-5a80-bd02-cc9678615d60" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048194} {:db/id 17592186049950}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231558} {:db/id 17592186231778} {:db/id 17592186377431} {:db/id 17592186377438} {:db/id 17592186377445} {:db/id 17592186377452}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Laplace Transform of a Second-Order ODE With Step Function Forcing"} :step/id #uuid "8145dfa8-c039-550b-be43-1fa940e25360" :step/math-academy-id 612668 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231842}} {:db/id 17592186231842 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231998 :tutorial/content "In the first-order case, we saw that a time delay in the forcing term appears in the $s$-domain as a factor of $e^{-as},$ and that we can handle this using the second shifting theorem.

The same idea applies when working with **second-order** differential equations.

Consider the initial value problem $$y'' + 4y = 7u_2(t)e^{-2(t-2)}, \qquad y(0)=0,\qquad y'(0)=0,$$ where $u_2(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.

Again, we begin by taking the Laplace transform of both sides and writing $$Y(s)=\mathcal L\{y(t)\}.$$ Using the initial conditions, the left-hand side becomes $$\mathcal L\{y''\}+4\mathcal L\{y\}=s^2Y(s)+4Y(s).$$

The forcing term has the form $$u_2(t)\,f(t-2),$$ where $$f(t-2)=7e^{-2(t-2)} \quad\text{and}\quad f(t)=7e^{-2t}.$$

As in the first-order case, we apply the **second shifting theorem**. That is, if $$F(s)=\mathcal L\{f(t)\},$$ then $$\mathcal L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)\}=e^{-as}F(s),$$ which is valid for $s>0.$

Here, using $a=2,$ we have $$F(s)=\mathcal L\{7e^{-2t}\}=\frac{7}{s+2},$$ so the transformed forcing term is $$\mathcal L\{7u_2(t)e^{-2(t-2)}\} = e^{-2s}\cdot\frac{7}{s+2}.$$

Substituting into the transformed differential equation gives $$s^2Y(s)+4Y(s)=\frac{7e^{-2s}}{s+2}.$$ We now solve algebraically for $Y(s){:}$ $$\begin{aligned}({s}^{2}+4)Y(s) & =\frac{7{e}^{-2s}}{s+2} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{7{e}^{-2s}}{(s+2)({s}^{2}+4)}\end{aligned}$$

Just as in the first-order case, the delay introduces the factor $e^{-as}.$ Once this factor is identified, the remaining steps follow the same algebraic process used for second-order equations without time delay." :tutorial/id #uuid "b7d1588f-46ce-5a23-a449-ceb6b8f25099" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14829 :tutorial/title "Time-Delayed Forcing and the Second Shifting Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "b88d3621-4e32-596f-9b38-b53f3da4d2ad" :step/math-academy-id 612671 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231843}} {:db/id 17592186231843 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231433 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231301 :question/id #uuid "9941d046-be37-5ada-8d98-ecedfcb9d7f0" :question/math-academy-id "e-21904"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "15ae93ce-c4dd-5b33-b9ff-381502364213" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049492}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231587} {:db/id 17592186231589} {:db/id 17592186377404} {:db/id 17592186377459} {:db/id 17592186377466} {:db/id 17592186377473} {:db/id 17592186518201}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Laplace Transform of a Second-Order ODE With Time-Delayed Forcing"} :step/id #uuid "0947db02-2bd3-50a0-803f-4e78e3ce7311" :step/math-academy-id 612672 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231844}} {:db/id 17592186231844 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231999 :tutorial/content "Once the Laplace transform has been found, solving a second-order initial value problem with step function forcing follows the same overall strategy as before: we take the inverse Laplace transform.

The key difference is handling terms that include a factor of $e^{-as}$.

Consider the initial value problem $$y'' + y = u_2(t), \qquad y(0)=0,\qquad y'(0)=0,$$ where $u_2(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.

We previously found the Laplace transform $$Y(s)=e^{-2s}\cdot\frac{1}{s(s^2+1)}.$$

To take the inverse Laplace transform, we first focus on the *base function* $$F(s)=\frac{1}{s(s^2+1)}.$$ Using partial fraction decomposition, we write $$\frac{1}{s(s^2+1)}=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{s^2+1}.$$

Now we compute the inverse transform of $F(s)$ and call it $f(t){:}$ $$f(t) = \mathcal L^{-1}\!\left\{\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{s^2+1}\right\} = 1-\cos t.$$

Next, we apply the **second shifting theorem**. Since $Y(s)=e^{-2s}F(s)$, we have $$\mathcal L^{-1}\{e^{-2s}F(s)\} = u(t-2)\cdot f(t-2).$$ Substituting our result for $f(t)$, the solution to the initial value problem is $$y(t)=u(t-2)\left(1-\cos(t-2)\right).$$

The important idea is that once the exponential factor $e^{-as}$ has been identified, we first find the inverse transform of the base function, then shift the result and multiply by the unit step function." :tutorial/id #uuid "10f6f136-0604-57e5-b635-1c8a5cfcf8da" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14830 :tutorial/title "Solving for the Laplace Transform With Step Function Forcing"} :step/id #uuid "3dff1d7e-fcee-5906-8723-2dbeac9f85ee" :step/math-academy-id 612676 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231845}} {:db/id 17592186231845 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231434 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231300 :question/id #uuid "029321f3-c767-5a77-95d7-5b4150e24f42" :question/math-academy-id "e-21903"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0459cf03-27db-5198-ab3a-1dbeecb675a9" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231588} {:db/id 17592186231590} {:db/id 17592186377480} {:db/id 17592186377483} {:db/id 17592186377514} {:db/id 17592186377517} {:db/id 17592186377520} {:db/id 17592186518206}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Second-Order Initial Value Problem With Step Function Forcing"} :step/id #uuid "f8a1577f-f7d4-5c2b-869b-f0ae315317fa" :step/math-academy-id 612677}] :activity/title "Solving Second-Order ODEs With Time-Delayed Forcing Using Laplace Transforms" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186231525} {:db/id 17592186231839 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231995 :tutorial/content "In previous lessons, we solved second-order initial value problems using Laplace transforms when the forcing term was an ordinary function of $t.$

We will see how to account for this delay and how it changes the algebraic equation for $Y(s).$ To do this, we first need to determine the transform of the step function itself. Let's find some Laplace transforms." :tutorial/id #uuid "932cf723-31f5-5d76-95e4-d384feb59c11" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14810 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186231840 :step/content {:db/id 17592186232000 :tutorial/content "Consider a second-order initial value problem with step function forcing, such as $$y'' + y = u_2(t), \qquad y(0)=0,\qquad y'(0)=0,$$ where $u_2(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.

**Step 1: Transform the left-hand side.**

We begin by taking the Laplace transform of both sides. Let $Y(s)=\mathcal L\{y(t)\}.$ Using the formula for the second derivative and the initial conditions, we have $$\mathcal L\{y''\}=s^2Y(s)-sy(0)-y'(0) = s^2Y(s).$$

**Step 2: Transform the right-hand side.**

From the table of Laplace transforms, the unit step function satisfies $$\mathcal L\{u_2(t)\}=\frac{e^{-2s}}{s},$$ which is valid for $s>0.$

**Step 3: Solve for $Y(s).$**

Substituting these results into the transformed equation gives $$s^2Y(s)+Y(s)=\frac{e^{-2s}}{s}.$$ We now collect terms and solve algebraically for $Y(s){:}$ $$\begin{aligned}({s}^{2}+1)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s({s}^{2}+1)}\end{aligned}$$

Aside from the exponential factor $e^{-2s},$ the steps are exactly the same as in problems without time delay." :tutorial/id #uuid "f7be86fb-5367-564f-906a-5ce064205685" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14834 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "f07d73a0-6354-56ab-81e4-4b5131af3c8c" :step/math-academy-id 612667 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231841}} {:db/id 17592186232000 :tutorial/content "Consider a second-order initial value problem with step function forcing, such as $$y'' + y = u_2(t), \qquad y(0)=0,\qquad y'(0)=0,$$ where $u_2(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.

The same idea applies when working with **second-order** differential equations.

Consider the initial value problem $$y'' + 4y = 7u_2(t)e^{-2(t-2)}, \qquad y(0)=0,\qquad y'(0)=0,$$ where $u_2(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.

Again, we begin by taking the Laplace transform of both sides and writing $$Y(s)=\mathcal L\{y(t)\}.$$ Using the initial conditions, the left-hand side becomes $$\mathcal L\{y''\}+4\mathcal L\{y\}=s^2Y(s)+4Y(s).$$

The forcing term has the form $$u_2(t)\,f(t-2),$$ where $$f(t-2)=7e^{-2(t-2)} \quad\text{and}\quad f(t)=7e^{-2t}.$$

As in the first-order case, we apply the **second shifting theorem**. That is, if $$F(s)=\mathcal L\{f(t)\},$$ then $$\mathcal L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)\}=e^{-as}F(s),$$ which is valid for $s>0.$

Here, using $a=2,$ we have $$F(s)=\mathcal L\{7e^{-2t}\}=\frac{7}{s+2},$$ so the transformed forcing term is $$\mathcal L\{7u_2(t)e^{-2(t-2)}\} = e^{-2s}\cdot\frac{7}{s+2}.$$

Substituting into the transformed differential equation gives $$s^2Y(s)+4Y(s)=\frac{7e^{-2s}}{s+2}.$$ We now solve algebraically for $Y(s){:}$ $$\begin{aligned}({s}^{2}+4)Y(s) & =\frac{7{e}^{-2s}}{s+2} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{7{e}^{-2s}}{(s+2)({s}^{2}+4)}\end{aligned}$$

Just as in the first-order case, the delay introduces the factor $e^{-as}.$ Once this factor is identified, the remaining steps follow the same algebraic process used for second-order equations without time delay." :tutorial/id #uuid "b7d1588f-46ce-5a23-a449-ceb6b8f25099" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14829 :tutorial/title "Time-Delayed Forcing and the Second Shifting Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "b88d3621-4e32-596f-9b38-b53f3da4d2ad" :step/math-academy-id 612671 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231843}} {:db/id 17592186231998 :tutorial/content "In the first-order case, we saw that a time delay in the forcing term appears in the $s$-domain as a factor of $e^{-as},$ and that we can handle this using the second shifting theorem.

The key difference is handling terms that include a factor of $e^{-as}$.

Consider the initial value problem $$y'' + y = u_2(t), \qquad y(0)=0,\qquad y'(0)=0,$$ where $u_2(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.

We previously found the Laplace transform $$Y(s)=e^{-2s}\cdot\frac{1}{s(s^2+1)}.$$

To take the inverse Laplace transform, we first focus on the *base function* $$F(s)=\frac{1}{s(s^2+1)}.$$ Using partial fraction decomposition, we write $$\frac{1}{s(s^2+1)}=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{s^2+1}.$$

Now we compute the inverse transform of $F(s)$ and call it $f(t){:}$ $$f(t) = \mathcal L^{-1}\!\left\{\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{s^2+1}\right\} = 1-\cos t.$$

Next, we apply the **second shifting theorem**. Since $Y(s)=e^{-2s}F(s)$, we have $$\mathcal L^{-1}\{e^{-2s}F(s)\} = u(t-2)\cdot f(t-2).$$ Substituting our result for $f(t)$, the solution to the initial value problem is $$y(t)=u(t-2)\left(1-\cos(t-2)\right).$$

The important idea is that once the exponential factor $e^{-as}$ has been identified, we first find the inverse transform of the base function, then shift the result and multiply by the unit step function." :tutorial/id #uuid "10f6f136-0604-57e5-b635-1c8a5cfcf8da" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14830 :tutorial/title "Solving for the Laplace Transform With Step Function Forcing"} :step/id #uuid "3dff1d7e-fcee-5906-8723-2dbeac9f85ee" :step/math-academy-id 612676 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231845}} {:db/id 17592186231999 :tutorial/content "Once the Laplace transform has been found, solving a second-order initial value problem with step function forcing follows the same overall strategy as before: we take the inverse Laplace transform.

:question/math-academy-id "q-345255" :question/problem "Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if

$$
{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+13y=6{u}_{1}(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-1)),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,
$$

where ${u}_{1}(t)=u(t-1)$ is the unit step function." :question/worked-solution "First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+13y\} & =L\{6{u}_{1}(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-1))\} \\ L\{{y}^{″}\}+4L\{{y}^{′}\}+13L\{y\} & =L\{6{u}_{1}(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-1))\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{′}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of the first derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=0$:

$$
L\{{y}^{′}\}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{″}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of the second derivative and the initial conditions $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0$:

$$
L\{{y}^{″}\}={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)
$$

For the right-hand side, we use the second shifting theorem:

$$
L\{u(t-a)f(t-a)\}={e}^{-as}F(s)
$$

Here, $a=1$ and $f(t-1)=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-1))$, so $f(t)=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$ The transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
F(s)=L\{6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\}=6\cdot \frac{3}{{s}^{2}+{3}^{2}}=\frac{18}{{s}^{2}+9}.
$$

Applying the shift, we get

$$
L\{6{u}_{1}(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-1))\}={e}^{-s}\cdot \frac{18}{{s}^{2}+9}=\frac{18{e}^{-s}}{{s}^{2}+9}.
$$

Substituting these into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)+4sY(s)+13Y(s) & =\frac{18{e}^{-s}}{{s}^{2}+9} \\ ({s}^{2}+4s+13)Y(s) & =\frac{18{e}^{-s}}{{s}^{2}+9} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{18{e}^{-s}}{({s}^{2}+9)({s}^{2}+4s+13)}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8ed0242a-2db9-5144-8e11-5ba6887b8361" :step/next {:db/id 17592186518313}} {:db/id 17592186518277 :step/content {:db/id 17592186518206 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9575d503-b33a-5aaf-a793-2497c79dc90a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{-5(t-4)}" :db/id 17592186517769}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186517769} :answer-field/id #uuid "5479ca0e-e235-5daf-9f78-3a7ac798d247" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186518011}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e0f1706f-269a-5658-8fd3-75993082b4c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-345300" :question/problem "Find the solution $y(t)$ given that the Laplace transform of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}(t)+6{y}^{′}(t)+5y(t)=20{u}_{4}(t),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,
$$

is given by

$$
{s}^{2}Y(s)+6sY(s)+5Y(s)=\frac{20{e}^{-4s}}{s}.
$$

The solution is $y(t)=u(t-4)\cdot (4-5{e}^{-(t-4)}\,+\,$
{{field-1}}
$).$" :question/worked-solution "Using the transformed equation, we solve for $Y(s)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)+6sY(s)+5Y(s) & =\frac{20{e}^{-4s}}{s} \\ ({s}^{2}+6s+5)Y(s) & =\frac{20{e}^{-4s}}{s} \\ (s+1)(s+5)Y(s) & =\frac{20{e}^{-4s}}{s} \\ Y(s) & ={e}^{-4s}\cdot \frac{20}{s(s+1)(s+5)}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the inverse transform, we first use partial fraction decomposition on the algebraic part:

$$
\frac{20}{s(s+1)(s+5)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{s+1}+\frac{C}{s+5}
$$

Solving for the constants, we find $A=4,$ $B=-5,$ and $C=1,$ giving:

$$
\frac{20}{s(s+1)(s+5)}=\frac{4}{s}-\frac{5}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s+5}
$$

Now, we apply the inverse Laplace transform. Let 

$$
F(s)=\frac{4}{s}-\frac{5}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s+5},
$$

then, we have

$$
f(t)=4-5{e}^{-t}+{e}^{-5t}.
$$

According to the second shifting theorem, 

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}={u}_{a}(t)f(t-a).
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-4s}F(s)\} \\ y(t) & ={u}_{4}(t)\,f(t-4) \\ y(t) & =u(t-4)\cdot (4-5{e}^{-(t-4)}+{e}^{-5(t-4)}).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "99b6edeb-bbfc-5c8b-b1c4-dd5efc3764aa"} {:db/id 17592186518287 :step/content {:db/id 17592186518201 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03a207cf-6ec4-5e6d-997d-39d88a243b9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y(s)=\frac{3{s}^{2}+7{e}^{-4s}}{{s}^{2}({s}^{2}+16)}" :db/id 17592186517496} {:answer/id #uuid "2a4db7a8-b2f3-5998-9cda-8fbb2aabb05f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y(s)=\frac{3{s}^{2}+7{e}^{-s}}{{s}^{2}({s}^{2}+16)}" :db/id 17592186517567} {:answer/id #uuid "8ddf6de9-76a1-580c-a0a5-04e50833b026" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y(s)=\frac{3s+7{e}^{-4s}}{{s}^{2}({s}^{2}+16)}" :db/id 17592186517752} {:answer/id #uuid "8f14cb64-f15c-5e63-97dc-cb8d52fe503e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y(s)=\frac{3{s}^{2}+7{e}^{-4s}}{{s}^{2}+16}" :db/id 17592186517757} {:answer/id #uuid "a5df1187-9902-5a00-900d-f4f5ec5cd0fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y(s)=\frac{3{s}^{2}+7{e}^{-4s}}{s({s}^{2}+16)}" :db/id 17592186517797}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186517496} :answer-field/id #uuid "96d0813c-5c54-5890-9610-b5222646eaaa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186518041}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d2f59173-bdb2-59d3-8bec-268e720e4bf5" :question/math-academy-id "q-345246" :question/problem "Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if

$$
{y}^{″}+16y=7{u}_{4}(t)\cdot (t-4)\,,\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=3,
$$

where ${u}_{4}(t)=u(t-4)$ is the unit step function." :question/worked-solution "First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{″}+16y\} & =L\{7{u}_{4}(t)\cdot (t-4)\} \\ L\{{y}^{″}\}+16L\{y\} & =L\{7{u}_{4}(t)\cdot (t-4)\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{″}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of the second derivative and the initial conditions $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=3:$

$$
L\{{y}^{″}\}={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)-3
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
7{u}_{4}(t)\cdot (t-4)
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=4$ and $f(t)=7(t-4).$

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\}={e}^{-as}\cdot L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

  

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{7u(t-4)\cdot (t-4)\} & ={e}^{-4s}\cdot L\{7((t+4)-4)\} \\  & ={e}^{-4s}\cdot L\{7t\} \\  & ={e}^{-4s}\cdot 7\cdot \frac{1!}{{s}^{1+1}} \\  & =\frac{7{e}^{-4s}}{{s}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(t)=4-5{e}^{-t}+{e}^{-5t}.

According to the second shifting theorem, 

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}={u}_{a}(t)f(t-a).
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-4s}F(s)\} \\ y(t) & ={u}_{4}(t)\,f(t-4) \\ y(t) & =u(t-4)\cdot (4-5{e}^{-(t-4)}+{e}^{-5(t-4)}).\end{aligned}

:question/math-academy-id "q-345246" :question/problem "Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if

$$
{y}^{″}+16y=7{u}_{4}(t)\cdot (t-4)\,,\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=3,
$$

where ${u}_{4}(t)=u(t-4)$ is the unit step function." :question/worked-solution "First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{″}+16y\} & =L\{7{u}_{4}(t)\cdot (t-4)\} \\ L\{{y}^{″}\}+16L\{y\} & =L\{7{u}_{4}(t)\cdot (t-4)\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{″}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of the second derivative and the initial conditions $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=3:$

$$
L\{{y}^{″}\}={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)-3
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
7{u}_{4}(t)\cdot (t-4)
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=4$ and $f(t)=7(t-4).$

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\}={e}^{-as}\cdot L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

  

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{7u(t-4)\cdot (t-4)\} & ={e}^{-4s}\cdot L\{7((t+4)-4)\} \\  & ={e}^{-4s}\cdot L\{7t\} \\  & ={e}^{-4s}\cdot 7\cdot \frac{1!}{{s}^{1+1}} \\  & =\frac{7{e}^{-4s}}{{s}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{″}\}+16L\{y\} & =L\{7{u}_{4}(t)(t-4)\} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s)-3+16Y(s) & =\frac{7{e}^{-4s}}{{s}^{2}} \\ ({s}^{2}+16)Y(s) & =3+\frac{7{e}^{-4s}}{{s}^{2}} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{3{s}^{2}+7{e}^{-4s}}{{s}^{2}({s}^{2}+16)}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b8b7f1db-a884-5b7a-8f66-cefcb30e2b44" :step/next {:db/id 17592186518270}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03a207cf-6ec4-5e6d-997d-39d88a243b9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186222306 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222473 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to compute the **matrix exponential**.

Recall that the scalar exponential function $e^t$ can be written as the power series 

$$
e^t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{t^k}{k!} = 1 + t + \dfrac{t^2}{2} + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!} + \cdots.
$$

Now, let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix. By definition, the matrix exponential $e^{At}$ is given by the analogous series

$$
e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k t^k}{k!} = I + tA + \dfrac{t^2}{2}A^2 + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!}A^k + \cdots.
$$

There are several approaches for computing matrix exponentials:

- The most direct approach is to use the definition above, but this is typically impractical.

- Another method, often covered in linear algebra courses, is to use the Jordan canonical form of $A$. This works, but it can also be tedious, especially for larger matrices.

Here, we will introduce a different method.

By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, every power $A^n, A^{n+1}, \ldots$ can be rewritten as a linear combination of 

$$
I, \: A, \: A^2, \: \ldots, \: A^{n-1}.
$$

As a result, $e^{At}$ can be written in the form

$$
e^{At}=\alpha_{n-1}A^{n-1} t^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2} A^{n-2}t^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1 At+\alpha_0 I,
$$

where $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{n-1}$ are functions of $t$ and $I$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix. 

Now, we define the polynomial 

$$
r(\lambda)=\alpha_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2}\lambda^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0.
$$

Then we have the following key fact:

> For any eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $At$, we have $r(\lambda) = e^{\lambda}.$

Let’s now see how this method works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "d78b3664-4117-56fc-bf30-5ca3acb28377" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14270 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f932ab79-9fa6-5a87-aa94-755b1685c4e3" :step/math-academy-id 588472 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222307}} {:db/id 17592186222307 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222482 :tutorial/content "Let's find $e^{At}$ for $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}$ 

By solving the characteristic polynomial $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we can find that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=2, \qquad
\lambda_2=7.
$$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=2t, \qquad
\lambda_2=7t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t) &={e}^{2t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,\Rightarrow \,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
5t\alpha_1 = e^{7t} - e^{2t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_1 = \dfrac{1}{5t}\bigl(e^{7t}-e^{2t}\bigr).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $7$ and subtracting twice the second one, we get

$$
5\alpha_0 = 7e^{2t} - 2e^{7t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_0 = \dfrac{1}{5}\bigl(7e^{2t}-2e^{7t}\bigr).
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((2{e}^{7t}-2{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & =-7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t \\  & =-\frac{7}{5}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{7}{5}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((7{e}^{7t}-7{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 7({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) & 5{e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6e5aa695-b237-54d4-9836-20514d70dc9e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14389 :tutorial/title "2x2 Matrices With Distinct Real Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "3c91134a-154b-5692-a2cc-fdc45c81af7e" :step/math-academy-id 588473 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222308}} {:db/id 17592186222308 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221408 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221150 :question/id #uuid "35a158c3-37b6-5123-ba90-1fd05218ce43" :question/math-academy-id "e-21271"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fee186e0-579f-5104-b0e1-50540abc0bdc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050001}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221925} {:db/id 17592186221994} {:db/id 17592186308532} {:db/id 17592186308533} {:db/id 17592186308644} {:db/id 17592186308645}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Real Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "ebe4cfdc-9e1a-577d-ad38-9d117b4cf820" :step/math-academy-id 588474 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222309}} {:db/id 17592186222309 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221409 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221151 :question/id #uuid "18064c11-63d3-599a-b504-7b589f46c3dc" :question/math-academy-id "e-21272"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a118fe4a-cd1f-52f7-aa33-59f5494e4905" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048305}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221932} {:db/id 17592186222002} {:db/id 17592186308654} {:db/id 17592186308655} {:db/id 17592186308656} {:db/id 17592186308657} {:db/id 17592186308658} {:db/id 17592186308659} {:db/id 17592186308660} {:db/id 17592186370129} {:db/id 17592186532679}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "ea0b2d60-3227-5e25-b6a9-171c0dc66319" :step/math-academy-id 588478 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222310}} {:db/id 17592186222310 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222481 :tutorial/content "Recall that the matrix exponential $e^{At}$ can be written as

$$
e^{At}=\alpha_{n-1} A^{n-1}t^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2} A^{n-2}t^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1 At+\alpha_0 I.
$$

If we define the polynomial

$$
r(\lambda)=\alpha_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2}\lambda^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0,
$$

then for any eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ of $At,$ we have

$$
r(\lambda_i) = e^{\lambda_i}.
$$

However, for *repeated eigenvalues*, we have the following additional fact:

> If $\lambda_i$ is an eigenvalue of multiplicity $k$ with $k>1,$ then 
> 
> 
> $$
> \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(\lambda ){|}_{\lambda ={\lambda }_{i}}={e}^{{\lambda }_{i}},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{\lambda }^{2}}r(\lambda ){|}_{\lambda ={\lambda }_{i}}={e}^{{\lambda }_{i}},\,…,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{k-1}}{\text{d}{\lambda }^{k-1}}r(\lambda ){|}_{\lambda ={\lambda }_{i}}={e}^{{\lambda }_{i}}\end{aligned}
> $$

Let's apply these facts to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "d7b15b25-b73f-5d5f-aa02-e4c1a5e9804e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14388 :tutorial/title "2x2 Matrices With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "855a741b-2bbe-5e04-b892-8d1d9c7d0e65" :step/math-academy-id 588481 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222311}} {:db/id 17592186222311 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221410 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221152 :question/id #uuid "40a6318a-a1c9-55f3-afdb-02b43891d7b5" :question/math-academy-id "e-21273"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0fd1d280-c768-5504-892e-a9a1948e1f1a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221933} {:db/id 17592186222003} {:db/id 17592186308670} {:db/id 17592186308671} {:db/id 17592186308672} {:db/id 17592186308673} {:db/id 17592186308674} {:db/id 17592186308675} {:db/id 17592186370138}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "de5a7d5c-0c01-5247-8ba6-a69a863c9cbb" :step/math-academy-id 588482 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222312}} {:db/id 17592186222312 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222505 :tutorial/content "Again, let $A$ be a constant $n\times n$ matrix. The matrix exponential satisfies

$$
\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\bigl(e^{At}\bigr)=A\,e^{At}.
$$

Indeed, recall that

$$
e^{At}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(At)^k}{k!}
=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k t^k}{k!}.
$$

To prove the formula, we differentiate the series above term-by-term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At}) & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k}\cdot k{t}^{k-1}}{k!} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k}{t}^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \\  & =A{\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{k-1}{t}^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} \\  & =A{\sum }_{j=0}^{\infty }\frac{{A}^{j}{t}^{j}}{j!} \\  & =A\,{e}^{At}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "739548ab-310c-5de3-a426-1fcaa3282478" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14526 :tutorial/title "Derivatives of Matrix Exponentials"} :step/id #uuid "fc10fbf4-2be0-5b3f-ad2e-0505b175d5a6" :step/math-academy-id 588485 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222313}} {:db/id 17592186222313 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221411 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221194 :question/id #uuid "c0213c76-94e8-5ab3-a260-8a78a205589a" :question/math-academy-id "e-21724"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d4fc3ba4-d488-5156-88dc-837369269cef" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221995} {:db/id 17592186222006} {:db/id 17592186308726} {:db/id 17592186308727} {:db/id 17592186308728} {:db/id 17592186308729} {:db/id 17592186308730} {:db/id 17592186308731} {:db/id 17592186308732} {:db/id 17592186370312} {:db/id 17592186370321}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Derivative of a Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "df4956ab-0323-513e-ab21-66734987f4d0" :step/math-academy-id 588486 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222314}} {:db/id 17592186222314 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222506 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials have other properties. We list a few of them:

- *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

$$
e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
$$

- *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

$$
(e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
$$

- *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

$$
e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
$$

- *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

$$
e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
$$

**Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute." :tutorial/id #uuid "2fcc3801-5d58-5c8e-b8c8-7be65b34f71a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14527 :tutorial/title "Properties of the Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "24b8ab46-a4b1-5358-abbd-db086f102dbf" :step/math-academy-id 588489}] :activity/title "Matrix Exponentials" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221467} {:db/id 17592186222306 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222473 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to compute the **matrix exponential**.

Recall that the scalar exponential function $e^t$ can be written as the power series 

$$
e^t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{t^k}{k!} = 1 + t + \dfrac{t^2}{2} + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!} + \cdots.
$$

Now, let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix. By definition, the matrix exponential $e^{At}$ is given by the analogous series

$$
e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k t^k}{k!} = I + tA + \dfrac{t^2}{2}A^2 + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!}A^k + \cdots.
$$

There are several approaches for computing matrix exponentials:

- The most direct approach is to use the definition above, but this is typically impractical.

- Another method, often covered in linear algebra courses, is to use the Jordan canonical form of $A$. This works, but it can also be tedious, especially for larger matrices.

Here, we will introduce a different method.

By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, every power $A^n, A^{n+1}, \ldots$ can be rewritten as a linear combination of 

$$
I, \: A, \: A^2, \: \ldots, \: A^{n-1}.
$$

As a result, $e^{At}$ can be written in the form

$$
e^{At}=\alpha_{n-1}A^{n-1} t^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2} A^{n-2}t^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1 At+\alpha_0 I,
$$

where $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{n-1}$ are functions of $t$ and $I$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix. 

Now, we define the polynomial 

$$
r(\lambda)=\alpha_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2}\lambda^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0.
$$

Then we have the following key fact:

> For any eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $At$, we have $r(\lambda) = e^{\lambda}.$

Let’s now see how this method works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "d78b3664-4117-56fc-bf30-5ca3acb28377" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14270 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f932ab79-9fa6-5a87-aa94-755b1685c4e3" :step/math-academy-id 588472 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222307}} {:db/id 17592186222473 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to compute the **matrix exponential**.

Recall that the scalar exponential function $e^t$ can be written as the power series 

$$
e^t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{t^k}{k!} = 1 + t + \dfrac{t^2}{2} + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!} + \cdots.
$$

Now, let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix. By definition, the matrix exponential $e^{At}$ is given by the analogous series

$$
e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^k t^k}{k!} = I + tA + \dfrac{t^2}{2}A^2 + \cdots + \dfrac{t^k}{k!}A^k + \cdots.
$$

There are several approaches for computing matrix exponentials:

- The most direct approach is to use the definition above, but this is typically impractical.

- Another method, often covered in linear algebra courses, is to use the Jordan canonical form of $A$. This works, but it can also be tedious, especially for larger matrices.

Here, we will introduce a different method.

By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, every power $A^n, A^{n+1}, \ldots$ can be rewritten as a linear combination of 

$$
I, \: A, \: A^2, \: \ldots, \: A^{n-1}.
$$

As a result, $e^{At}$ can be written in the form

$$
e^{At}=\alpha_{n-1}A^{n-1} t^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2} A^{n-2}t^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1 At+\alpha_0 I,
$$

where $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{n-1}$ are functions of $t$ and $I$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix. 

Now, we define the polynomial 

$$
r(\lambda)=\alpha_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\alpha_{n-2}\lambda^{n-2}+\cdots+\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0.

> For any eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $At$, we have $r(\lambda) = e^{\lambda}.$

Let’s now see how this method works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "d78b3664-4117-56fc-bf30-5ca3acb28377" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14270 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186222307 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222482 :tutorial/content "Let's find $e^{At}$ for $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}$ 

By solving the characteristic polynomial $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we can find that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=2, \qquad
\lambda_2=7.
$$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=2t, \qquad
\lambda_2=7t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t) &={e}^{2t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,\Rightarrow \,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
5t\alpha_1 = e^{7t} - e^{2t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_1 = \dfrac{1}{5t}\bigl(e^{7t}-e^{2t}\bigr).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $7$ and subtracting twice the second one, we get

$$
5\alpha_0 = 7e^{2t} - 2e^{7t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_0 = \dfrac{1}{5}\bigl(7e^{2t}-2e^{7t}\bigr).
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((2{e}^{7t}-2{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ -7{\alpha }_{1}t & =-7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t \\  & =-\frac{7}{5}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{7}{5}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7(\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{7t}-{e}^{2t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((7{e}^{7t}-7{e}^{2t})+(7{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{7t})) \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 7({e}^{2t}-{e}^{7t}) & 5{e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6e5aa695-b237-54d4-9836-20514d70dc9e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14389 :tutorial/title "2x2 Matrices With Distinct Real Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "3c91134a-154b-5692-a2cc-fdc45c81af7e" :step/math-academy-id 588473 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222308}} {:db/id 17592186222482 :tutorial/content "Let's find $e^{At}$ for $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -7 & 7\end{bmatrix}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(3t) &={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$

$$

$$

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=(2+3\text{i})t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=(2-3\text{i})t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((2+3\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(2+3\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(2+3\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\ (2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+3{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5\cdot \frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t+{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3\cdot \frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t \\  & =-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].
