17592186230029 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230153 :tutorial/content "We know how to apply the implicit Euler method to initial value problems

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y_0 = y(x_0),
$$

that are linear in $y,$ that is, where $f(x,y) = a(x)y + b(x).$
However, in general, $f$ can be a nasty, nonlinear function in $y.$ For example, consider the following initial value problem:

$$
y' = x^2 - xy^4,\qquad y(0)=1
$$

Can we apply the implicit Euler method with step size $\Delta x = 0.5$ to this IVP to approximate the value of $y(0.5)?$

Yes, we can! However, doing so requires defining a function $g$ to which the next $y$-value $y_\text{new}$ is a solution of the equation $g(y_\text{new})=0.$ Then, we apply a root-finding method to solve for $y_\text{new}.$

To see how, let's start by applying the implicit Euler method as we normally would. In general, the change $\Delta y$ for our ODE is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{'}\cdot Δx \\  & =(({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{4})\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into the update formula $y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y$ and move all terms to the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{4} \\ 0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{4}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, with terms such as $0.5x_\text{new}(y_\text{new})^4$ and $y_\text{new},$ there’s no simple algebraic rearrangement, and solving exactly is impractical.

Instead, let's define a new function $g$ of $y_\text{new}$ by the expression on the left-hand side:

$$
g(y_\text{new}) = 0.5x_\text{new}(y_\text{new})^4 + y_\text{new} - y - 0.5(x_\text{new})^2
$$

Note that, at any step, $y$ and $x_\text{new}$ are known constants, so $g$ is truly a one-variable function in $y_\text{new}.$

Then, the next $y$-value $y_\text{new}$ is a root of this function: $g(y_\text{new}) = 0.$ Therefore, to find $y_\text{new},$ we apply a root-finding method, such as Newton's method.

For instance, in the first step, the new $x$-value is $x_\text{new}=0+0.5=0.5.$ So, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5\cdot 0.5\cdot ({y}_{\text{new}})^{4}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1-0.5\cdot (0.5)^{2} \\  & =0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{4}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1.125.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we would proceed to use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g(y_\text{new}) = 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "84c89e00-0b30-5678-80a1-4471ec2526da" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14291 17592186222338 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222489 :tutorial/content "Can we apply Euler's method to approximate solutions to second-order initial value problems, such as the one below?

$$
xy'' - y' - y = 2x, \qquad y(1) = -1, \quad y'(1) = 1
$$

Well, for a second-order initial value problem,

$$
y'' = f(x, y, y'), \qquad y(a) = c, \quad y'(a) = d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{'} &=f(x,y,z),\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}Δy &={y}^{'}\cdot Δx \\ Δz &={z}^{'}\cdot Δx\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The new values are then given by $y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y$ and $z_\text{new} = z + \Delta z.$

In the example above, we set up Euler's method by first isolating $y''$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{''}-{y}^{'}-y & =2x \\ x{y}^{''} & =y+{y}^{'}+2x \\ {y}^{''} & =\frac{y+{y}^{'}}{x}+2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z=y',$ $z'=y''$ in the above. This gives the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} &=z,\, && y(1)=-1 \\ {z}^{'} &=\frac{y+z}{x}+2,\, && z(1)=1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

On the next slide, we will approximate values for this system using step size $\Delta x = \dfrac12.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6d9782a2-388c-59cd-bb4e-165619f75de3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14485 "5277b709-6b41-5099-b1a2-e16d03ed909a" :step/math-academy-id 594428} {:db/id 17592186222396 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222529 :tutorial/content "We now apply the update rules $\Delta y = y' \cdot \Delta x$ and $\Delta z = z' \cdot \Delta x$ to our system below starting at $x=1$ with step size $\Delta x = \dfrac12.$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} &=z,\, && y(1)=-1 \\ {z}^{'} &=\frac{y+z}{x}+2,\, && z(1)=1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=-1$ and $z(1)=1.$

| $x$ | $y$ | $y'$ | $\Delta y$ | $z$ | $z'$ | $\Delta z$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ |  |  | $1$ |  |  |

We compute $y'$ and $\Delta y,$ $z'$ and $\Delta z$ (using the values of $x$, $y,$ and $z,$ in the first row), and the values of $x_\text{new},$ $y_\text{new},$ and $z_\text{new}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =z=1 \\ {z}^{'} & =\frac{y+z}{x}+2=\frac{-1+1}{1}+2=2 \\ Δy & ={y}^{'}\cdot Δx=1\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ Δz & ={z}^{'}\cdot Δx=2\cdot \frac{1}{2}=1 \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=-1+\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{1}{2} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=1+1=2\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | $y'$ | $\Delta y$ | $z$ | $z'$ | $\Delta z$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $\dfrac12$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ |
| $\dfrac32$ | $-\dfrac12$ |  |  | $2$ |  |  |

After several steps, we obtain the following table of values.

| $x$ | $y$ | $y'$ | $\Delta y$ | $z$ | $z'$ | $\Delta z$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $\dfrac12$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ |
| $\dfrac32$ | $-\dfrac12$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $\dfrac32$ |
| $2$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac72$ | $\dfrac74$ | $\dfrac72$ | $4$ | $2$ |
| $\dfrac52$ | $\dfrac94$ |  |  | $\dfrac{11}2$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y\left(\dfrac52\right) \approx \dfrac94$ and $y'\left(\dfrac52\right) = z\left(\dfrac52\right) \approx \dfrac{11}2.$

$$
xy'' - y' - y = 2x, \qquad y(1) = -1, \quad y'(1) = 1
$$

Well, for a second-order initial value problem,

$$
y'' = f(x, y, y'), \qquad y(a) = c, \quad y'(a) = d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} &=z,\, && y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{'} &=f(x,y,z),\, && z(a)=d,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}Δy &={y}^{'}\cdot Δx \\ Δz &={z}^{'}\cdot Δx\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The new values are then given by $y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y$ and $z_\text{new} = z + \Delta z.$

In the example above, we set up Euler's method by first isolating $y''$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{''}-{y}^{'}-y & =2x \\ x{y}^{''} & =y+{y}^{'}+2x \\ {y}^{''} & =\frac{y+{y}^{'}}{x}+2\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} &=z,\, && y(1)=-1 \\ {z}^{'} &=\frac{y+z}{x}+2,\, && z(1)=1.\end{aligned}\right.

Indeed, we could apply any numerical method component-wise to approximate the solution to a second-order ODE once split into a system of first-order ODEs!" :tutorial/id #uuid "23470bd2-647f-5c35-b30d-10e88b4b7c3c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14856 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:activity/expected-seconds 1080.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186222294} :activity/id #uuid "0db2ac37-787f-5ca2-b7bf-324550d93a1d" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186051034 :topic/id #uuid "7c092bea-3614-5bca-b402-7742647e083b" :topic/math-academy-id 6399} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186222294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222498 :tutorial/content "Each step of a numerical method produces a local truncation error $\tau,$ which, over multiple steps, accumulates into a global truncation error $e.$ Both LTE and GTE depend on step size $\Delta x.$

The **order** of a numerical method describes how fast these errors shrink as $\Delta x$ decreases.
A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the *largest positive* integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^p\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0.
$$

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately $k^p{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}e(\frac{Δx}{k}) & ≈K{(\frac{Δx}{k})}^{p}=\frac{K(Δx)^{p}}{{k}^{p}}≈\frac{e(Δx)}{{k}^{p}}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's demonstrate with an example. Suppose a numerical method is used to approximate the solution to an initial value problem.

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.21,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.21) = 0.785.$

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.07,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.07) = 0.010.$

Using this data, we can estimate the order of the numerical method.

The step size decreases from $0.21$ to $0.07.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k = \dfrac{0.21}{0.07} = 3.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the GTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
k^p = 3^p.
$$

On the other hand, the GTE actually decreases from $0.785$ to $0.010.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\dfrac{0.785}{0.010} = 78.5.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the GTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{p} & ≈78.5 \\ p & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(78.5) \\ p & ≈3.97….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the approximate order of the method is $4.$

But why is order important? Well, a higher order means that the error decreases faster as $\Delta x$ decreases. As a result, higher-order methods can achieve a target accuracy *with fewer steps*. In this way, order predicts the accuracy you gain when you make steps smaller." :tutorial/id #uuid "40e84a8b-32df-5566-99ff-2b37f338d69f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14500 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ec16a00b-18c7-517a-94d1-35859655f930" :step/math-academy-id 585132 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222295}} {:db/id 17592186222295 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221401 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221184 :question/id #uuid "fb9baafb-4eca-593f-ad3e-34744fdfd3f4" :question/math-academy-id "e-21684"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "48cd517d-be8a-5dc2-91af-fbd19231363c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049053} {:db/id 17592186049611} {:db/id 17592186049621}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221972} {:db/id 17592186221974} {:db/id 17592186308639} {:db/id 17592186308640} {:db/id 17592186308641} {:db/id 17592186308642} {:db/id 17592186391487} {:db/id 17592186443231} {:db/id 17592186443235} {:db/id 17592186443236} {:db/id 17592186443240}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Order of a Numerical Method By Comparing GTE for Different Step Sizes"} :step/id #uuid "8b58215f-a6df-5452-b05c-85bfbc0fd9f2" :step/math-academy-id 585133 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222296}} {:db/id 17592186222296 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222499 :tutorial/content "An alternative, but equivalent, definition for the **order** can be made in terms of the local truncation error.

A numerical method has **order** $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
\tau(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0.
$$

In other words, a numerical method has **order** $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately $k^{p+1}.$

But why is the power $p+1$ for LTE but only $p$ for GTE?

Each local truncation error measures the error made in *one step* of the method. If a method has order $p,$ then the error made in a single step shrinks like

$$
\tau(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right).
$$

However, on a fixed interval, using step size $\Delta x$ requires about

$$
N \approx \dfrac1{\Delta x}
$$

steps. The global truncation error results from *accumulating* these local errors over all steps.

Heuristically, adding up $N$ local errors of size $(\Delta x)^{p+1}$ gives

$$
e(\Delta x) \sim N \cdot (\Delta x)^{p+1} \sim \dfrac1{\Delta x} \cdot (\Delta x)^{p+1} = (\Delta x)^p.
$$

Thus, the local truncation error is one power of $\Delta x$ higher than the global truncation error.

Next, we will apply this definition to determine the order of a given numerical method." :tutorial/id #uuid "b5d4a6f3-fc92-557f-be1f-b14832313c21" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14501 :tutorial/title :tutorial/content "We'll now show that the definition of order with respect to LTE is the same as with respect to GTE.

Indeed, suppose a numerical method with increment formula $\Delta y = \Phi(x, y, \Delta x) \cdot \Delta x$ satisfies the following:

$$
\tau(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0
$$

On a fixed interval of length $L,$ the number of steps is $N \approx \dfrac{L}{\Delta x}.$ So,
$N = \mathcal O\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\Delta x}\right)$ as $\Delta x \to 0.$

Now, recall the relationship between GTE and LTE, given by

$$
e(\Delta x) = e_N = e_{N-1} + \left[ \Phi(x_{N-1}, y(x_{N-1}), \Delta x) - \Phi(x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, \Delta x) \right] \cdot \Delta x + \tau_N.
$$

Since $y(x_{N-1}) - y_{N-1} = e_{N-1},$ it is natural to say that changing the input $y$ by $e_{N-1}$ changes $\Phi$ by about a constant multiple of $e_{N-1}.$ So, heuristically,

$$
\Phi(x_{N-1}, y(x_{N-1}), \Delta x) - \Phi(x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, \Delta x) \approx Ce_{N-1}
$$

for some $C$ that *doesn't* depend on $\Delta x$ (on a fixed interval). Hence, the GTE satisfies approximately

$$
e(\Delta x) = e_N \approx (1+C\Delta x)e_{N-1} + \tau_N.
$$

After $N$ steps, we get

$$
e(\Delta x) \approx (1+C\Delta x)^N e_0 + \sum_{n=1}^N(1+C\Delta x)^{N-n}\tau_n.
$$

Next, note that $(1+C\Delta x)^N \approx e^{CN\Delta x} \approx e^{CL},$ which is $\mathcal O(1)$ as $\Delta x \to 0.$ So, the weights $(1+C\Delta x)^{N-n}$ don't change the *power* of $\Delta x.$

So, we can treat the GTE as roughly the sum of the per-step local errors. Therefore,

$$
e(\Delta x) \approx \sum_{n=1}^N \tau_n
$$

With $\tau_n = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right)$ for each $n=1,\ldots,N,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}e(Δx) & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{N}O\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\  & =N\cdot O\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\  & =O\,(\frac{1}{Δx})\cdot O\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\  & =O\,((Δx)^{p}).\end{aligned}
$$

Note that since $p$ is maximal in the LTE definition, this shows the GTE has order $p$ as well." :tutorial/id #uuid "380a28f7-f36f-50b0-982b-365f87b068bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14656 :tutorial/title "Connecting the Definitions of the Order of Numerical Methods"} :step/id #uuid "a05640d9-1389-5d1b-b299-1230e633c270" :step/math-academy-id 593404}] :activity/title "Order of Numerical Methods" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221478} {:db/id 17592186222294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222498 :tutorial/content "Each step of a numerical method produces a local truncation error $\tau,$ which, over multiple steps, accumulates into a global truncation error $e.$ Both LTE and GTE depend on step size $\Delta x.$

The **order** of a numerical method describes how fast these errors shrink as $\Delta x$ decreases.
A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the *largest positive* integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^p\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0.
$$

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately $k^p{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}e(\frac{Δx}{k}) & ≈K{(\frac{Δx}{k})}^{p}=\frac{K(Δx)^{p}}{{k}^{p}}≈\frac{e(Δx)}{{k}^{p}}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's demonstrate with an example. Suppose a numerical method is used to approximate the solution to an initial value problem.

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.21,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.21) = 0.785.$

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.07,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.07) = 0.010.$

Using this data, we can estimate the order of the numerical method.

The step size decreases from $0.21$ to $0.07.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k = \dfrac{0.21}{0.07} = 3.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the GTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
k^p = 3^p.
$$

On the other hand, the GTE actually decreases from $0.785$ to $0.010.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\dfrac{0.785}{0.010} = 78.5.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the GTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{p} & ≈78.5 \\ p & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(78.5) \\ p & ≈3.97….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the approximate order of the method is $4.$

But why is order important? Well, a higher order means that the error decreases faster as $\Delta x$ decreases. As a result, higher-order methods can achieve a target accuracy *with fewer steps*. In this way, order predicts the accuracy you gain when you make steps smaller." :tutorial/id #uuid "40e84a8b-32df-5566-99ff-2b37f338d69f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14500 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ec16a00b-18c7-517a-94d1-35859655f930" :step/math-academy-id 585132 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222295}} {:db/id 17592186222498 :tutorial/content "Each step of a numerical method produces a local truncation error $\tau,$ which, over multiple steps, accumulates into a global truncation error $e.$ Both LTE and GTE depend on step size $\Delta x.$

A numerical method has **order** $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
\tau(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0.
$$

In other words, a numerical method has **order** $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately $k^{p+1}.$

But why is the power $p+1$ for LTE but only $p$ for GTE?

Each local truncation error measures the error made in *one step* of the method. If a method has order $p,$ then the error made in a single step shrinks like

$$
\tau(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right).
$$

However, on a fixed interval, using step size $\Delta x$ requires about

$$
N \approx \dfrac1{\Delta x}
$$

steps. The global truncation error results from *accumulating* these local errors over all steps.

Heuristically, adding up $N$ local errors of size $(\Delta x)^{p+1}$ gives

$$
e(\Delta x) \sim N \cdot (\Delta x)^{p+1} \sim \dfrac1{\Delta x} \cdot (\Delta x)^{p+1} = (\Delta x)^p.
$$

Thus, the local truncation error is one power of $\Delta x$ higher than the global truncation error.

Next, we will apply this definition to determine the order of a given numerical method." :tutorial/id #uuid "b5d4a6f3-fc92-557f-be1f-b14832313c21" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14501 :tutorial/title "Order From Local Truncation Error"} :step/id #uuid "7d7d7ca0-178c-5ff6-b4a4-b9cd8fd8f8c0" :step/math-academy-id 585136 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222297}} {:db/id 17592186222499 :tutorial/content "An alternative, but equivalent, definition for the **order** can be made in terms of the local truncation error.

{:db/id 17592186222331 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222512 :tutorial/content "We'll now show that the definition of order with respect to LTE is the same as with respect to GTE.

Indeed, suppose a numerical method with increment formula $\Delta y = \Phi(x, y, \Delta x) \cdot \Delta x$ satisfies the following:

$$
\tau(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0
$$

On a fixed interval of length $L,$ the number of steps is $N \approx \dfrac{L}{\Delta x}.$ So,
$N = \mathcal O\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\Delta x}\right)$ as $\Delta x \to 0.$

Now, recall the relationship between GTE and LTE, given by

$$
e(\Delta x) = e_N = e_{N-1} + \left[ \Phi(x_{N-1}, y(x_{N-1}), \Delta x) - \Phi(x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, \Delta x) \right] \cdot \Delta x + \tau_N.
$$

Since $y(x_{N-1}) - y_{N-1} = e_{N-1},$ it is natural to say that changing the input $y$ by $e_{N-1}$ changes $\Phi$ by about a constant multiple of $e_{N-1}.$ So, heuristically,

$$
\Phi(x_{N-1}, y(x_{N-1}), \Delta x) - \Phi(x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, \Delta x) \approx Ce_{N-1}
$$

for some $C$ that *doesn't* depend on $\Delta x$ (on a fixed interval). Hence, the GTE satisfies approximately

$$
e(\Delta x) = e_N \approx (1+C\Delta x)e_{N-1} + \tau_N.
$$

After $N$ steps, we get

$$
e(\Delta x) \approx (1+C\Delta x)^N e_0 + \sum_{n=1}^N(1+C\Delta x)^{N-n}\tau_n.
$$

Next, note that $(1+C\Delta x)^N \approx e^{CN\Delta x} \approx e^{CL},$ which is $\mathcal O(1)$ as $\Delta x \to 0.$ So, the weights $(1+C\Delta x)^{N-n}$ don't change the *power* of $\Delta x.$

So, we can treat the GTE as roughly the sum of the per-step local errors. Therefore,

$$
e(\Delta x) \approx \sum_{n=1}^N \tau_n
$$

With $\tau_n = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right)$ for each $n=1,\ldots,N,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}e(Δx) & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{N}O\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\  & =N\cdot O\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\  & =O\,(\frac{1}{Δx})\cdot O\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\  & =O\,((Δx)^{p}).\end{aligned}
$$

Note that since $p$ is maximal in the LTE definition, this shows the GTE has order $p$ as well." :tutorial/id #uuid "380a28f7-f36f-50b0-982b-365f87b068bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14656 :tutorial/title "Connecting the Definitions of the Order of Numerical Methods"} :step/id #uuid "a05640d9-1389-5d1b-b299-1230e633c270" :step/math-academy-id 593404} {:db/id 17592186222512 :tutorial/content "We'll now show that the definition of order with respect to LTE is the same as with respect to GTE.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.25$ to $0.10.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.25}{0.10}=2.5.
$$

Now, since the numerical method is of order $3,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of

$$
{k}^{3}=(2.5)^{3}=15.625.
$$

Therefore, using a step size of $Δx=0.10,$ the expected GTE is

$$
e(0.10)≈\frac{0.125}{15.625}=0.008.
$$

So,

$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.25.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.5}{0.25}=2.
$$

Now, since the numerical method is of order $1,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of

$$
{k}^{1+1}={2}^{2}=4.
$$

Therefore, using a step size of $Δx=0.25,$ the expected LTE is

$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-334724" :question/problem "The local truncation error (LTE) of a numerical method with step size $Δx$ is

$$
τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}.
$$

Complete the following sentences.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Decreasing from $Δx=0.5$ to $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is reduced by a factor of $≈$
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ According to this data, the order of the method is approximately
{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =8(0.5)^{5}+2(0.5)^{6} \\  & =8\cdot 0.031\,25+2\cdot 0.015\,625 \\  & =0.281\,25 \\  & ≈0.281.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.2) & =8(0.2)^{5}+2(0.2)^{6} \\  & =8\cdot 0.000\,32+2\cdot 0.000\,064 \\  & =0.002\,688 \\  & ≈0.003.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.2.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.5}{0.2}=2.5.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={2.5}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.281\,25$ to $0.002\,688.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.281\,25}{0.002\,688}=104.631\,69…≈104.632.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2.5}^{p+1} & ≈104.631\,69… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2.5}⁡(104.631\,69…) \\ p+1 & ≈5.075… \\ p & ≈4.075….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$4.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:

$$
τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{5})=O\,((Δx)^{4+1}),\,Δx\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $4.$"} :step/id #uuid "d1344963-f111-577e-9b39-d9ba8d2a6219" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482618}}] :activity/title "Order of Numerical Methods" :activity/type {:db/id {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.25$ to $0.10.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.25}{0.10}=2.5.
$$

Now, since the numerical method is of order $3,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of

$$
{k}^{3}=(2.5)^{3}=15.625.
$$

Therefore, using a step size of $Δx=0.10,$ the expected GTE is

$$
e(0.10)≈\frac{0.125}{15.625}=0.008.
$$

So,

$τ(0.25)≈$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.25.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.5}{0.25}=2.
$$

Now, since the numerical method is of order $1,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of

$$
{k}^{1+1}={2}^{2}=4.
$$

Therefore, using a step size of $Δx=0.25,$ the expected LTE is

$$
τ(0.25)≈\frac{0.2}{4}=0.05.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "110acc7d-2f94-5af9-b727-c5d13e21f510"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4c42e845-2d37-5c62-8435-55cbffc5e702" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :question/math-academy-id "q-334724" :question/problem "The local truncation error (LTE) of a numerical method with step size $Δx$ is

$$
τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}.
$$

Complete the following sentences.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Decreasing from $Δx=0.5$ to $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is reduced by a factor of $≈$
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ According to this data, the order of the method is approximately
{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =8(0.5)^{5}+2(0.5)^{6} \\  & =8\cdot 0.031\,25+2\cdot 0.015\,625 \\  & =0.281\,25 \\  & ≈0.281.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.2) & =8(0.2)^{5}+2(0.2)^{6} \\  & =8\cdot 0.000\,32+2\cdot 0.000\,064 \\  & =0.002\,688 \\  & ≈0.003.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.2.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.5}{0.2}=2.5.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={2.5}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.281\,25$ to $0.002\,688.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.281\,25}{0.002\,688}=104.631\,69…≈104.632.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2.5}^{p+1} & ≈104.631\,69… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2.5}⁡(104.631\,69…) \\ p+1 & ≈5.075… \\ p & ≈4.075….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$4.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:

$$
τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{5})=O\,((Δx)^{4+1}),\,Δx\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $4.$"} :step/id #uuid "d1344963-f111-577e-9b39-d9ba8d2a6219" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482618}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "87976b3b-af1b-5fcb-8c01-533b581f6a90" :question/math-academy-id "q-334826" :question/problem "A numerical method for approximating a solution to an initial value problem is known to be order $4.$  Suppose that using step size $Δx=0.25$ produces a global truncation error (GTE) of $e(0.25)≈0.3125.$  If we instead use a step size $Δx=0.10,$ what GTE should we expect?

$e(0.10)≈$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.25$ to $0.10.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.25}{0.10}=2.5.
$$

Now, since the numerical method is of order $4,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of

$$
{k}^{4}=(2.5)^{4}=39.0625.
$$

Therefore, using a step size of $Δx=0.10,$ the expected GTE is

$$
e(0.10)≈\frac{0.3125}{39.0625}=0.008.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0a696d2d-bcf2-5d59-8cbe-c8b94fa6e1c7"} {:db/id 17592186512963 :step/content {:db/id 17592186512881 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03959187-9418-5be5-ac79-7e4967d9b00d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186512109} {:answer/id #uuid "585966c4-0f5a-5998-b590-6b01a0ed43b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186512301} {:answer/id #uuid "82ff2bc6-4ad2-5485-9688-6c45d0274b48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186512405} {:answer/id #uuid "c274000b-29cf-5c45-9c94-1b409cdb85c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186512563} {:answer/id #uuid "c735b7b9-b2be-5342-be94-4a2ee43a5709" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186512579}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186512563} :answer-field/id #uuid "01277570-5a55-57cd-b355-f92266d0d444" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186512722}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "288ecca2-4a65-5e47-af70-06519e1d4ea1" :question/math-academy-id "q-334747" :question/problem "Which of the following global truncation error expressions represent a third-order numerical method?

With that in mind, let's check each option in turn:

$$

$$

$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={3}^{p+1}.
$$

$$
\frac{0.54}{0.003}=180.
$$

$$

method for approximating a solution to an initial value problem is known to be order $2.$  Suppose that using step size $Δx=0.15$ produces a global truncation error (GTE) of $e(0.15)≈0.0225.$  If we instead use a step size $Δx=0.10,$ what GTE should we expect?

$e(0.10)≈$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.15$ to $0.10.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.15}{0.10}=1.5.
$$

Now, since the numerical method is of order $2,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of

$$
{k}^{2}=(1.5)^{2}=2.25.
$$

Therefore, using a step size of $Δx=0.10,$ the expected GTE is

$$
e(0.10)≈\frac{0.0225}{2.25}=0.01.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "77da484d-f99e-564b-b4c3-19d24cde8a96" :step/next {:db/id 17592186535091}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d077e1b-69a5-5689-b7f2-27863f84eb6e" :answer/type {:db/id (4{x}^{2}+1)+(2{x}^{2})=6{x}^{2}+1,
$$

which is a binomial.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
(3{x}^{2}-2x)+(5)=3{x}^{2}-2x+5,
$$

which is *not* a binomial (it's a trinomial).

- Statement III is true. The sum of a binomial and a monomial *could be* a binomial (see, for example, statement I). 

 However, the sum of a binomial and a monomial is *not always* a binomial (see, for example, statement II). 

 So, the sum of a binomial and a monomial is *sometimes* binomial.

The factors of $25$ are

$$
1,\,5,\,25.
$$

The factors of $10$ are

$$
1,\,2,\,5,\,10.
$$

The common factors of $25$ and $10$ are

$$
1,\,5.
$$

The greatest of these common factors is $5.$

Now we look at the variable factors. Both $25z$ and $10z$ contain $z.$

$$

$$

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

- To create a numerator of $12,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $3:$

$$
\frac{4\times 3}{7\times 3}=\frac{12}{21}
$$

- To create a denominator of $35,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $5:$

$$
\frac{4\times 5}{7\times 5}=\frac{20}{35}
$$

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:

| $4$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- |
| $12$ | $21$ |
| $20$ | $35$ |

$$

$$

:question/problem "Gerry, a gardener, is planting roses. He knows he needs $1$ cup of water for every $4$ seeds he plants. So, Gerry creates a ratio table to determine the ratio of water to seeds for different quantities.

| Water (cups) | Seeds |
| --- | --- |
| $1$ | $4$ |
| $7$ | $?$ |
| $12$ | $48$ |

$$

$$

How many seeds can Gerry plant with $7$ cups of water?" :question/worked-solution "We start with the ratio $1:4$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{1}{4}
$$

So the numerator represents the number of cups of water ($1$), and the denominator represents the number of seeds ($4$).

We can make a numerator of $7$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $7$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1\times 7}{4\times 7} & =\frac{7}{28}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our ratio table:

| Water (cups) | Seeds |
| --- | --- |
| $1$ | $4$ |
| $7$ | $28$ |
| $12$ | $48$ |

$$

$$

So, Gerry can plant $28$ seeds with $7$ cups of water."} {:db/id 17592186049405} {:db/id 17592186050948 :topic/id #uuid "7447137e-4148-57e3-9e8c-8ef64742b913" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id What is the ratio of crushed stone to cement in its simplest form?" :question/worked-solution "One of the points belonging to the graph is $(60,15).$ Let's write the ratio $60:15$ as a fraction:

$$
\frac{60}{15}
$$

We can simplify this fraction by dividing both the numerator and the denominator by $15:$

$$
\frac{60÷15}{15÷15}=\frac{4}{1}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{\frac{125}{8}} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{\frac{{5}^{3}}{{2}^{3}}} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{\frac{5\cdot 5\cdot 5}{2\cdot 2\cdot 2}} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2}} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{{(\frac{5}{2})}^{3}} & = \\ \frac{5}{2} & \end{aligned}

$$
100%+45%=145%.
$$

$$
145%=\frac{145}{100}=1.45
$$

$$

$$

"Notice that the expression we need to subtract from $5$ must be expanded using the distributive law. 

So first, let's write some big brackets around the expression in parentheses, keeping the minus sign *outside*.

$$
5-[3(x+1)]
$$

Next, we expand the expression inside the brackets using the distributive law. This gives

$$
5-[3x+3].
$$

Now, we remove the brackets by distributing the negative sign. This gives

$$
5-3x-3.
$$

Finally, we collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}5-3x-3 & = \\ (5-3)-3x & = \\ 2-3x & \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186188974 :question/id #uuid "bbcff71d-a7ed-5825-a0e9-f89171d22dde" :question/math-academy-id "q-75692"} {:db/id 17592186475946 :question/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 3754} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180639 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180661 :tutorial/content "If we start with the formula

$$
\textrm{percentage}\times \textrm{whole} = \textrm{part} ,
$$

we can use the relationship between multiplication and division to write down a formula to calculate a percentage:

$$
\textrm{percentage} = \textrm{part} \div \textrm{whole}
$$

Let's demonstrate how to apply this formula using a real-world example.

Suppose that $54$ out of $300$ boxes of grapes in a supermarket contain red grapes. What percentage of the boxes contain red grapes?

In this case, the part is the number of red grapes, which is $54$, and the whole is the total number of grapes, which is $300.$

Substituting our numbers into the above formula, we get

$$
\textrm{percentage} = 54 \div 300 = \dfrac{54}{300}.
$$

To write this fraction as a percentage, we create an equivalent fraction with $100$ as the denominator:

$$
\dfrac{54}{300} = \dfrac{54 \div 3}{300 \div 3} = \dfrac{18}{100}
$$

Now we can write this fraction as a percentage:

$$
\dfrac{18}{100} = 18 \%
$$

Therefore, $18 \%$ of the boxes contain red grapes." :tutorial/id #uuid "73bca8be-ae46-5214-9ba6-2beb553be49f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2082 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "bdf65be2-4038-5c62-b8e0-2362d10939cc" :step/math-academy-id 7964 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180640}} {:db/id 17592186180640 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179819 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179496 :question/id #uuid "75ac9866-6b0f-5736-a592-0bade16b8814" :question/math-academy-id "e-2333"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ddf13639-8d18-5909-a26d-aeda1e011ac0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050776}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180240} {:db/id 17592186180243} {:db/id 17592186459213} {:db/id 17592186459256} {:db/id 17592186538994}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Missing Percent Given Two Numbers Without Simplification"} :step/id #uuid "2a3797e0-441d-5d87-adba-4fa2a33a82b4" :step/math-academy-id 7965 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180641}} {:db/id 17592186180641 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179820 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179497 :question/id #uuid "2f3270cc-d191-5282-b9f7-cf63dcd69d70" :question/math-academy-id "e-2334"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6f67408f-f019-5365-b4a0-6f60ac23cc1d" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180242} {:db/id 17592186180244} {:db/id 17592186459298} {:db/id 17592186459309} {:db/id 17592186544865}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Missing Percent Given Two Numbers Using Simplification"} :step/id #uuid "d0c640ea-bd66-5449-a695-d9913915d65f" :step/math-academy-id 7966}] :activity/title "Finding a Percentage Given Two Numbers: Word Problems" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179897} {:db/id 17592186180639 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180661 :tutorial/content "If we start with the formula

Substituting our numbers into the above formula, we get

$$
\textrm{percentage} = 54 \div 300 = \dfrac{54}{300}.
$$

To write this fraction as a percentage, we create an equivalent fraction with $100$ as the denominator:

$$
\dfrac{54}{300} = \dfrac{54 \div 3}{300 \div 3} = \dfrac{18}{100}
$$

Now we can write this fraction as a percentage:

$$
\dfrac{18}{100} = 18 \%
$$

Therefore, $18 \%$ of the boxes contain red grapes." :tutorial/id #uuid "73bca8be-ae46-5214-9ba6-2beb553be49f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2082 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186180640 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179819 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179496 :question/id #uuid "75ac9866-6b0f-5736-a592-0bade16b8814" :question/math-academy-id "e-2333"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ddf13639-8d18-5909-a26d-aeda1e011ac0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050776}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180240} {:db/id 17592186180243} {:db/id 17592186459213} {:db/id 17592186459256} {:db/id 17592186538994}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Missing Percent Given Two Numbers Without Simplification"} :step/id #uuid "2a3797e0-441d-5d87-adba-4fa2a33a82b4" :step/math-academy-id 7965 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180641}} {:db/id 17592186180641 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179820 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179497 :question/id #uuid "2f3270cc-d191-5282-b9f7-cf63dcd69d70" :question/math-academy-id "e-2334"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6f67408f-f019-5365-b4a0-6f60ac23cc1d" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180242} {:db/id 17592186180244} {:db/id 17592186459298} {:db/id 17592186459309} {:db/id 17592186544865}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Missing Percent Given Two Numbers Using Simplification"} :step/id #uuid "d0c640ea-bd66-5449-a695-d9913915d65f" :step/math-academy-id 7966} {:activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186199284} :activity/id #uuid "ea08cd43-7cea-59a6-a6eb-b25618d785bd" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048429 :topic/id #uuid "9eaae820-5193-5702-9ef4-efac567af4b5" :topic/math-academy-id 4136} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186199284 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199466 :tutorial/content "Every division problem can be written as a fraction and vice-versa. This corresponds to applying a so-called **percentage increase.**

To apply a percentage increase, we add the increase to $100\%,$ convert the result to a decimal multiplier, and then find the product of the multiplier and the original number.

To demonstrate, let's consider the following problem.

What number is $25\%$ *greater than* $160?$

The key words here are "$\boldsymbol{25\%}$ **greater than.**" This means we need to apply a percentage increase, increasing the original number by $25\%.$

To find a number $25\%$ greater than $160,$ we apply a new percentage of

$$
100\% + 25\% = 125\%.
$$

This means that our new number is $125\%$ of $160.$ 

So, first, we convert this percentage to a decimal:

$$
125\% = \dfrac{125}{100} = 1.25
$$

To find a number that is $25\%$ greater than $160,$ we multiply $160$ by $1.25{:}$

$$
1.25 \cdot 160 = 200
$$

Therefore, the number that is $25\%$ *greater than* $160$ is $200.$

This method applies to *any* percentage increase, including those greater than $100\%{;}$ add the increase to $100\%$ before converting to a decimal multiplier." :tutorial/id #uuid "83dbd64f-3ab9-5239-b54b-ae6d91816248" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14336 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "547ba33b-b6b3-5bae-b2dc-eacefe1e81a4" :step/math-academy-id 615692 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153299}} {:db/id 17592186153299 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152295 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151899 :question/id #uuid "2cfd1ed7-8249-5970-9ddc-1bb69929951c" :question/math-academy-id "e-21450"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "125ed0b3-14ad-5af8-8370-ca6f83d93c35" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050716}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152552} {:db/id 17592186152553} {:db/id 17592186455458} {:db/id 17592186455469}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying a Percentage Increase"} :step/id #uuid "a946c7fa-5aee-54d2-b223-0a3b560b3401" :step/math-academy-id 615693 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153300}} {:db/id 17592186153300 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152296 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151900 :question/id #uuid "95c3dedd-accd-57dc-91ee-4ee8fdb2f3a4" :question/math-academy-id "e-21451"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f90ea994-79f2-5409-bf96-306803b4ef01" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049467}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152554} {:db/id 17592186152555} {:db/id 17592186455451} {:db/id 17592186455478} {:db/id 17592186455495} {:db/id 17592186455498} {:db/id 17592186486395} {:db/id 17592186486445} {:db/id 17592186534011} {:db/id 17592186542120}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying a Percentage Increase: Word Problems"} :step/id #uuid "fd57418f-a99a-5c17-9192-9191eca0084b" :step/math-academy-id 615696 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153301}} {:db/id 17592186153301 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153340 :tutorial/content "It's possible to increase a number by $100\%$ or more.

Increasing by $9.5%$ means that we must apply a new percentage of

$$
100%+9.5%=109.5%=1.095
$$

Now, we multiply the original price by $1.095:$

$$
12\times 1.095=13.14.
$$

Increasing by $45%$ means that we must apply a new percentage of

$$
100%+45%=145%.
$$

We begin by converting the percentage to a decimal:

$$
145%=\frac{145}{100}=1.45
$$

Finally, we compute the new value by multiplying the original amount by $1.45:$

$$
3,\,500,\,000\times 1.45=5,\,075,\,000
$$

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186055697 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055997 :tutorial/content "Polynomials with one, two, or three terms have special names.

- A polynomial with one term is called a **monomial**. For example:
 

$$
1, \qquad y,	\qquad	2x^3,	\qquad	5a^{4}
$$

However, the following expressions are not monomials because they can't be called polynomials:
 

$$
\dfrac{1}{y},	\qquad	5t^{-1},	\qquad \sqrt{x}, \qquad 	2z^{1/4}
$$

- A polynomial with two terms is called a **binomial**. For example:

$$
x+3,	\qquad	7n^2 +n,	\qquad	p^{32} -1
$$

- A polynomial with three terms is called a **trinomial**. For example:
 

$$
z^2 -z +1,	\qquad	x^3 -2x -1,	\qquad	2c^{4} - 3c^{3} +4c^2
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5e82b56d-3e2d-582a-b73f-3c5c98830a58" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6660 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d5ad5bf3-9168-540f-8492-ce7c9fc4b988" :step/math-academy-id 40308 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055698}} {:db/id 17592186055698 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054710 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054348 :question/id #uuid "b8742776-1dc7-5816-afb6-9a72142ecb5c" :question/math-academy-id "e-10650"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d3a71018-8f67-53cb-aa6c-7f17e0af9ef9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050306}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055300} {:db/id 17592186055301} {:db/id 17592186475965} {:db/id 17592186475967}] :knowledge-point/title "Categorizing a Polynomial by the Number of Terms It Has"} :step/id #uuid "38cccf7d-917a-5a79-aa78-f1a2b54e1a10" :step/math-academy-id 40309 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055699}} {:db/id 17592186055699 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055998 :tutorial/content "Each type of polynomial of degree between $0$ and $5$ has a specific name. These are shown in the table below.

| Degree | Name | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | Constant | $7$ |
| $1$ | Linear | $3x + 2$ |
| $2$ | Quadratic | $2x^2 - 6x + 1$ |
| $3$ | Cubic | $x^3 + 4x^2 + 9x$ |
| $4$ | Quartic | $3x^4 - 5x^2$ |
| $5$ | Quintic | $7x^5 + 3x^4 - x^4 + x - 6$ |

We can combine these with the names we learned earlier. 

For example:

- $2x+1$ is a *linear binomial* because its degree equals $1,$ and it has $2$ terms.

- $x^2$ is a *quadratic monomial* because its degree equals $2,$ and it has $1$ term.

- $2x^3+x+1$ is a *cubic trinomial* because its degree equals $3,$ and it has $3$ terms.

If a polynomial contains more than three terms, then we refer to it by its degree only.

For example:

- $x^3+2x^2+x-1$ is a *cubic polynomial.*

- $x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1$ is a *quartic polynomial.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "ed2578f7-b1e4-5f83-b963-d66d7b97fa9a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6661 :tutorial/title "Names of Polynomials Based on Their Degree"} :step/id #uuid "ac189d1f-bdee-52ff-86b2-d371b3d6e1c6" :step/math-academy-id 40312 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055700}} {:db/id 17592186055700 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054711 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054349 :question/id #uuid "6270e77f-6ccb-5304-90da-2419fa309007" :question/math-academy-id "e-10651"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3b8feb96-7432-5fe7-a6c7-b2d8ebe7e766" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048406}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055361} {:db/id 17592186055442} {:db/id 17592186234398} {:db/id 17592186475918} {:db/id 17592186475973} {:db/id 17592186493944} {:db/id 17592186493954} {:db/id 17592186533990}] :knowledge-point/title "Categorizing a Polynomial by Its Degree and Number of Terms"} :step/id #uuid "08e0cbe9-22f1-5b66-a44f-4af1547552f5" :step/math-academy-id 40313 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055701}} {:db/id 17592186055701 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054712 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054350 :question/id #uuid "3400928d-9463-56f2-af47-e193a1e18a47" :question/math-academy-id "e-10652"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0bd2d5a4-73de-51ad-9f9f-070d1d4f31a5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048524}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055015} {:db/id 17592186055016} {:db/id 17592186475925} {:db/id 17592186475927} {:db/id 17592186493921}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements"} :step/id #uuid "227abef4-c6c1-5c73-9556-5ca01a686b40" :step/math-academy-id 40316}] :activity/title "Monomials, Binomials and Trinomials" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186054924} {:db/id 17592186055697 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055997 :tutorial/content "Polynomials with one, two, or three terms have special names.

If a polynomial contains more than three terms, then we refer to it by its degree only.

We express the cube root using the **radical symbol** $\sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}.$

For example, the "cube root of $8$" equals $\color{blue}2$ since 

$$
{\color{blue}2}^3 = {\color{blue}2}\cdot {\color{blue}2}\cdot {\color{blue}2} = 8.
$$

So, we write $\sqrt[3]{8}={\color{blue}2}.$

Some basic cube roots are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{0} & = & \sqrt[3]{{0}^{3}} & = & 0 \\ \sqrt[3]{1} & = & \sqrt[3]{{1}^{3}} & = & 1 \\ \sqrt[3]{8} & = & \sqrt[3]{{2}^{3}} & = & 2 \\ \sqrt[3]{27} & = & \sqrt[3]{{3}^{3}} & = & 3 \\ \sqrt[3]{64} & = & \sqrt[3]{{4}^{3}} & = & 4 \\ \sqrt[3]{125} & = & \sqrt[3]{{5}^{3}} & = & 5 \\ \sqrt[3]{1\,000} & = & \sqrt[3]{{10}^{3}} & = & 10\end{aligned}
$$

A **perfect cube** is a number whose cube root is a whole number. So, the numbers 

$$
0,\qquad 1,\qquad  8,\qquad  27,\qquad  64,\qquad 125, \qquad 1\,000
$$

 are all perfect cubes. For example, $\sqrt[3]{-8}={\color{blue}{-2}}$ because

$$
-8 = ({\color{blue}{-2}})^3 = ({\color{blue}{-2}})\cdot ({\color{blue}{-2}})\cdot ({\color{blue}{-2}}).
$$

Some basic cube roots of negative numbers are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{-1} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-1)^{3}} & = & -1 \\ \sqrt[3]{-8} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-2)^{3}} & = & -2 \\ \sqrt[3]{-27} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-3)^{3}} & = & -3 \\ \sqrt[3]{-64} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-4)^{3}} & = & -4 \\ \sqrt[3]{-125} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-5)^{3}} & = & -5 \\ \sqrt[3]{-1\,000} & = & \sqrt[3]{(-10)^{3}} & = & -10\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the numbers 

$$
-1,\qquad  -8,\qquad  -27,\qquad  -64,\qquad -125, \qquad -1\,000
$$

are all perfect cubes." :tutorial/id #uuid "02c87b9c-9741-553f-a98b-da7832928f6a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8378 :tutorial/title "The Cube Root of a Negative Perfect Cube"} :step/id #uuid "8b332403-62f5-5fe0-ac76-52a66e2c10b5" :step/math-academy-id 554696 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120938}} {:db/id 17592186120938 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119960 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119526 :question/id #uuid "5c5c9efb-7bff-5177-a736-b21ce6410871" :question/math-academy-id "e-13376"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4b9e5026-ab54-5f35-a8da-b647c0f68c1e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120157} {:db/id 17592186120249} {:db/id 17592186120465} {:db/id 17592186475915} {:db/id 17592186475964} {:db/id 17592186533980}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Cube Root of a Negative Perfect Cube"} :step/id #uuid "b172821f-393c-54f4-bec3-98560d9d0245" :step/math-academy-id 554697 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120939}} {:db/id 17592186120939 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121144 :tutorial/content "Let's calculate $(\sqrt[3]{64})^3$ by performing each operation one step at a time:

$$
\left(\sqrt[3]{\color{blue}64}\right)^3 = \left(\sqrt[3]{{\color{red}4}^3}\right)^3 = {\color{red}4}^3 = {\color{blue}64}
$$

Notice that cubing the cube root gives the number under the cube root:

$$
\left( \sqrt[3]{64} \right)^3 = 64
$$

This result holds in general. If $\color{blue}\square$ is any number, then

$$
\left(\sqrt[3]{\color{blue}\square}\right)^3 = {\color{blue}\square}.
$$

The cube and the cube root cancel each other out, and we're left with the number that we started with.

into separate terms.

For example, 

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac {x + 2} {3} &= \
		\dfrac x 3 + \dfrac 2 3
	}
$$

and

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac {3a - 4b + 1} {5} &= \
		\dfrac {3a} 5 - \dfrac {4b} 5 + \dfrac 1 5.
	}
$$

Often, we're able to simplify the fractions in the individual terms, as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac {10x + 9} {2} &= \
		\dfrac {10x} {2} + \dfrac 9 2 &= \
		\dfrac {10} {2} \cdot x + \dfrac 9 2 &= \	
		5 \cdot x + \dfrac 9 2 &= \
		5x + \dfrac 9 2 
	}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0a37b6ec-6750-5aea-ae26-ad82d059a0ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3375 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "871a576b-9882-5cab-a267-5bfaae09bb5c" :step/math-academy-id inequality that consists of multiple different inequalities put together. For example, the compound inequality 

$$
x \leq 0 \hspace{.25cm} \text{ or } \hspace{.25cm} x \gt  3
$$

 states that $x$ is less than or equal to $0$, or greater than $3$.

For the compound "or" inequality to be satisfied, at least one of the separate inequalities must be satisfied. To illustrate:

- $x=-1$ satisfies the inequality because it satisfies $x \leq 0.$

- $x=5$ satisfies the inequality because it satisfies $x > 3.$

- $x=1$ does not satisfy the inequality because it does not satisfy $x \leq 0$ and it also does not satisfy $x > 3.$

To graph a compound inequality involving the word "or," we graph the two separate inequalities on the same number line. In this particular case,

- the inequality $x \leq 0$ consists of a closed circle at $0$ and an arrow to the left, while

- the inequality $x >3$ consists of an open circle at $3$ and an arrow to the right.

The resulting graph is as follows:

$$
-4 \leq x < -1
$$

 means that $-4 \leq x$ and $x < -1.$

For the compound "and" inequality to be satisfied, both of the separate inequalities must be satisfied. To illustrate:

- $x=-3$ satisfies the inequality because it satisfies both $-4 \leq x$ and $x < -1.$

- $x=-5$ does not satisfy the inequality because it does not satisfy $-4 \leq x.$

17592186111598 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111900 :tutorial/content "We can organize all mentioned types of quadrilaterals into the following hierarchy diagram:

![](images/1d/1dbe4c3e8ea97c0ac077c37143802366c5817d86965ab1dbc5abf54cd01d27c3.png)

Each shape below another is a specific type of the one above it. For example, every square is a rectangle, and every rectangle is a parallelogram. This means every square is also a parallelogram." :tutorial/id #uuid "d9d3be2f-753b-5a4b-9f26-20b34ab8f89a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5931 :tutorial/title "Classifying Quadrilaterals"} :step/id #uuid "eab37537-55a4-56e5-9fd6-7ee823f295bb" :step/math-academy-id 36207 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111765}} {:db/id 17592186111763 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111845 :tutorial/content "There are lots of different types of quadrilaterals. Let's look at some examples.

- A **trapezoid** is a quadrilateral with exactly ![](images/95/95836ae470c61ab15bfb67d6f0c92d2ad8d03d400b04473e81e58de3ee44bf32.svg) pair of opposite sides that are parallel to each other. 
The parallel sides are called the **bases**. The other two sides are called the **legs**.

![](images/9f/9fa09c46a2119d35c796065a696954931e20062fd5b3677a5484bef92bc2b0d8.png)

- An **isosceles trapezoid** is a  trapezoid with congruent legs.

![](images/b6/b6b2b2012c1d724f9da8b23551ec4f978f190d86875d7db7a3074635d7f40c02.png)

- A **parallelogram** is a quadrilateral with ![](images/f5/f5f3224583db57b9cfe323c8489ef5e5271000002b5ea253eb98fd067a858b2d.svg) pairs of parallel sides.

 

![](images/5d/5d0f383f3510f54b415a7ab99ef52fb30270924f97b8afec59534a96cd3edcef.png)

 Opposite sides and opposite angles of a parallelogram are always congruent. Moreover, if a quadrilateral has ![](images/f5/f5f3224583db57b9cfe323c8489ef5e5271000002b5ea253eb98fd067a858b2d.svg) pairs of opposite congruent sides or  ![](images/f5/f5f3224583db57b9cfe323c8489ef5e5271000002b5ea253eb98fd067a858b2d.svg) pairs of opposite congruent angles, it is always a parallelogram.

![](images/39/39ccf26333785f9ef47eed68a96bc40005a6ba025fdb6e250beefe14f10b043d.png)

- A **rectangle** is a parallelogram where all angles are right.

 

![](images/55/55a16e0ba93bf1f01d576cca558805aaea9631d1fa8e43b149509d4f8eb4c834.png)

$$
6x-(3+2x)
$$

In this example, we're subtracting the entire group of terms in parentheses from $6x.$ In such cases, we distribute the negative sign to each term in the parentheses *first* and then simplify by collecting like terms.

Removing the parentheses by distributing the negative sign, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-(3+2x) & = \\ 6x-3-2x & .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-3-2x & = \\ (6x-2x)-3 & = \\ 4x-3 & \end{aligned}
$$

For example, let's simplify the following expression:

$$
7-4(y+2)
$$

First, let's write some big brackets around the expression in parentheses, keeping the minus sign *outside*.

$$
7 - \Big[4(y+2)\Big]
$$

Next, we expand the expression inside the brackets using the distributive law. This gives

$$
7 - \Big[4y+8\Big].
$$

Now, we proceed as before. Removing the brackets by distributing the negative sign gives

$$
7 - 4y - 8.
$$

Finally, we collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}7-4y-8 & = \\ (7-8)-4y & = \\ -1-4y & \end{aligned}

:step/math-academy-id 8892} {:db/id 17592186074901 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074978 :tutorial/content "The distance between two points in the coordinate plane is the number of units between them. Let's explore two methods for calculating the horizontal distance between two points with the points $(1,1)$ and $(5,1).$

**Method 1** 

The distance between two points is the length of the line segment that connects them.

First, we plot the given points in the coordinate plane.

![](images/19/196c50295e8d8a95084c31226fb9319ede7b70603d894b6939e4615df583c29c.png)

From the diagram, we see that the length of the segment is $4$ units, so the distance equals $4.$

![](images/4b/4b531e29616f3e8d7ea0c65761e59cfea224b9c0e756c68b7647c7271dc09493.png)

**Method 2**

We can find the distance between the two points by finding the distance of each point from the $y$-axis and then subtracting.

![](images/6d/6d5c6760e15098dc381e639cd806b6410f2fa6d9049d11d5467427635c9872b6.png)

The point $({\color{blue}{1}},1)$ is at a distance of $\color{blue}{1}$ from the $y$-axis, and the point $({\color{red}{5}},1)$ is at a distance of $\color{red}{5}$ from the $y$-axis. Therefore, the distance between the two points is ${\color{red}{5}} - {\color{blue}{1}} = 4.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "aeee8d0d-20f6-5700-8c35-c66e0eef8daa" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2199 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1961bdcc-cea7-5d78-88c1-4f69e1dab833" :step/math-academy-id 8895 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074898}} {:db/id 17592186074902 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074979 :tutorial/content "When we want to find the distance between two points in different quadrants, method 1 works exactly the same, but method 2 is slightly different.

We can find the distance between the two points by finding the distance of each point from the $y$-axis for a horizontal distance, or $x$-axis for a vertical distance, and then *adding*. 

So, what's the distance between $(-3,2)$ and $(1,2)?$

**Method 1** 

We plot the given points in the coordinate plane.

![](images/e0/e0fec8fca43b421b62efc3d6d892563c80beaab3c2816be47aa7563868555268.png)

The distance between two points is the length of the line segment that connects them.

From the diagram, we see that the length of the segment is $4$ units, so the distance equals $4.$

![](images/dd/ddc1e6cec323fe245ff2a115a587e773d408dc0115ba5002c02ac1d238620c63.png)

**Method 2**

We can find the distance between the two points by finding the distance of each point from the $y$-axis and then adding.

![](images/0b/0bbb91fc8c0e7ad577261dcdbc8e7aaa16a44e8be2e937e2d6870aae58af4ccf.png)

The point $({\color{blue}{1}},2)$ is at a distance of $\color{blue}{1}$ from the $y$-axis, and the point $({\color{red}{-3}},2)$ is at a distance of $\color{red}{3}$ from the $y$-axis. Therefore, the distance between the two points is ${\color{red}{3}} + {\color{blue}{1}} = 4.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a1233efd-87e1-5707-9b70-24c24ed47418" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2204 :tutorial/title "The Distance Between Two Points in Different Quadrants"} :step/id #uuid "d97c5e30-e125-5cba-9973-1e1898eca20e" :step/math-academy-id 8947 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074900}}] :activity/title "Distances Between Points in the Coordinate Plane" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186073991} {:db/id 17592186074901 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074978 :tutorial/content "The distance between two points in the coordinate plane is the number of units between them. | --- | --- |
| ${\color{blue}10}$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}\textrm{?}}$ |

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}5}}{{\color{red}10}}.
$$

The numerator represents the left-hand entry (${\color{blue}5}$), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry (${\color{red}10}$).

To find the missing number, we need to make a numerator of ${\color{blue}10}.$ We can do this by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5\times 2}{10\times 2} & =\frac{10}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

We now add this to our ratio table:

| ${\color{blue}5}$ | ${\color{red}10}$ |
| --- | --- |
| ${\color{blue}10}$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}20}$ |
| ${\color{blue}20}$ | ${\color{red}40}$ |

17592186176625 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176970 :tutorial/content "Let's calculate $(\sqrt{100})^2$ by performing each operation one step at a time:

$$
(\sqrt{\color{blue}100})^2 = \left(\sqrt{{\color{red}10}^2}\right)^2 = ({\color{red}10})^2 = {\color{blue}100}
$$

Notice that the squaring the square root gives the number under the square root:

$$
\left( \sqrt{100} \right)^2 = 100
$$

This result holds in general for any non-negative number. If $\color{blue}\square$ is any positive number or zero, then

$$
(\sqrt{\color{blue}\square})^2 = {\color{blue}\square}\,.
$$

The square and the square root cancel each other out, and we're left with the number that we started with.

![](images/1f/1fa29ca192dc3fb99f4180c300aa3120064e3682361d175a698b1d457a569ba0.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "871b272d-6a05-5ad2-b443-785a6abbd186" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3093 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e1e25251-ada4-572c-af12-8dec4f2cc93b" :step/math-academy-id 16791 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176626}} {:db/id 17592186176626 :step/content {:db/id 17592186175916 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175774 :question/id #uuid "a4796dd0-e8ee-5ffe-b96c-6646c209d4be" :question/math-academy-id "e-4609"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5a937bb0-da50-5be0-a007-dce431a84282" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050358}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176484} {:db/id 17592186176489} {:db/id 17592186447326} {:db/id 17592186447328}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Square of a Square Root"} :step/id #uuid "8bcb8880-f2b7-5129-b867-7a66c1a6f8d9" :step/math-academy-id 16792 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176627}} {:db/id 17592186176627 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176971 :tutorial/content "We must be careful when taking the square root of a negative number that's been squared.

For example, $\sqrt{(-9)^2}$ is *not* equal to $-9!$ We can write this using a **not equal to** symbol $\neq$ as

$$
\sqrt{(-9)^2}  \neq -9.
$$

This is because the square root of a number can *only* be positive or zero, never negative.
Let's work it out the long way:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{(-9)^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{(-9)\cdot (-9)} & = \\ \sqrt{81} & = \\ \sqrt{{9}^{2}} & = \\ 9\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\sqrt{(-9)^2}=\sqrt{9^2} = 9.
$$

For any positive perfect square, we always have exactly two numbers whose squares equal that number. Here, we have

$$
9^2=81\quad \textrm{and} \quad (-9)^2=81.
$$

But *by definition* the square root is always *positive* (or zero) and *cannot* be negative. So here, $\sqrt{81}=+9,$ and for any non-negative $\color{blue}\square$ we get

$$
\sqrt{\color{blue}\square} \geq 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "27f63bb3-bf90-584e-b96c-d999c482f4e4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3094 :tutorial/title "The Square Root of a Negative Number Squared"} :step/id #uuid "b53578db-d74c-51c3-a032-b84c8468af3c" :step/math-academy-id 16793 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176628}} {:db/id 17592186176628 :step/content {:db/id 17592186175917 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175775 :question/id #uuid "0e96044b-b1f8-5d33-85ec-6a6a7f1fec6c" :question/math-academy-id "e-4610"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0f524f08-137f-56e6-8a6d-a45c3dae2635" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176482} {:db/id 17592186176483} {:db/id 17592186447327} {:db/id 17592186447329} {:db/id 17592186482577} {:db/id 17592186482600}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Square Root of a Negative Number Squared"} :step/id #uuid "b246c6a3-8aeb-5a46-904f-bf555b6a6441" :step/math-academy-id 16794}] :activity/title "Squaring a Square Root" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176103} {:db/id 17592186176625 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176970 :tutorial/content "Let's calculate $(\sqrt{100})^2$ by performing each operation one step at a time:

17592186168094 :tutorial/content "Recall the following derivatives of the inverse reciprocal hyperbolic functions:
$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x) & =-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,0)\cup (0,\infty ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡x) & =-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}, &  & \,x\in (0,1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x) & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )\end{aligned}
$$

Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we arrive at the following basic integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x+C, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,0)\cup (0,\infty ) \\ \int \frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡x+C, &  & \,x\in (0,1) \\ \int \frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x+C, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )\end{aligned}
$$

We can now use these formulas for finding integrals. For example, let's find the integral

$$
\int \left(\dfrac{2}{3x\sqrt{1-x^2}} + \cos x \right) \textrm d x.
$$

Using the properties of integration and the formulas above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{2}{3x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{3}\int \frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "77d4740c-3cac-5695-aa67-597e3c0ce164" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5213 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "36d709c0-168f-57e9-9ba0-9651411edeb8" :step/math-academy-id 32698 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167601}} {:db/id 17592186167712 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168102 :tutorial/content "Recall that 
$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{1-x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = {\color{blue}\artanh{x}} + C, \qquad {\color{blue}x\in(-1,1)}.
$$

But we have just seen that

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{1-x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = {\color{red}\arcoth{x}} + C, \qquad {\color{red}x\in(-\infty,-1) \cup (1,\infty)}.
$$

Notice that the integral on the left-hand side is the same but we used different functions on the right. What is the difference, and how do we know which hyperbolic function to use?

The difference is the domain of the variable $x.$ When the $|x| < 1,$ we use the antiderivative $\artanh{x},$ otherwise we use the antiderivative $\arcoth{x}.$

For instance, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡x\,{|}_{-1/2}^{1/2} \\  & =\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{artanh}⁡(-\frac{1}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Note that since the limits of integration lie in the interval $(-1,1),$ we used the antiderivative $\artanh{x}.$

While, on the other hand, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x\,{|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(3)-\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x+C, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,0)\cup (0,\infty ) \\ \int \frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡x+C, &  & \,x\in (0,1) \\ \int \frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x+C, &  & \,x\in (-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )\end{aligned}
$$

We can now use these formulas for finding integrals. For example, let's find the integral

$$
\int \left(\dfrac{2}{3x\sqrt{1-x^2}} + \cos x \right) \textrm d x.
$$

Using the properties of integration and the formulas above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{2}{3x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{3}\int \frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "77d4740c-3cac-5695-aa67-597e3c0ce164" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5213 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "36d709c0-168f-57e9-9ba0-9651411edeb8" :step/math-academy-id $$

But we have just seen that

Notice that the integral on the left-hand side is the same but we used different functions on the right. What is the difference, and how do we know which hyperbolic function to use?

Note that since the limits of integration lie in the interval $(-1,1),$ we used the antiderivative $\artanh{x}.$

While, on the other hand, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x\,{|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(3)-\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$

Instead, a function $f(x)$ might get bigger and bigger, increasing without bound, as shown in the graph below.

![](images/99/99d75e971e3ac33723bd6a012806af08ae69a5677a7a44553569bdf6706a81ac.png)

In this case, we say that the limit of the function is infinity:

$$
\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x) = \infty
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c3614f64-54f5-51dd-8908-af9d99f7da31" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2584 :tutorial/title "Infinite Limits"} :step/id #uuid "8f7c3cbf-6b88-5be0-b80b-aa8a91f57ff6" :step/math-academy-id 12028 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125505}} {:db/id 17592186125504 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125714 :tutorial/content "Until now, we have considered limits at individual points:

> $\lim\limits_{x \to a} f(x)$ is the value that $f(x)$ approaches as $x$ approaches the point $a$.

However, the idea of a limit extends beyond individual points. For instance, it might also be the case that $f(x)$ approaches some value as $x$ gets bigger and bigger, growing without bound.

To illustrate, consider the function

$$
f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x} + 1
$$

whose graph is shown below.

![](images/71/71fdfd68ce32097cac17da935f0422b471b28d804f4108c62783d0ffc1e96f24.png)

On the right side of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets bigger and bigger, $f(x)$ approaches the horizontal asymptote $y=1$. In other words, as $x$ increases to infinity ($\infty$), the value of $f(x)$ approaches a limit of $1$. We can write this symbolically as

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to \infty} f(x) = 1
$$

Likewise, on the left side of the graph, as $x$ decreases to negative infinity ($-\infty$), the value of $f(x)$ approaches the same horizontal asymptote $y=1$. Consequently, we also have that

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to -\infty} f(x) = 1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7f754170-0622-5c95-a522-eab185c0e2d0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 152 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3a7a7874-637c-5af9-9935-68417a30cf66" :step/math-academy-id 285 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125315}} {:db/id 17592186125505 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124579 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124193 :question/id #uuid "a5050a89-0b53-5499-8a78-9d5d7c5a78c2" :question/math-academy-id "e-11"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ea4038bf-34f0-58cc-a7b6-6a4c1890570f" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124917} {:db/id 17592186125166} {:db/id 17592186233389} {:db/id 17592186235377}] :knowledge-point/title "The Limit at Infinity for an Unbounded Function"} :step/id #uuid "f069f004-01b3-5bd3-845a-6e1c33680f54" :step/math-academy-id 286}] :activity/title "Limits at Infinity from Graphs" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124686} {:db/id 17592186125504 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125714 :tutorial/content "Until now, we have considered limits at individual points:

> $\lim\limits_{x \to a} f(x)$ is the value that $f(x)$ approaches as $x$ approaches the point $a$.

However, the idea of a limit extends beyond individual points. For instance, it might also be the case that $f(x)$ approaches some value as $x$ gets bigger and bigger, growing without bound.

To illustrate, consider the function

$$
f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x} + 1

whose graph is shown below.

![](images/71/71fdfd68ce32097cac17da935f0422b471b28d804f4108c62783d0ffc1e96f24.png)

On the right side of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets bigger and bigger, $f(x)$ approaches the horizontal asymptote $y=1$. In other words, as $x$ increases to infinity ($\infty$), the value of $f(x)$ approaches a limit of $1$. We can write this symbolically as

Likewise, on the left side of the graph, as $x$ decreases to negative infinity ($-\infty$), the value of $f(x)$ approaches the same horizontal asymptote $y=1$. Consequently, we also have that

> $\lim\limits_{x \to a} f(x)$ is the value that $f(x)$ approaches as $x$ approaches the point $a$.

However, the idea of a limit extends beyond individual points. For instance, it might also be the case that $f(x)$ approaches some value as $x$ gets bigger and bigger, growing without bound.

To illustrate, consider the function

$$
f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x} + 1
$$

whose graph is shown below.

![](images/71/71fdfd68ce32097cac17da935f0422b471b28d804f4108c62783d0ffc1e96f24.png)

On the right side of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets bigger and bigger, $f(x)$ approaches the horizontal asymptote $y=1$. In other words, as $x$ increases to infinity ($\infty$), the value of $f(x)$ approaches a limit of $1$. We can write this symbolically as

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to \infty} f(x) = 1
$$

Likewise, on the left side of the graph, as $x$ decreases to negative infinity ($-\infty$), the value of $f(x)$ approaches the same horizontal asymptote $y=1$. Consequently, we also have that

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to -\infty} f(x) = 1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7f754170-0622-5c95-a522-eab185c0e2d0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 152 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186050688 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186429350 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency.
