"2c32a996-4944-5e2d-afe2-519907ae493e" :question/math-academy-id "q-140962" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}2\sqrt{6} & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}2\sqrt{2} \\ 2\sqrt{2} \\ 2\sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \\ -\sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3} &=0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "07212635-5697-56eb-b073-186df2f19fe5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500455}} {:db/id 17592186500396 :step/content {:db/id 17592186381942 :question/answer-fields </table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{10}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "32c2748a-bc08-575b-86a6-b7980b2a85bb"} {:db/id 17592186500432 :step/content {:db/id 17592186399322 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c77702da-2dc8-56b5-9db1-be0b111ea63a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186399324} {:answer/id #uuid "cb23530e-d73c-5fed-bfb2-d794a091435b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186399325} {:answer/id #uuid "affdcd79-dc85-53c4-b26a-150695001bdb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186399326} {:answer/id #uuid "675e4916-c043-5a86-94e0-b5ce7ed867f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186399327} {:answer/id #uuid "66a239a8-93d6-518d-96e1-a3a28f06e1cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186399328}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186399326} :answer-field/id #uuid "5ca4d33a-4ff2-52b4-8aee-3fbddebc35d0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186399323}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ea8f7f21-702e-5433-ab10-60c9a800aee5" :question/math-academy-id "q-98765" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeros outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}-\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}+\frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3} &=0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a62f00a7-f0ed-5a86-8683-e47c15c066ab" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500386}} {:db/id 17592186500455 :step/content {:db/id 17592186408021 :question/answer-fields - $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}-\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}+\frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3} &=0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}

$$

$$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-\sqrt{5} \\ 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f9037d14-7ae0-5acc-b20c-d657e5c950ec" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500396}} {:db/id 17592186500396 :step/content {:db/id 17592186381942 :question/answer-fields </table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{10}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "32c2748a-bc08-575b-86a6-b7980b2a85bb"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3deee69f-3a09-5221-985a-bd0ac7deae81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$  select the correct options in the computations of the matrix $U$ below.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$

Now, we compute the $1$st column of $U.$ It is given by:

|  |  | {{field-1}} |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${u}_{1}=\,\,$ |  | $0$ |  |  |
|  |  | {{field-2}} |  |  |

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal.

Hence, we must find vectors $u=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}]^{T}$ such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to 

$$
{{field-3}}.
$$

Choosing ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ as free variables, the general solution is given by:

|  |  | $2{x}_{3}$ |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |
|  |  | {{field-5}} |  |  |

that we can rewrite as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the two linearly independent solutions are already mutually orthogonal, we only need to normalize them. Hence, we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$

</table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "16918a72-6401-5b9a-b63c-2cb335c81055" :step/next {:db/id 17592186505851}} {:db/id 17592186505851 :step/content {:db/id 17592186423858 :question/answer-fields - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{2}{3}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 5 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{3} & 0 & \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "178233a0-87c7-5ef5-b337-71bf319396d4"} {:db/id 17592186505859 :step/content {:db/id 17592186399329 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a220f89c-3d0a-5463-b736-64bfc352bad4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186399331} {:answer/id #uuid "293c8357-8265-5b01-b470-7d517f25aa72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186399332} {:answer/id #uuid "35a514cb-7982-5a31-a007-45f908842ccc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186399333} {:answer/id #uuid "e92e99cd-068f-5ddb-b8d3-1c72fa9118b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186399334} {:answer/id #uuid "63e3470d-66bf-5e47-8c08-2675fd0d4713" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186399335}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186399331} :answer-field/id #uuid "b3279ea5-57df-56e5-a59e-a9baf5354ec3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186399330}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4670b2c4-578c-543d-913f-4a2e02949175" :question/math-academy-id "q-98768" :question/problem "$$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -4 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{4}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}-\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\frac{4}{5} & 0 & -\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} & 0 & \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "35cd0852-1006-5820-b30d-c2a976014373" :step/next {:db/id 17592186505850}} {:db/id 17592186505877 :step/content {:db/id 17592186408020 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4a847e10-ad2a-5e19-bffe-4f473d1f4614" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407950} {:answer/id #uuid "53b3d1ac-5ba6-5b42-802f-34c001d2a3eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407952} {:answer/id #uuid "7ba9bbe0-a4bd-5d08-aca1-3c1661cf6c5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407966} {:answer/id #uuid "e36cd36f-f51a-505a-8f73-b691e55977cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407993} {:answer/id #uuid "e71af25d-d057-558a-8db8-29ad46847b17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407996}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407996} :answer-field/id #uuid "1e3568eb-62d3-583e-93bd-bbecf0a0149d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186408002}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "256724b0-7532-517f-89d9-acc3daa6cf56" :question/math-academy-id "q-98766" :question/problem "$$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}-\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}

A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}-\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7f3114bf-a6be-5b7f-9354-2b9bd578a3a3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186505859}} {:db/id 17592186505850 :step/content {:db/id 17592186430360 :question/answer-fields - $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "16918a72-6401-5b9a-b63c-2cb335c81055" :step/next {:db/id 17592186505851}} {:db/id 17592186505851 :step/content {:db/id 17592186423858 :question/answer-fields </table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{2}{3}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{1}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 5 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix},\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{3} & 0 & \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "178233a0-87c7-5ef5-b337-71bf319396d4"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1bb23bb5-3483-5614-b88a-de724eaace0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "q-98768" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -4 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{4}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{5}{x}_{2}-\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\frac{4}{5} & 0 & -\frac{3}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} & 0 & \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "35cd0852-1006-5820-b30d-c2a976014373" :step/next {:db/id 17592186505850}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a220f89c-3d0a-5463-b736-64bfc352bad4" :answer/type {:db/id - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{10} \\ 2\sqrt{10} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2ae9fbe8-190e-52f6-9c10-192410ac4065"} {:db/id 17592186511611 :step/content {:db/id 17592186511512 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a42c0f3-23fe-54b3-9812-4384378e4fdf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186510842} {:answer/id #uuid "2ea8b7cd-7674-5bdd-be23-c96008f18ef2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186510882} {:answer/id #uuid "a39bb8ab-4347-5457-ac3e-775c486b4c6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186511126} {:answer/id #uuid "c0ca0393-d174-5ef6-b704-b99b7d145991" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186511183} {:answer/id #uuid "f50be767-9717-528b-bc60-edef8d33bf76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186511289}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186511183} :answer-field/id #uuid "c4360e51-0f64-590c-bba8-917045fffada" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186511418}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "79df1f11-1c43-51b8-8e99-4f8efb003972" :question/math-academy-id "q-140961" :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-6I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-1I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $V:$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "392eb1aa-9b69-5309-8d5f-16ee0b5603a3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186511603}} {:db/id 17592186511613 :step/content {:db/id 17592186443406 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6d08e6f7-0c8c-5a19-bed7-db8dc41af65e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186443350} {:answer/id #uuid "7e31c437-06d1-5826-9cb1-4684802533dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186443354} {:answer/id #uuid "89017994-b329-5175-a753-3bf33a611163" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186443358} {:answer/id #uuid "c6c810b0-869e-5ce1-8f1a-3a1e0dbb11d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186443367} {:answer/id #uuid "dd9ebd11-88f5-552e-b5e4-2988eb8b37a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186443377}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186443377} :answer-field/id #uuid "5c8bfdef-6f81-5a7f-8190-7d981c16e459" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186443393}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "77278df4-e113-5900-8941-27a77a33d7c4" :question/math-academy-id "q-98696" :question/problem "$$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{10} \\ 2\sqrt{10} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$

A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-6I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-1I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $V:$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "392eb1aa-9b69-5309-8d5f-16ee0b5603a3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186511603}} {:db/id 17592186511652 :step/content {:db/id 17592186371436 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d3ca5a0b-c8af-5e70-962f-1f5f6f4b7f7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186371438} {:answer/id #uuid "1a8785d7-c5ad-518a-acd1-9f9ada9bd015" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186371439} {:answer/id #uuid "88254370-bfae-5dc3-81e7-adc53cf53476" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186371440} {:answer/id #uuid "7be15a9b-8f59-5064-9812-d260abe9e0d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186371441} {:answer/id #uuid "2cc59cf3-c247-5942-a9f5-c1997970aef5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186371442}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186371440} :answer-field/id #uuid "77e9283f-fec6-5979-96c1-f6617f8a4d62" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186371437}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1fbce2d1-be2d-5c6a-bfaf-0486d4c0daa8" :question/math-academy-id "q-98772" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=6$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{10}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{8}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{8}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}+\frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3} &=0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} & 0 & -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ada82642-7b26-53dc-9e04-7877d6ceb00a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186511611}} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046658} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186526150} :activity/id #uuid A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 4 & 4 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=6$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 4 & 4 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{8}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 4 & 4 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+{x}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{30}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}[\begin{aligned}-2\sqrt{5} \\ -\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{(-1)}{5}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\frac{2}{5}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 & \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c7d0e522-c0f3-5784-84ea-d620614fe1b5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186526147}} {:db/id 17592186526147 :step/content {:db/id 17592186443407 :question/answer-fields - $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e1f66dfa-3760-5612-bfad-a3090a4dcb42"} {:db/id 17592186526150 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162712 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "46ec70b2-790d-582b-8940-37eea292ae4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430279} {:answer/id #uuid "4d30fcb9-4e9c-5480-91f8-be9027ba4304" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430281} {:answer/id #uuid "5ea213a0-7cb0-59f5-98bd-30dcad60aa90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430287} {:answer/id #uuid "84575063-53ca-5b2a-94b3-9e965df7c601" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430299} {:answer/id #uuid "d346a1ab-d6ee-5497-ae67-93ca1862ead9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430325}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186430325} :answer-field/id #uuid "53075006-3bde-5335-a07e-7b2f11fef0a6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186161564}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0acab5c5-194e-580b-922b-276032b93c12" :question/math-academy-id "q-97365" :question/problem "$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 4 & 4 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{8}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 4 & 4 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{30}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}[\begin{aligned}-2\sqrt{5} \\ -\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,-2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. 

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are *not* mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let 

$$
{c}_{1}={b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={b}_{2}-\frac{{b}_{2}\cdot {c}_{1}}{{c}_{1}\cdot {c}_{1}}{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{(-1)}{5}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\frac{2}{5}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{30}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{30}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 & \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c7d0e522-c0f3-5784-84ea-d620614fe1b5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186526147}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "21cd4f8b-9498-5d21-baab-074e7d02e4bd" :answer/type {:db/id Hence, we must find vectors $u=[{x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}]^{T}$ such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to 

$$

|  |  | {{field-4}} |  |  |

</table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}={x}_{2}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\,{u}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e1f66dfa-3760-5612-bfad-a3090a4dcb42"} {:db/id 17592186048829 :topic/id #uuid "c4140dd8-d457-5cdb-8b51-1b7b952642cd" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186119950
