:knowledge-point/title "Constructing a Recursive Formula for a Geometric Sequence"}] :question/problem "What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence?
$1, \: 4, \: 16, \: \ldots$" :question/worked-solution "The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form

$$
a_{n+1} = r \cdot a_{n}
$$

In this case, the first term is

$$
a_1={\color{blue}1}
$$

and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac 4 1 = {\color{red}4}
$$

Therefore, the recursive formula is

$$
a_{n+1} = {\color{red}4} \cdot a_{n}, \qquad a_1 = {\color{blue}1}, \qquad n\geq 1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050380} {:db/id 17592186050977} {:db/id 17592186120169 :question/id #uuid "5fa37a9a-c70f-58d1-aee2-fc8ed450adfe" :question/math-academy-id "q-249792"} {:db/id 17592186120170 :question/id #uuid "e3c0fa68-397d-5b64-ab7c-38e981283bef" :question/math-academy-id "q-249795"} {:db/id 17592186120469 :question/id #uuid "be068788-b8e8-533c-8904-f3a99e38c619" :question/math-academy-id "q-44818"} {:db/id 17592186119951 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119537 :question/id #uuid "25a92b77-314f-5e6a-8a26-5e631d10e4d0" :question/math-academy-id "e-1507"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6aee1b1d-3cb6-5f52-8973-13b067b1c41a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120165 :question/id #uuid "bf38b717-cda3-5a9d-aaeb-00b9d1a95709" :question/math-academy-id "q-233046"} {:db/id 17592186120171 :question/id #uuid "385a6fb7-8690-582d-88d4-8765c8c27e63" :question/math-academy-id "q-249805"} {:db/id 17592186120470 :question/id #uuid "ca8e8dd5-30dc-5108-8bf2-005f91e7f3ba" :question/math-academy-id "q-44819"}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Term of a Geometric Sequence Given Its Recursive Formula"} {:db/id 17592186119537 :question/id #uuid "25a92b77-314f-5e6a-8a26-5e631d10e4d0" :question/math-academy-id "e-1507" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186119951 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6aee1b1d-3cb6-5f52-8973-13b067b1c41a" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Term of a Geometric Sequence Given Its Recursive Formula"}] :question/problem "What is the $4$th term of the geometric sequence given below?
$a_{n+1} = -3 a_n,\qquad a_1 = 2,\qquad n \geq 1$" :question/worked-solution "We use the recursive formula to compute the terms of the sequence up to the $4$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{1} &= 2 \\
a_{2} &= -3a_{1} =-3(2) =-6 \\
a_{3} &= -3a_{2} =-3(-6) = 18 \\
a_{4} &= -3a_{3} =-3(18) =-54
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a_4 = -54$."} {:db/id 17592186120165 :question/id #uuid "bf38b717-cda3-5a9d-aaeb-00b9d1a95709" :question/math-academy-id "q-233046"} {:db/id 17592186120171 :question/id #uuid "385a6fb7-8690-582d-88d4-8765c8c27e63" :question/math-academy-id "q-249805"} {:db/id 17592186120470 :question/id #uuid "ca8e8dd5-30dc-5108-8bf2-005f91e7f3ba" :question/math-academy-id "q-44819"} {:db/id 17592186119952 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119584 :question/id #uuid "ae9a3613-9e84-53bd-ad35-48394adfdc30" :question/math-academy-id "e-4232"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aae4cf92-f456-5b5f-bf92-1c4aed5ee4f6" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120166 :question/id #uuid "3723e0d8-6d2b-5a3d-a0ff-f03c2d8686df" :question/math-academy-id "q-233070"} {:db/id 17592186120472 :question/id #uuid "b6c8e1bb-8aeb-5633-b1bf-9ed2faf34afe" :question/math-academy-id "q-44957"} {:db/id 17592186120473 :question/id #uuid "bbe09394-9961-5a1b-bfe0-a116320c40d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-44958"}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Term of a Geometric Sequence Given a Recursive Formula in Function Notation"} {:db/id 17592186119584 :question/id #uuid "ae9a3613-9e84-53bd-ad35-48394adfdc30" :question/math-academy-id "e-4232" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186119952 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aae4cf92-f456-5b5f-bf92-1c4aed5ee4f6" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Term of a Geometric Sequence Given a Recursive Formula in Function Notation"}] :question/problem "What is the $5$th term of the geometric sequence given below?

$f(n+1) = -5f(n),\quad f(1) = -1,\quad n\geq 1$" :question/worked-solution "We use the recursive formula to compute the terms of the sequence up to the $4$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(1) &= -1 \\
f(2) &= -5f(1) =-5(-1) = 5 \\
f(3) &= -5f(2) =-5(5) =-25 \\
f(4) &= -5f(3) =-5(-25) = 125 \\
f(5) &= -5f(4) =-5(125) =-625
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
f(5)=-625
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120166 :question/id #uuid "3723e0d8-6d2b-5a3d-a0ff-f03c2d8686df" :question/math-academy-id "q-233070"} {:db/id 17592186120472 :question/id #uuid "b6c8e1bb-8aeb-5633-b1bf-9ed2faf34afe" :question/math-academy-id "q-44957"} {:db/id 17592186120473 :question/id #uuid "bbe09394-9961-5a1b-bfe0-a116320c40d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-44958"} {:db/id 17592186119953 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119538 :question/id #uuid "33621cf4-4508-51d5-958b-18a6ec1ebc73" :question/math-academy-id "e-1508"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "76437951-0d71-548b-b330-e494aa12c6a1" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120413 :question/id #uuid "73859e24-723f-5cfe-bfb6-acaba3c39e8f" :question/math-academy-id "q-39313"} {:db/id 17592186120471 :question/id #uuid "8e320c2f-640c-53dc-a6d6-b04a67d6047a" :question/math-academy-id "q-44824"}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Geometric Sequences"} {:db/id 17592186119538 :question/id #uuid "33621cf4-4508-51d5-958b-18a6ec1ebc73" :question/math-academy-id "e-1508" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186119953 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "76437951-0d71-548b-b330-e494aa12c6a1" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Geometric Sequences"}] :question/problem "Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

1. $10, \: 20, \: 30, \: 40, \: \dots$
2. $a_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{6}a_n,\quad a_1 = 36,\quad n\geq 1$
3. $f(n+1) = 2f(n)-1,\quad f(1) =2,\quad n\geq 1$" :question/worked-solution "A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:
$\frac{a_{2}}{a_{1}} = \frac{20}{10}|= 2; \frac{a_{3}}{a_{2}} = \frac{30}{20}|= \frac{3}{2}$
- Sequence II is a geometric sequence. The recursive rule $a_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{6}a_n$ tells us that each term is $\dfrac{1}{6}$ times the previous term, so the common ratio is $r=\dfrac{1}{6}$.
- Sequence III is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first $3$ terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms.
$f(1)|= 2; f(2)|= 2 \cdot f(1) - 1 = 2 \cdot 2 - 1 = 3; f(3)|= 2 \cdot f(2) - 1 = 2 \cdot 3 - 1 = 5$
The first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios:
$(f(2))/(f(1)) = \frac{3}{2}; (f(3))/(f(2)) = \frac{5}{3}$

 What is the value of $x?$

First, note that $\angle DIF$ and $\angle BJI$ are corresponding angles. Therefore, they are congruent and thus have the same measure. This means we can write down the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠DIF & =m∠BJI \\ 3x-{20}^{∘} & =x+{10}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this equation, we first subtract $x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-{20}^{∘} & =x+{10}^{∘} \\ 3x-{20}^{∘}-x & =x+{10}^{∘}-x \\ 2x-{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we add $20^\circ$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘} \\ 2x-{20}^{∘}+{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘}+{20}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={30}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides by $2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ={30}^{∘} \\ \frac{2x}{2} & =\frac{{30}^{∘}}{2} \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & ={15}^{∘} \\ x & ={15}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=15^\circ.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1983a72b-cd06-525b-8a7f-820171f631c1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7640 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "c53425c9-93f8-50f1-ba9b-c5137c0d9d3e" :step/math-academy-id 44334 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069790}}] :activity/title "Corresponding Angles" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068954} {:db/id 17592186069781 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070002 :tutorial/content "A line that crosses two parallel lines is called a **transversal**. $$

Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?" :question/worked-solution "Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} & 2t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-1}}.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$"} {:db/id 17592186311648 :question/id #uuid "3d9725c1-fcc5-57a9-8b5a-bd5efbda8207" :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A\,Φ(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $[a,\,b]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $a$ and $b.$*

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L4}$ and substitution from lines {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ and substitution from line {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\text{L3}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular, 

$$
{x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that ${x}_{2}\text{ is a solution of the system}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L5}.$ By definition, the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column,

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}^{′}(t) & {x}_{2}^{′}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$ from $\text{L3},$ we substitute each derivative into the matrix to get

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ A{x}_{1}(t) & A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substitution from $\text{L2}\text{ and }\text{L3}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ From $\text{L6}$ we have

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)].
$$

Using the definition $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$ from $\text{L1},$ we substitute to obtain

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t).
$$

"Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line {{field-4}} by the properties of determinants." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Recall that a matrix has linearly independent columns if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for any particular $t,$

$$
det(Φ(t))\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by the properties of determinants."} {:db/id 17592186221422 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221192 :question/id #uuid :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-5\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((5\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(5\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(5\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+5\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308611 :question/id #uuid "ff10c64d-19c8-5825-958b-92dcd06d6e53" :question/math-academy-id "q-334387" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186221422 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "66c99cda-25a5-50f2-903b-bfb1fdc5fa10" :knowledge-point/title "Computing Fundamental Matrices Using Matrix Exponentials"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b642857-d5c7-5354-9582-e84b796c8d0c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186305568}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "2b642857-d5c7-5354-9582-e84b796c8d0c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186305568} :answer-field/id #uuid "191d5551-a712-5140-91a3-ad273a6ad519" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186307600} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bfdf9ccd-6d68-52b8-90d2-de98adb98891" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186306941}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "bfdf9ccd-6d68-52b8-90d2-de98adb98891" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186306941} :answer-field/id #uuid "69784144-c83c-5567-a773-771397a8e2ee" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186307859}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-3t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-3t) &={e}^{-3t} \\ r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-3t} \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-6t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308634 :question/id #uuid "691520cf-4380-50be-8b5c-ac8a181c7472" :question/math-academy-id "q-334499"} {:db/id 17592186365659 :question/id #uuid </tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365668 :question/id #uuid "162963ac-9899-549d-9b3f-b09605170db6" :question/math-academy-id "q-334389"} {:db/id 17592186365673 :question/id #uuid "93c5b9c1-d3c4-52c5-af95-03ae43585aaf" :question/math-academy-id "q-334497" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5728e179-6831-5401-a928-e641db0a06b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-4t}" :db/id 17592186365675}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365675} :answer-field/id #uuid "afbc2e57-8b1b-5ce4-9b27-cb6cab8bfe1d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365674} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "979acb26-7ddd-5b55-9211-9925729aa071" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186365677}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365677} :answer-field/id #uuid "43739f8d-9cc2-5a3f-8f44-3fd681edf8db" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365676} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8029db2d-8bde-50dd-9836-f39ca854a3bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t{e}^{-4t}" :db/id 17592186365679}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365679} :answer-field/id #uuid "faaddf78-a1db-5496-a708-d82d0e79d47b" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365678} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6356927b-4df6-547a-97be-5637f834898e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-4t}" :db/id 17592186365681}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186365681} :answer-field/id #uuid "c911bdd1-5a68-53a2-90c8-77d2d0783bc8" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186365680}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-4t{e}^{-4t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}(1+4t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-4{e}^{-4t}t+{e}^{-4t}(1+4t) \\  & ={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{-4t}t \\  & =t{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} & t{e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186442558 :question/id #uuid "9ce1dad2-2fca-5e8c-94e6-f02fef65fbf6" :question/math-academy-id "q-334378"} {:db/id 17592186442559 :question/id #uuid $$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186534093 :question/id #uuid "f69ba2b0-76ef-5087-a5bf-906e0adf24a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-334388" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a54e01d-d3da-520d-a71e-fb2b3d3a8bd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{6t}+e^{-6t}" :db/id 17592186533275}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533275} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ec158fd-889b-5066-b795-fdf52e06926c" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186533801} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f40c120d-2ef8-574c-b604-70f11f9600d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{6t}+e^{-6t}" :db/id 17592186533740}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533740} :answer-field/id #uuid "5ac691a2-04d5-52ef-bc49-8d3327cd84e3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186533851}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "$$

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-6t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-6t)={e}^{-6t} \\ r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-12t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot (-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} \\ {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048231} {:answer-field/id #uuid "aa786690-2dc1-59f3-a44d-639db8237f3d" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} system

$$
\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix.

A **fundamental matrix** for this system is an $n\times n$ matrix $\Phi(t)$ whose columns are $n$ linearly independent solutions of the system.

If $\mathbf{x}_1(t),\dots,\mathbf{x}_n(t)$ are linearly independent solutions, then one fundamental matrix is

$$
\Phi(t)=\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\dots,\mathbf{x}_n(t)\big].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $\Phi(t)$ can be written in any order.

$$
\Phi_0(0)=I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

For constant matrices $A,$ the standard fundamental matrix is given by

$$
\Phi_0(t)=e^{At}.
$$

This matrix satisfies

$$
\Phi_0'(t)=A\,\Phi_0(t)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\Phi_0(0)=I_n.
$$

**Note:** Any other fundamental matrix $\Phi(t)$ for the same system can be written in the form

$$
\Phi(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,C,
$$

where $C$ is an invertible constant matrix.

:question/math-academy-id "q-336093" :question/problem "Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ states the independence of the columns of {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L3}$ by the {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L2}.$ Line $\text{L2}$ states that the two columns of $Φ(t)$ are linearly independent, which is required of a fundamental matrix. Thus, $\text{L2}$ states independence of the columns of $Φ(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Recall that a square matrix is invertible when its determinant is nonzero. Since in $\text{L3}$ we have that $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t,$ it follows that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$ Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by the $\text{properties of invertible matrices}.$"} :step/id #uuid "0d32e49b-f44f-5aaf-b893-9c5777c8ec8a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498653}} {:db/id 17592186498619 :step/content {:db/id 17592186498522 :question/answer-fields $$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<td align="center"></td>

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ad30acf-66b9-5977-ad36-2183bb8c58c8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498619}} {:db/id 17592186498623 :step/content {:db/id 17592186365659 :question/answer-fields </tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ea51f6a-6ea8-5162-ad6a-900689393007" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498620}} {:db/id 17592186498653 :step/content {:db/id 17592186498584 :question/answer-fields {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d656b9e3-27c9-51a6-a70f-c9d56643be83" :question/math-academy-id "q-336108" :question/problem "Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$"} :step/id #uuid "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$</td>

</tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ea51f6a-6ea8-5162-ad6a-900689393007" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498620}} {:db/id 17592186498607 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311648 :question/answer-fields $\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<table align="l" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center"></td>
<td align="center">{{field-3}}</td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-4}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ad30acf-66b9-5977-ad36-2183bb8c58c8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498619}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "dae93f70-eae4-559e-a461-fdfe0abd280a" :answer/type {:db/id system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line {{field-4}} by the properties of determinants." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Recall that a matrix has linearly independent columns if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for any particular $t,$

$$
det(Φ(t))\ne 0.
$$

$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?" :question/worked-solution "Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} & 2t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order."} :step/id #uuid "24523b4e-4e57-53cd-8b40-7f56c7c2589e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534142}} {:db/id 17592186534127 :step/content {:db/id A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$

$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

A=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |

The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-4t{e}^{-4t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}(1+4t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-4{e}^{-4t}t+{e}^{-4t}(1+4t) \\  & ={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{-4t}t \\  & =t{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} & t{e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6372c740-c40b-54b4-b2d8-d67db30bf1d4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534109}} {:db/id 17592186534142 :step/content {:db/id 17592186534093 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a54e01d-d3da-520d-a71e-fb2b3d3a8bd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{6t}+e^{-6t}" :db/id 17592186533275}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533275} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ec158fd-889b-5066-b795-fdf52e06926c" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186533801} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f40c120d-2ef8-574c-b604-70f11f9600d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{6t}+e^{-6t}" :db/id 17592186533740}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533740} :answer-field/id #uuid "5ac691a2-04d5-52ef-bc49-8d3327cd84e3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186533851}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f69ba2b0-76ef-5087-a5bf-906e0adf24a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-334388" :question/problem "$$

<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="80px">${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>

</tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-6t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-6t)={e}^{-6t} \\ r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-12t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot (-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} \\ {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a9bd7aaf-ed47-5adf-8e37-bc1f645e1959" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534128}}] :activity/title "Fundamental Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident $$

$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} & 2t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<table align="l" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="80px">${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-6t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-6t)={e}^{-6t} \\ r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-12t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot (-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} \\ {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a9bd7aaf-ed47-5adf-8e37-bc1f645e1959" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534128}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b918900-9d47-501a-8fe9-03921f6ed92d" :answer/type {:db/id "93c5b9c1-d3c4-52c5-af95-03ae43585aaf" :question/math-academy-id "q-334497" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-4t{e}^{-4t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}(1+4t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-4{e}^{-4t}t+{e}^{-4t}(1+4t) \\  & ={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{-4t}t \\  & =t{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} & t{e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6372c740-c40b-54b4-b2d8-d67db30bf1d4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534109}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5728e179-6831-5401-a928-e641db0a06b5" :answer/type {:db/id 3. $\rho = 0.9$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the linear correlation coefficient $\rho$ satisfies the inequality

$$
-1 \leq \rho \leq 1
$$

where $\rho = 1$ indicates a perfect positive correlation, and $\rho = -1$ indicates a perfect negative correlation.

With that in mind, let's examine our scatter plot.

![](images/06/06dcc617bbbc07fea756f35975146a238bd4cb9c4ce437f1b9300a7c05ded7b6.png)

We note the following:

- The points in the scatter plot seem to follow a straight line with a *positive* slope. So, the correlation coefficient must be *positive*. Thus, we disregard the following value:
$\rho = -0.8$
- The points lie pretty close to the corresponding trend line. So, the correlation coefficient must be closer to $1$. Thus, we disregard the following value:
$\rho = 0.3$

Therefore, the best approximation of the correlation coefficient from the given options is $\rho= 0.9$."} {:db/id 17592186083518 :question/id #uuid "f3e1cea1-0dea-5f3c-a617-a3cfcf6a3eac" :question/math-academy-id "q-133918" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186083338 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b973aca4-f9fc-5b5c-ab75-2329204993ce" :knowledge-point/title "Estimating the Correlation Coefficient"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b279d816-33ea-51a8-b628-a6a16c8981d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "ρ \approx 0.9" :db/id 17592186080004} {:answer/id #uuid "d4740f4f-6a5e-5ef0-8e17-22f8fc4f2207" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "ρ \approx 0.1" :db/id 17592186080005} {:answer/id #uuid "4e3a85f6-e92b-50f2-b089-fa17524a19f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "ρ \approx 0" :db/id 17592186080006} {:answer/id #uuid "53c15a0c-3339-593c-b0cc-5b781144b799" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "ρ \approx - 0.8" :db/id 17592186080007} {:answer/id #uuid "7d162b83-6f4d-5c4e-9e53-97590fd7b985" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "ρ \approx - 0.2" :db/id 17592186080008}] :answer-field/id #uuid "5d7eb7fd-32f7-5271-8c12-8630ddb9702e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186080003}] :question/problem "![](images/04/0432f45ba5b0652edc7f620233e9d2095c6e6836e98cecddf9ebc6f8c4cf99a5.png)

between two sets of paired observations if the data points on the corresponding scatter plot are located along a straight line.

We say that the correlation is **positive** if the corresponding trend line has a *positive slope*. Similarly, we say that the correlation is **negative** if the corresponding trend line has a *negative slope*.

We have a **strong** correlation if the data points lie *close* to the corresponding trend line. Similarly, we have a **weak** correlation if the data points are scattered *far* from the corresponding trend line.

17592186084293 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084490 :tutorial/content "The linear **correlation coefficient** $\rho$ (the Greek letter rho, pronounced "row") is a real number between $-1$ and $1$ that shows the strength of a linear correlation. It has the following properties:

- $\rho = 1$ indicates a perfect positive correlation
- $\rho = -1$ indicates a perfect negative correlation
- $\rho = 0$ indicates no (linear) correlation

The approximate value of $\rho$ can be determined from the scatter plot.

| ![](images/09/09d585da995df4e5a67b022816eec246113171d3aad15dcb57d82c766dcb7d18.png) | For a strong positive correlation, we have $0.7 \leq \rho \leq 1$. |
| --- | ---: |
| ![](images/9b/9b288c25fb0993a714768e3e2e9caf23a11f2629950eb03b138acfc0aa6c17cf.png) | For a weak positive correlation, we have $0.3 \leq \rho \lt 0.7$. |
| ![](images/36/3680700a5e4e4e196db6ffe106535ad784567b9fbed85e5005cbb6e49a476860.png) | For a strong negative correlation, we have $-1 \leq \rho \leq -0.7$. |
| ![](images/92/92b65a115fd1621303a248de8ae03d05392827914f5200f267d368867d511ae5.png) | For a weak negative correlation, we have $-0.7 \lt \rho \leq -0.3$. |

- $\rho = 1$ indicates a perfect positive correlation
- $\rho = -1$ indicates a perfect negative correlation
- $\rho = 0$ indicates no (linear) correlation

The approximate value of $\rho$ can be determined from the scatter plot.

"Find the volume of the solid $R$ given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,-2\le y\le 2,\,0\le z\le \operatorname{sin}⁡x\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we have a three-dimensional type I region.

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-2}^{2}[z]_{z=0}^{z=\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-0\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x[y]_{y=-2}^{y=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(2-(-2))\,dx \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =-4[\operatorname{cos}⁡x]_{x=0}^{x=\pi } \\  & =-4(-1-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129764 :question/id #uuid "cfdc548b-2292-576d-ab60-511ad802a9dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-40327"} {:db/id 17592186281285 :question/id #uuid "edd7e04c-fb5f-5755-adfd-ac7811c6b1ad" :question/math-academy-id "q-161653" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b3410aa-3741-574c-a561-ca42745d30c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "39" :db/id 17592186278698} {:answer/id #uuid "27773d7f-25a8-52fe-bf01-68d9f7772331" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{33}{2}" :db/id 17592186278943} {:answer/id #uuid "355cd015-3c29-5af2-b4f6-238cf9b24f2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "27" :db/id 17592186279057} {:answer/id #uuid "4bc0b319-2b34-5da0-9a70-f1965d979755" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{32}{3}" :db/id 17592186279268} {:answer/id #uuid "51b7c11f-8dbf-5b54-9513-c9741d294524" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186279336}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186278698} :answer-field/id #uuid "862cee1d-edf0-59fb-96ad-6bf304ab07ea" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281077}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find the volume of the solid $R$ given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le 4,\,2\le z\le 3y+x\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we have a three-dimensional type I region.

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{2}^{3y+x}\,dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}[z]_{z=2}^{z=3y+x}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}3y+x-2\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+xy-2y]}_{y=1}^{y=4}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\,[(24+4x-8)-(\frac{3}{2}+x-2)]\,dx \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2}3x+\frac{33}{2}\,dx \\  & ={[\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{33}{2}x]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{3(2)^{2}}{2}+\frac{33}{2}(2)-0 \\  & =39.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281286 :question/id #uuid "c5e848fc-72d6-53a2-850c-9178b4b8b816" :question/math-academy-id "q-161656"} {:db/id 17592186281287 :question/id #uuid "2cb18357-7f8d-5c17-b356-ff0cf34ef3fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-161657"} {:db/id 17592186281288 :question/id #uuid "92ae0dd1-b6f7-54c8-bc54-cc5a6fb1fbb3" :question/math-academy-id "q-161659"} {:db/id 17592186412195 :question/id #uuid "341b5b80-395a-52ac-87f9-9ef65cfdd0e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-161658"} {:db/id 17592186412201 :question/id #uuid "89162549-49ec-507f-b56c-dea9e66a6c30" :question/math-academy-id "q-161654" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6ec6ec01-733e-5f02-af23-9cc8caaac3a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186412118} {:answer/id #uuid "7908b9c9-85f1-5fb7-8993-c1b1c1be6014" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186412124} {:answer/id #uuid "b9a79b99-32b0-5d67-90f5-be49d7031cdb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{10}{3}" :db/id 17592186412146} {:answer/id #uuid "bc206240-eb24-501d-9e9e-fc7fd50a7902" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186412147} {:answer/id #uuid "d8ffd103-8f74-5398-842a-0cf2cb86197a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186412160}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186412147} :answer-field/id #uuid "3acdc6ec-2a12-547a-88f2-73cc8411f0a8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186412179}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find the volume of the solid $R$ given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,1-x\le y\le 1+x,\,0\le z\le xy\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we have a three-dimensional type I region.

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-x}^{1+x}{\int }_{0}^{xy}\,dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-x}^{1+x}[z]_{z=0}^{z=xy}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-x}^{1+x}xy\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=1-x}^{y=1+x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{x}{2}((1+x)^{2}-(1-x)^{2})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{x}{2}((1+2x+{x}^{2})-(1-2x+{x}^{2}))\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{x}{2}(4x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186412202 :question/id #uuid "9b5b7d1e-4726-5549-b494-2d265b26d8f0" :question/math-academy-id "q-161661"} {:db/id 17592186412205 :question/id #uuid "aad5f44f-02bf-597c-9fc6-961b47dea0e4" :question/math-academy-id "q-161655"} {:db/id 17592186412210 :question/id #uuid "e95b54dd-6268-5c5c-a490-a7470ea8eb6e" :question/math-academy-id "q-40305"} {:db/id 17592186521539 :question/id #uuid "b01530fa-080b-571d-ad1e-cd03aad8ce73" :question/math-academy-id "q-161660" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "343954e9-c53f-5136-9342-da031d631171" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{10}{3}" :db/id 17592186520872} {:answer/id #uuid "5f8618f2-a4c1-5463-ab9a-c3032c367b51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186520980} {:answer/id #uuid "9cfbf36d-43f4-55af-88f8-c9911c1d33e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186521120} {:answer/id #uuid "a0a41433-b3e1-5c92-a9c4-ccd8e0742151" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186521124} {:answer/id #uuid "ff83ce28-20eb-50da-bedd-918638dace6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{2}" :db/id 17592186521326}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520872} :answer-field/id #uuid "8a20ef1d-6ee3-5383-abac-10a8cde3ea7a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186521393}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the volume of the solid $R,$ given by
